News.title: Bikers fined nearly £1000 after stopping for ice cream at popular tourist lake
News.content:
Bikers fined nearly £1000 after stopping for ice cream at popular tourist lake

A group of eight motorcyclists from Devon say they had to pay a total fine of £960 after twice stopping for ice creams at Llyn Tegid, Bala, Snowdonia, where new parking charges are in place

View Image The fines were given at a car park by Llyn Tegid (Image: Ian Cooper/North Wales Live)

Eight bikers who stopped for ice creams at a North Wales beauty spot have been hit by fines totalling near £1,000.

‌



The group from Devon were caught out by new cameras at Llyn Tegid, Bala, in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia, which are designed to stop overnight camping.

‌



The eight motorcyclists are now each in the process of receiving two lots of £60 fines after twice stopping to buy ice creams before realising the new parking fees and so it reaches a total of £960 for the group.

‌



One of the bikers said on a local message board, he said: “I’ve been visiting Llyn Tegid for many years from my home in Devon. This year I brought seven friends with me on motorcycles to introduce them to this beautiful area.

"We stopped here twice to buy an ice-cream from the lovely lady in the ice cream van – this is something I’ve been doing for getting on for 10 years." He added: “In that time I have never been aware of a parking fee for motorcycles in the bay just as you enter. Now we have been home for a week we have started to receive the fines.

Suffolk wildfire: National Trust launches emergency appeal to restore Dunwich Heath READ MORE :

UK drought maps turn red but temperatures set to drop after record dry July READ MORE :

"As we visited twice, we are all expecting £120 each in fines...for apparently missing £2 in parking fees! None of us remembers seeing any new signage in that motorcycle area. We would of course have paid the measly £1 charge if we had been made aware of it. Sadly, it has put a bitter taste in our mouths after visiting your beautiful countryside.”

‌



A petition has been raised with Eryri National Park Authority (ENPA) demanding free access to the lake’s car parks, reports NorthWalesLive.

Other motorists have also claimed to have been hit with £60 fines after visiting on July 12, the day before ANPR cameras were activated. They are contesting the penalties but are pessimistic about their chances with a private operator now managing the car parks.

At the same time there have been chaotic scenes on local roads in recent summers as Bala grapples with over-tourism and in response, capacity was boosted at Llyn Tegid's two car parks. Fees were hiked and solar-powered ANPR (automatic number plate recognition) cameras were installed.

‌



Parking now costs £5 for up to four hours with a daily rate of £8. Separate tariffs apply for watersports users, while Blue Badge holders get double the standard time allowance. Meanwhile, motorcyclists are now charged £1 to park in a spot they say was previously free.

Overnight parking bans at nine other Eryri car parks were paused in June following a public backlash. But the bans were retained at the two Bala facilities which now form part of a “pilot scheme”.

In protest at the arrangements, Bala residents launched the petition and began a letter-writing campaign demanding greater access. Fed up of lakeside littering, noise and illicit camping, many had campaigned for tighter restrictions - but the subsequent changes have now come back to haunt them.

‌



They too must pay higher parking charges and, potentially, punitive fines. As a concession - billed a “local benefit” - they are permitted a free hour of off-peak parking.

But locals claim the times available to them are a slap in the face. In change.org petition, they noted the hour’s free parking is only between 2am and 8am, or 5.30pm and midnight. “Nobody’s socialising by the lake at 3am,” they fumed. “Calling that a benefit isn’t generous, it’s insulting.”

In a letter to ENPA, petitioner Elin Pritchard added: “That’s not a meaningful concession for anyone trying to visit after work, at the weekend, or with children, it’s a token window designed to let you say one exists.”

‌



The petition argues Llyn Tegid and its two car parks have “belonged to this community for generations”. Demanding free 24-hour access, it added: “This lake is where this community meets, not a place we should have to pay to stand in.”

Elin voiced further concerns. She said: “We are constantly told, by government, by health bodies, by the outdoor sector itself, that people, and especially children, need more time outdoors, not less. A charge like this does not encourage that. It quietly discourages it, and it does so most for the people who already have the least room in their budget to absorb it."

Also causing local alarm is the enforcement model. Elin said: "This scheme is being managed on the authority’s behalf by Initial Parking, a private company. Whatever the safeguards, the practical effect for residents is that access to a public lake is now gated by a private firm whose income depends on charges and penalty notices being issued.

‌



“That is a significant change to how this land is used, and it deserved real consultation with residents and community councils before it began, not after.”

Within six days the petition has raised 534 signatures, more than a quarter of the town’s population. One supporter said it was “awful that people are being pushed away from beautiful natural spaces”.

In response to Elin’s letter, Bethan Wyn Hughes, ENPA’s director of corporate services, said the pilot would run until the end of the October half-term. Thereafter, the ANPR system would remain operational - but changes could be introduced.

Article continues below

She added: “The purpose of the pilot is to gather evidence of the effectiveness of ANPR of dealing with both overnight camping and general non-payment of parking fees.

“The findings from the pilot, including operational ANPR data, resident feedback, community council views and other relevant information, will be evaluated as part of the overall review, and will help inform any future decisions. It would be premature at this stage to speculate on what conclusions may be reached or what changes, if any, may result from that process.”

ENPA said the pilot scheme was introduced to help it manage its car parks more effectively and to ensure the correct parking charges are paid. It’s hoped the new arrangements will also “improve the visitor experience” and contribute towards the sites’ ongoing maintenance. To clamp down on overnight parking, both car parks are now closed from 12am-2am each day.

News.title: Prince Edward melts hearts as rare public moment is caught on camera
News.content:
Prince Edward melts hearts as rare public moment is caught on camera

Prince Edward has shown his sweet side in an adorable moment caught on camera, and people picked up on the subtle things he did that make him deemed an "invaluable" member of the Royal Family

View 2 Images Prince Edward was hailed as a "gentleman" (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

Prince Edward has been caught on camera in an adorable moment while meeting a fan, and he handled it like a "true gentleman". Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh, is perhaps less in the public eye compared to King Charles III, Anne, Princess Royal and other royals. But, when he is seen, people are reminded why he's one of their favourite members of the Royal Family.

‌



Prince Edward is widely admired for his dedication to public service and drama-free lifestyle, and he has a very low-key approach to Royal life, very much keeping himself to himself. That's why the 62-year-old is adored by many, including one young boy who had the pleasure of meeting him.

‌



TikToker @lollystoun, who regularly shares videos of the Royals, shared a clip of a young, blind boy named Corey, meeting Prince Edward - and he came prepared with a gift to show how much he likes him.

‌



Prince Edward sweetly touched Corey to let him know that he was there, and then someone explained that Corey had made a card for Prince Edward, and he replied: "Oh, really?"

"That's all he wanted to do, is give you a card," they explained, and Prince Edward seemed touched by the kind gesture.

"That's very kind, thank you very much indeed," he gushed, as he opened the card Corey had made for him. He also acknowledged that they'd been "trying desperately to keep it out of the rain" so he wouldn't ruin it, as it was clear how much effort had gone into it.

‌



View 2 Images Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh and Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh have become Royal fan favourites (stock image) (Image: Pool, Getty Images)

"Very good, excellent, well, that's very, very kind," Prince Edward told Corey, admiring the card again before the heartwarming clip ends.

In the comments, people fawned over the interaction, with one praising him by writing: "Prince Edward is an amazing gentleman".

‌



Others were floored by the fact that once he knew the boy was blind, he "touched his hand," saying it was "lovely".

"I think Edward and Sophie [Prince Edward's wife] are the best royals. No drama, very down to earth," a third wrote.

A fourth said: "I'm not a royalist, but I think Edward and Sophie should be in charge".

‌



Back in June, Edward and Sophie went to Portugal with King Charles III on a landmark tour of Portugal to celebrate the UK's ties with the country.

The couple spent three days in Lisbon and Porto carrying out a string of engagements, with many reflecting causes close to their heart, such as the Duke of Edinburgh Award for Edward and women’s rights for Sophie.

In recent years, they've enjoyed a slightly bigger public profile, especially since the likes of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stepped down from royal duties, allowing the Edinburghs to take more of the spotlight.

Article continues below

Away from their royal roles, the pair appear to prefer life away from publicity, living under the radar, away from the cameras at their Bagshot Park estate in Surrey.

News.title: Sir John Curtice: The "Burnham bounce" is real but it's not massive
News.content:
But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons' authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

News.title: Labour's Bev Craig elected Greater Manchester mayor, succeeding Andy Burnham
News.content:
In the first round, Craig secured 47% of the vote, compared with Astley's 21%.

This meant the ballot papers from voters who did not select either of them as their first choice were brought back into play.

They were checked to see if the second-preference votes were for either the Labour or Reform candidate.

They were then added to the first-preference votes.

Craig expanded her already significant lead.

More than two million people across Greater Manchester's 10 boroughs were eligible to vote in the contest but turnout was just under 25%.

Analysis of the votes showed that Craig came top of the poll in the first round of voting in all the 10 local authority areas that make up Greater Manchester.

Astley came second in eight of the 10 areas, while the Green candidate Geraldine Coggins came second in Manchester and the Conservative candidate Phil Eckersley was second in Trafford.

In her speech, Craig said: "For too many people across our region, life is simply too hard. The generational belief that we had, that if you work hard and do the right thing, your life will be better and the life of the community will be better, is something that many people just don't feel at the minute."

She continued: "Everyone deserves a quality home in a good neighbourhood."

Craig added that people should be able to plan for their future and for that of their children.

She added: "We have to move away from divisive politics, and we'll do it together."

Congratulations came from Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell, the MP for Manchester Central, who posted on X, external: "Huge congratulations to @bevcraig our fantastic new Mayor of Greater Manchester.

"Thank you to our tireless activists who have worked so hard to help deliver this win."

News.title: Decades-long search ends with discovery of new marine species
News.content:
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.

Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.

And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.

The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.

News.title: He thought a fitness supplement was safe, but it sent him into psychosis
News.content:
Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.

But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.

Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.

The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.

The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country.

His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.

Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.

Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.

News.title: What is Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and why does Trump say he wants to bomb it?
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb a suspected underground nuclear site in Iran known as Pickaxe Mountain, where recent satellite images appear to show construction work taking place.

Pickaxe Mountain is one of the few Iranian sites linked to the country's nuclear programme that has not been the target of US and Israeli strikes. There have been unproven claims that some of Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium may be kept there, which could be further enriched for use in nuclear weapons.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Trump told reporters on 21 July. And on 28 July he said: "I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem - we took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take out Pickaxe if we don't make a deal."

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on 22 July that "no nuclear activity is taking place" at Pickaxe Mountain, and described US threats as "a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage".

BBC Verify and BBC Persian have spoken to experts and analysed satellite imagery to piece together what we know about the site, and the potential impact of any strike.

News.title: Former workers fight for wages they say they're owed: 'It makes me sick'
News.content:
What happens when your boss is also the HR department, the grievance handler and the person deciding whether you get paid?

"I just want my wages. It's my hard work. I just want what I'm owed."

Sonia Garcia Monuz is one of several workers trying to recover money she believes she is owed by a catering firm based in Berkshire.

Latest figures show early conciliation cases involving unpaid wages rose by about 17% between 2024 and 2025, according to Acas â the independent body that helps resolve workplace disputes.

Acas says nearly half of hospitality workers, 49%, experience problems at work.

News.title: Who is Greater Manchester's new Mayor Bev Craig?
News.content:
Having grown up on a council estate in Belfast, Craig moved to Manchester in 2003 at the age of 18 to study politics and modern history at the University of Manchester.

After graduating, she began her career in local government. She went on to work in higher education and then at a national trade union, leading on social care.

Craig was first elected as a councillor for the Burnage ward on Manchester City Council in 2011.

She was executive member for adult social care and health throughout the Covid-19 global pandemic, before becoming deputy council leader in 2021.

Craig soon took over as leader when Sir Richard Leese stood down after 25 years in the role.

Her promotion made her the local authority's first female boss and the council's first openly gay leader.

The 41-year-old has also held the role of deputy mayor for economy, business and inclusive growth on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

She was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the New Year Honours List in 2025 for services to local government.

News.title: Soap star Shane Richie facing drink-drive charge
News.content:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie is to appear in court charged with drink-driving, police have said.

Essex Police confirmed it was called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the Church Langley Way area of Harlow, shortly before 23:20 BST on Wednesday.

A force spokesman confirmed the 62-year-old, of Tadworth, Surrey, was arrested and a charge of drink-driving had been authorised against him.

It added Richie, real name Shane Roche, was due to appear at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 9 September.

Richie plays Alfie Moon in EastEnders, making his first appearance in the BBC soap in 2002.

The Sun reported he was arrested, external at a Tesco petrol station forecourt.

Essex Police said: "Officers were called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the area of Church Langley Way, Harlow, shortly before 23:20 on Wednesday, 29 July.

"On arrival, officers arrested a man.

"A charge of drink-driving has subsequently been authorised against Shane Roche, 62, of Tadworth, Surrey."

Richie's representative has been contacted for comment.

Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.

News.title: Stick to spending limits, PM and chancellor tell ministers in joint memo
News.content:
Healey said the budget would "meet our fiscal rules" and "give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future".

A report in the Times says the joint letter told ministers they must "within the budgets they have already got" even while "pay[ing] for new things they want to do this year and next".

While the ongoing war in Iran is pushing up inflation and borrowing costs, senior Treasury sources confirmed the government is determined to stay "well within the fiscal rules" inherited from Sir Keir Starmer and his chancellor Rachel Reeves.

But Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

He also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this, and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain should lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

Questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

Reeves left a Â£22bn buffer in her last budget, but persistent inflation due to the Iran war could have eroded it.

On Friday, the PM said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his efforts to move power out of London.

Reeves had previously said that regional mayors could be given control of some tax revenue to spend on their local priorities.

Labour pledged to devolve more powers to local councils and mayors as part of its 2024 election manifesto, in areas such as housing and transport.

More details of Burnham's plan are expected to be announced in the Budget, but the government said the rate of income tax will not change as a direct result of the reforms.

AJ Bell public policy director Tom Selby said Healey "doesn't have the luxury of pointing the finger of blame at the last administration".

"Healey will likely spend a chunk of his time leafing through the thesaurus looking for new ways to rephrase the 'tough choices' message of his predecessor," he said.

Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the announcement of the budget date meant "89 more days of unfunded spending commitments and damaging tax speculation until we get some details".

"89 more days for Brits to wait before they know how much their taxes are going to go up to fund Burnham's spending addiction", he said.

News.title: CPS to target assets of jailed funeral director
News.content:
A disgraced funeral director's bank accounts and assets have been frozen, as prosecutors seek to recover cash fleeced from his victims.

Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years at Hull Crown Court on Friday for 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial and giving families the ashes of strangers.

Bush, 48, who ran Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull, stole up to Â£12,000 from charities and sold fake funeral plans.

Laura Tams KC, deputy chief crown prosecutor at the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said: "We will be looking at him, at the financial aspects of this case, to see if we can confiscate any of the proceeds of his crimes and try to compensate the families."

Sentencing Bush following a five-day hearing, Mr Justice Hilliard said it was clear that he "benefited very substantially" and "obviously lived very well".

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Tams said it "was not a case of somebody that had recently fallen on hard times".

She added: "I think the scale of the offending, the length of time it had gone on for, showed that really this had become something of his business model."

News.title: Victims of disgraced funeral boss demand industry regulation
News.content:
Tristan Essex is standing on the steps of Hull Crown Court, shoulder to shoulder with several others whose lives have been devastated by disgraced funeral director Robert Bush.

The 27-year-old is fighting alongside his sister Claire for regulation of the funeral industry, a journey that has seen them take their campaign to Downing Street and resulted in a new pledge from the government "to take urgent action to crack down on rogue funeral operators".

Their grandmother Jessie Stockdale was one of Bush's victims â her body one of the 35 found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, five months after her funeral was held.

The news knocked the family off its feet, Tristan said. Even worse, they learned the ashes they had been given were not Jessie's remains.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

News.title: Commonwealth Games boxing official suspended over headbutt probe
News.content:
A boxing official has been banned from serving at the Commonwealth Games over allegations he headbutted a teenage fighter in the ring.

Jon-Paul Hynd also faces claims he struck another child with an unknown object during a training session at Beath Boxing Club in Cowdenbeath, Fife.

Hynd was appointed as a technical official for the games in Glasgow, but Boxing Scotland said he had been suspended pending an investigation.

Beath Boxing Club did not respond when asked for comment by BBC Scotland News.

Complaints lodged with the sport's governing body detail claims Hynd "physically assaulted" one boxer, aged 15, by "striking him with his head" after the fighter responded to "verbal belittlement" last year.

Police Scotland investigated the incident but found no evidence of criminality.

News.title: I was in a coma for 42 days after a tick bite on a holiday to Greece
News.content:
A woman has been left with memory loss and seizures and has to take 18 tablets a day after a tick bite on a Greek holiday left her in a coma for nearly six weeks.

Victoria Stellas, from Anglesey, had flu-like symptoms while on the island of Syros in 2019, then - once back home - started having night seizures.

She went to hospital but "no-one knew what was wrong" so had an MRI scan and was flown by helicopter to Liverpool's Walton Centre, external, where she was put in an induced coma for 42 days.

From there Victoria was diagnosed with tick-borne encephalitis, external (TBE), a potentially fatal brain inflammation.

"It's changed my life completely. Apart from the work I don't go out as much," the 51-year-old said.

Mum-of-one Victoria believes she was bitten when she was at her brother-in-law's home as he has goats that can attract ticks.

She said: "I just kept on having seizures and no-one knew what was wrong. It was an unusual infection, and they didn't have the experts I think to diagnose this.

"Altogether it was about six months from when I was in hospital, the treatment afterwards.

"Sometimes I just keep quiet. I was outgoing before."

Victoria said she lost her jobs in a pub and as a teaching assistant at a school for children with special educational needs and disabilities, due to her symptoms.

News.title: Tortoise that ended up at tip reunited with owner
News.content:
An adventurous tortoise is home safe and well after being rescued from a recycling and garden waste centre.

Arnold ventured into owner Jacqueline Sear's garden waste bag before she was unknowingly taken to St Erth Household Waste and Recycling Centre in Cornwall on Tuesday.

Suez, which runs the facility, sent out emails asking customers who had been at the centre on Tuesday if they had lost a tortoise.

Arnie's owner said she was relieved her "very curious" tortoise was found alive after initially fearing the worst.

News.title: Meet the people keeping endangered skills alive
News.content:
Some skills have survived for centuries, passed carefully from one pair of hands to the next using historic techniques that have changed little over time.

But many traditional crafts are now on the brink of extinction, as advances in technology render them obsolete and valuable knowledge fades into the past.

Heritage Crafts' red list reveals those with limited training opportunities and low financial viability are at "serious risk" of disappearing within a generation or two.

While artificial intelligence (AI) and mass production take over, artisans across the west of England are determined to prevent these skills from disappearing forever.

News.title: Two more small boat pilots jailed for Channel crossings
News.content:
Two men who piloted overcrowded small boats have been jailed for endangering others while crossing the Channel.

Omar Heidari, a 34-year-old Afghan national who steered a dinghy carrying 95 people to the UK in June, has been jailed for two years.

Manas Yuk, an 18-year-old Sudanese national, was sentenced to 18 months in youth detention after piloting a boat carrying 81 people - including a number of children - just days prior.

The men were sentenced at Canterbury Crown Court on Friday having earlier pleaded guilty to endangerment.

It means 10 people have now been sentenced under a law targeting those who risk the safety of others by piloting small boats since it came into force in January.

The Home Office said Heidari had endangered the largest number of lives of anyone so far sentenced for the offence.

The boat was overcrowded during the crossing on 23 June, with some passengers hanging their legs over the sides of the vessel, it said. A number of the passengers were not wearing life jackets.

He was jailed for endangering others as well as arriving in the UK without valid entry clearance.

The renowned Nepal-born British mountaineer Nirmal Purja is among those confirmed dead after his team were hit by an avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak, according to the climber’s expedition company.

Purja was leading a 10-person expedition to summit Broad Peak, the world’s 12th tallest mountain located on the border with China, when the avalanche struck at midday on Thursday.

Elite Exped said in a statement on social media that the company “also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive”.

“No words can ease the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects [their families’] privacy as they grieve,” it said.

open image in gallery File. Nirmal Purja ( Reuters )

Earlier, the regional government in Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan said three members of the team had been confirmed dead after their bodies or partial remains were recovered from the mountain.

They were identified as Sarah Mallory Geis from Texas, Nadhira Ahmed ​Abdullah ⁠Al Harthy from Oman and Nepalese citizen Pur Bahadur Gurung.

Drone footage on Friday showed signs of several more bodies in the search area, officials said, although attempts to reach them on the ground have been hampered by bad weather.

The remains of the three mountaineers recovered so far have been taken to hospital by helicopter for "legal formalities regarding identification", according to the Information Department of Gilgit-Baltistan, the local region.

open image in gallery In this photo released by the Alpine Club of Pakistan on Friday, members of a mountaineers rescue team prepare to depart from an airbase on a search operation for climbers missing after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak ( AP )

Regional police said the rescue operation ⁠was suspended on Friday night because of weather conditions.

"We hope to continue our operations, both aerial search and the ​ground rescue, ⁠till the time we find the survivors ‌or the dead bodies," said Irfan Arshad, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan.

The area ‌in which the search is taking place is "remote and difficult", said Sajid Hussain, deputy director of the tourism department in Gilgit-Baltistan.

The Alpine Club of Pakistan earlier reported that four bodies had been located on the mountain, but later clarified that two bodies had been recovered as well as a body part of a climber.

Geis, 39, a resident of San Antonio, was an avid traveller who loved being outdoors, according to her Instagram page.

She announced on social media earlier this year that she was closing her Pilates studio to take “a giant leap of faith into the unknown to see where life goes. I have a sneaking suspicion there will be lots of helmets, harnesses, and crampons involved.”

With an altitude of 8,051 metres (26,414 feet), Broad Peak is considered one of the most challenging mountains to climb in Pakistan. It saw its first successful ascent in 1957 when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

The team of 10 was last in contact with their tour operator at 9am local time on Thursday. An avalanche struck the team when they were ascending from Camp II to Camp III at an approximate altitude of 6,600 metres, the commissioner of Gilgit-Baltistan announced late that night.

open image in gallery Members of a mountaineers rescue team pose for photo with honorary general secretary of Alpine Club of Pakistan Ayaz Ahmed Shigri, center, before departing from an airbase on a search operation for climbers missing after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, in Skardu ( AP )

The rescue mission began at 8.30am on Friday after the tour agency made a formal request to the Pakistan army, which then deployed three helicopters to join the effort.

But later on Friday it was announced that rescue teams were stuck at base camp because of challenging weather conditions. “Due to inclement weather, the search and rescue operation for the day has been suspended and will resume the following day, with additional Sherpas from other expeditions joining the effort,” a statement said.

Alongside Purja, Geis, Al Harthy and Gurung, the other missing members of the expedition to Broad Peak are Wang Zhong, a Chinese climber, Gyalu Sherpa, Nima Sherpa, Kili Pemba, Pur Bahadur Gurung (also known as Yukta) and Suhail Shahzad.

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a news briefing on Friday that Chinese authorities were “urgently verifying the situation and gathering information” and that they were “willing to offer help based on the requirements of the Pakistan side”.

If you want to pack the most into a summer road trip, consider the national park which gives back an hour of your time without crossing its borders.

Tucked into the North Dakota Badlands, Theodore Roosevelt National Park offers roaming bison and canyons carved by water.

The North Unit of the park is on Central Time and the South Unit on Mountain Time. Separated by around an hour’s drive, if you take U.S. Highway 85 from the North Unit at 9 a.m. C.T., you could make it to the South Unit by 9 a.m. M.T.

There are campgrounds in both areas but if you only have a day to enjoy the park, there is still tons to do.

The North Unit has a 14-mile drive through the Little Missouri River Valley, rising out of the canyon to the River Bend Overlook, and then along the upper rim of the Badlands to Oxbow Overlook.

open image in gallery Theodore Roosevelt National Park offers roaming bison and canyons carved by water ( AFP via Getty Images )

Visitors often see bison on the drive, and mule deer usually appear around dawn and dusk. Bighorn sheep may also be spotted on the adventure. For those who wish to experience nature on foot, the North Unit also offers backcountry trails, including the Buckhorn, Caprock Coulee, and Achenbach Trails. There are also easier nature trails for more casual hikers.

The South Unit has a 36-mile drive where visitors can spot bison, mule deer, prairie dogs and horses. There are also two self-guided nature trails in the South Unit, the Ridgeline Nature Trail and Coal Vein Trail, as well as backcountry trails.

There are several tips to keep in mind when visiting Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

You must make a reservation if you’d like to stay at the campgrounds, and overnight backcountry hiking requires a permit. The park is completely cashless, so entrance fees and other in-person sales will require a mobile payment, credit card or debit card.

open image in gallery Theodore Roosevelt National Park’s North Unit and South Unit are in two different time zones, allowing you to arrive in one area before leaving the other ( Getty Images )

Theodore Roosevelt National Park has a rich history, dating back to the death of “the conservation president” in 1919. America wanted a way to honor Roosevelt, who doubled the number of sites within the National Park system during his tenure.

In 1947, President Harry Truman signed a bill creating the Theodore Roosevelt National Memorial Park, which included the land that roughly makes up the South Unit and Elkhorn Ranch. The North Unit was added in 1948. The land was given national park status in 1978 with the signing of a law by President Jimmy Carter, slightly changing its name to Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

If you aren’t planning on visiting North Dakota anytime soon, there are dozens of other national parks across the U.S. to choose from.

Yellowstone National Park stands at No. 1 on U.S. News & World Report’s ranking of the best national parks for 2026. The ranking was based on scenery, activities and the opinions of travel experts and park visitors.

open image in gallery If you aren’t planning on visiting North Dakota anytime soon, there are dozens of other national parks to choose from, including the famed Yellowstone National Park ( Getty Images )

Holding the title of America’s first national park, Yellowstone offers hiking, fishing, backcountry camping and horseback riding. The park, which stretches across Wyoming, Montana and Idaho, is also home to more than half of the world’s active geysers.

Montana’s Glacier National Park and California’s Yosemite National Park follow Yellowstone, respectively, on U.S. News’ ranking.

Visitors at Glacier National Park can drive down its “Going-to-the-Sun Road,” a 50-mile stretch with views of glacier-carved mountains, alpine lakes and dense forests. Yosemite National Park is best known for its waterfalls and granite rock formations.

Manchester United continue their pre-season tour of Scandinavia as they take on fellow European heavyweights Atletico Madrid in Stockholm.

United bounced back from their surprise opening defeat to Wrexham with a rampant 5-0 win over Norwegian outfit Rosenborg.

They now face their biggest test of pre-season so far, with Atletico coming into the clash off their 4-1 triumph of their LaLiga rivals Getafe, which saw Ademola Lookman bag a brace.

It kicks off a run of exciting friendlies for Michael Carrick’s side, who will also face Paris Saint-Germain, fierce rivals Leeds and AC Milan before their Premier League curtain-raiser at Hull City.

Here’s everything you need to know.

When is Man United vs Atletico Madrid?

Manchester United’s pre-season friendly against Atletico Madrid kicks off at 2pm BST on Saturday 1 August at the Strawberry Arena in Stockholm, Sweden.

How can I watch it?

Fans can watch the match on MUTV, with an annual subscription costing £29.99.

Team news

Man United look set to be without Benjamin Sesko along with Manuel Ugarte and Matthijs de Ligt due to injury, but there is a boost in the form of Amad Diallo’s return. New boy Andrey Santos is likely to start again while there is a slim chance of a debut for Youri Tielemans, who has finally arrived at Carrington off the back of the World Cup.

Atletico are without their Argentine and Spanish stars that featured in the World Cup final - all those other than Marcos Llorente, who is already back for the squad despite his involvement for La Roja.

Predicted line-ups

Man United XI: Heaton; Yoro, Maguire, Heaven, Shaw; Mount, Santos; Mbeumo, Lacey, Dorgu; Zirkzee.

Atletico Madrid XI: Oblak; Llorente, Le Normand, Hancko, Ruggeri; Koke, Hjulmand, Martin; Mendoza; Lookman, Cubo.

Arsenal take their pre-season campaign in front of fans for the first time with a trip to Catalonia as they take on LaLiga outfit Girona.

The Gunners eased past MK Dons in a 3-0 behind-closed-doors win a few days ago, with Mikel Arteta hoping to go two for two as preparations continue for their Premier League title defence.

Fans have been whipped up into a frenzy by the Vinicius Jr transfer saga but all eyes will be on Christos Tzolis, the new arrival from Club Brugge who is set to get his first official run-out.

A number of World Cup stars have also rejoined the squad so could be in line to feature for the first time since the end of last term, with the last sight of Arsenal being their Champions League final shootout defeat to Paris Saint-Germain.

When is Girona vs Arsenal?

Arsenal’s pre-season friendly with Girona kicks off at 7pm BST on Saturday 1 August at Estadi Montilivi.

How can I watch it?

Fans can watch the clash on Arsenal.com by purchasing the pre-season pass, which costs £14.99 - or £9.99 if purchased before 9am on the day of the match. This will also allow you to stream the club’s remaining pre-season fixtures against Real Betis, Borussia Dortmund and Como.

Team news

Arsenal are already lumbered with defensive injury problems after Ben White and Jurrien Timber left the camp nursing fresh woes, joining William Saliba who is out for a number of months with a back issue picked up at the World Cup. Piero Hincapie, Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres have all joined up with the squad after the World Cup so could be in contention.

Girona, meanwhile, welcomed back Morocco midfielder Azzedine Ounahi from World Cup duty who could feature in a midfield against one-time Manchester United flop Donny van de Beek.

You’ve likely been warned at least once, with little explanation, not to drink water from a disposable plastic bottle left in a hot car. But what is the science behind these concerns?

Single-use plastic water bottles are typically made from PET, a durable synthetic polymer that is generally considered safe. However, research suggests there are several reasons to avoid drinking water that has been left in a heated PET-containing water bottle.

Chemical exposure

When plastic containers are left in the heat or direct sunlight, certain chemicals used in plastics can more easily migrate into food or drinks.

Phthalates, which are synthetic chemicals that are used to make plastics soft and flexible, can quickly leach from some plastic packaging when exposed to heat, Emily Barrett, an associate professor of biostatistics and epidemiology at Rutgers School of Public Health, told HuffPost in 2022.

open image in gallery Single-use plastic water bottles can leach chemicals and microplastics if exposed to heat or direct sunlight for too long ( Getty Images )

Phthalates — along with other chemicals used to make hard plastics — are endocrine disruptors. This means “they interfere with the natural hormones in our body,” Jaime Ross, a neuroscientist at the University of Rhode Island, said in 2025 to The New York Times.

Exposure to these types of chemicals, such as BPAs (a chemical used to make polycarbonate plastics), has been linked to many health concerns, “including infertility, thyroid dysfunction, various types of cancer, metabolic issues, as well as behavioral problems in children,” Dani Lebovitz, M.S., RDN, a food and nutrition education expert based in Tennessee, said in 2023 to EatingWell.

The Food and Drug Administration’s position is that the current levels of BPA and certain phthalates used in food packaging are safe. Yet, multiple experts explained to HuffPost that, given the traces found in everyday objects, it’s best to limit additional exposure where possible.

A popular claim that has circulated on social media is that heated plastic water bottles release toxic, cancer-causing chemicals called dioxins. This urban myth, however, has been debunked by Dr. Nicole Deziel, an environmental epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health. They do not, she insisted to The Times.

Risk of microplastics

open image in gallery Experts say it’s best to dump out bottled water left inside hot cars ( Getty )

There is, however, also the potential for tiny pieces of plastic, known as microplastics, to migrate into the water. While bottled water often already contains microplastics, heat can accelerate the process by which bottles shed billions of microscopic fragments into their contents, Food & Wine reported in 2025.

The current literature about the effect microplastics can have on our bodies is still quite limited. “There are so many unknowns,” said Bernardo Lemos, an adjunct professor of environmental epigenetics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, in the University’s medical magazine, Harvard Medicine, “but we are seeing more data that suggest microplastics affect human biology.”

According to Harvard Medicine, studies done on cell cultures, marine wildlife and animal models indicate that “microplastics can cause oxidative damage, DNA damage, and changes in gene activity, known risks for cancer development.”

The magazine cited a few studies conducted in mice that found that microplastics harmed reproductive organs, causing ovarian scarring, reduced sperm count and quality, and metabolic disorders in offspring.

Bacterial growth

Another concern is that hot environments create a breeding ground for bacteria.

“Bacteria grow in bottles due to moisture, warmth and nutrients, from saliva or drink residue,” Dr. Bruno Silvester Lopes, a lecturer in microbiology and epidemiology at England’s Teesside University, shared with The Independent last year.

They can “start multiplying in as little as 20 minutes,” he shared, “and in 24 hours can reach a staggering billion or even trillions of cells.”

Consuming that water can lead to an upset stomach or, worse, make you sick, according to Jackson Health System, an online nonprofit academic medical system.

Safer alternatives

open image in gallery Health professionals and scientists recommend keeping water in stainless steel or glass bottles when you’re on the go ( Siobhan Grogan/The Independent )

In recent years, there has been a shift toward reusable water bottles over disposable plastic ones. Not only is this better for the environment, as it reduces the amount of single-use plastic that will end up in landfills, but it can also be beneficial to your health.

The safest option is an insulated water bottle, such as the trendy Stanley or Hydro Flask. They are generally made from food-grade stainless steel, an alloy primarily composed of iron, chromium and nickel, and avoid many of the concerns associated with plastic bottles, including BPA exposure and microplastic release from the container itself. Glass water bottles are another similar option.

However, if you prefer a lighter-weight water bottle — like the popular Nalgene, made of harder plastics — these are still safer than single-use plastic bottles, since they are less likely to break down and leach plastic and chemicals when exposed to heat or direct sunlight, Dr. Deziel shared with The Times.

But the expert reminded readers that any type of plastic can be degraded by time, heat or general wear.

One catch for both stainless-steel and reusable plastic bottles is that you must regularly give them a good wash. Otherwise, bacteria and mold can grow inside.

Stainless-steel bottles remain a better choice, Dr. Suzanne Wylie, a GP and medical adviser for IQdoctor, noted in 2025 to The Independent because they “are generally more hygienic than plastic ones, as they are less likely to develop microabrasions that can harbor bacteria.”

It was 1989, George H.W. Bush was in the White House, Madonna was on the radio and the country was in the grips of its last major measles outbreak - until today.

“People were scared to death to come to the city. I mean, schools canceled trips to the city. We were pulling one dead child out of the house after another,” pediatrician Dr. Paul Offit, an infectious disease expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia who was working in the city as cases exploded, told The Independent.

By the time the outbreak ended nearly three years later, there had been 55,467 cases and 166 deaths across the country, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention records show.

It was the worst outbreak the country had seen since the measles vaccine, which also targeted preventable illnesses mumps and rubella, was introduced in 1963. Public health officials blamed the crisis on low vaccine coverage.

Now - with more than 2,300 cases of the potentially-deadly disease in the U.S. and numbers rising weekly - there are no such vaccine barriers. But different obstacles exist: beginning with the White House.

open image in gallery College students stand in line for measles vaccinations at Georgia’s Auburn University in April 1989 - the year of the last major measles outbreak in the US - until today ( AP )

A skeptical White House

President Donald Trump’s public health agenda, spearheaded by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has seen vaccine skeptics added to advisory panels and conspiracy theories about vaccines spoken about inside the federal government.

Trump himself has repeatedly claimed that young children are given 80 different vaccines.

"They give — I mean, for a little baby to be injected with that much fluid?" Trump told reporters in September. "Even beyond the actual ingredients, they have sometimes 80 different vaccines … It’s like you’re shooting up a horse."

The number of vaccinations before the age of 18 is typically between 30 to 50, doctors say.

The president has also recently pushed Kennedy - long known as a vaccine skeptic - to be more aggressive on cutting federal recommendations for annual child vaccines over the debunked ties to autism, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month.

open image in gallery Measles is a nasty virus that can lead to life-threatening brain swelling in children who are unvaccinated. Distrust in vaccines has been at the heart of America’s measles resurgence, with vaccine skepticism rising 15 percent since 2019 ( CDC )

open image in gallery President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. have both made misleading comments that are skeptical of vaccines for children, including related to debunked ties between vaccines and autism ( Getty )

Last year, Kennedy said he directed the CDC to abandon its longstanding position that vaccines do not cause autism.

“The whole thing about ‘vaccines have been tested and there’s been this determination made,’ is just a lie,” he told The New York Times in November.

White House spokesperson Kush Desai also previously told the The Independent that people worried about “skyrocketing autism rates have long been ignored if not mocked.”

He added that the administration is “committed to leaving no stone unturned to finally address these concerns with Gold Standard Science.”

In vaccines we distrust

Distrust in vaccines in the U.S. came long before Trump but has grown in recent years because of misinformation that circulated online during the Covid-19 pandemic and in podcasts and social media since then.

That distrust has been at the heart of America’s measles resurgence, with vaccine skepticism rising 15 percent since 2019, according to a study from the University of Arkansas.

About one in five parents are not confident childhood vaccines have been tested enough or that the annual vaccine schedule for kids is safe, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey.

“Here we have a skeptical, mistrustful, conspiratorial population goaded on by people like Bobby Kennedy Jr. And now we have a very different kind of problem – and a dangerous one,” Dr. Irwin Redlener, co-founder of non-profit healthcare organization Children's Health Fund with the musician Paul Simon, told The Independent.

open image in gallery This map from the CDC shows measles cases across the U.S. so far this year. The states with the highest case levels are shown in darker blues and those with the lowest levels are shown in lighter blues ( CDC )

Since last year, there have been several large measles outbreaks affected by vaccine skepticism, including in a Mennonite community in West Texas and an evangelical Christian community in South Carolina. There were two child deaths reported in Texas.

Measles appears as an angry red rash dotting all areas of the skin, with cases causing a high fever, pink eye and runny nose. Normal cases typically last for a week or two but some who are infected develop a progressive brain disorder that is often fatal.

The virus spreads quickly through the air after an infected person coughs or sneezes - even if they are no longer in the room a couple of hours later.

Fortunately, the answer to stopping the spread is the same as it was 35 years ago: vaccines.

open image in gallery Ethan Turner holds his 14-month-old son, Niko, while he gets the measles vaccine at a clinic in Lubbock, Texas, in March 2025. Increased vaccination helped to end the measles outbreak in Texas last August ( Getty )

open image in gallery Medical workers assess a patient with symptoms of the measles in a parking lot in Spartanburg, South Carolina, in January. Spartanburg was the site of one of the nation’s biggest outbreaks since last year ( The Washington Post/Getty )

A deadly cost

During the last major outbreak, Philadelphia saw 1,400 cases, with about a third in middle-class Christians, accounting for six deaths in under a year, according to Offit.

Religious exemptions to vaccines were legal in Pennsylvania, as remains the case across more than 40 states, and these communities “just didn’t believe in modern medicine,” he recalled.

“And you know, they believed in prayer. And if you prayed and your child died, then you hadn’t gotten close enough to God,” Offit said.

Several months into the 1991 outbreak, Philadelphia doctors were issued an order from a judge to vaccinate children, regardless of the parents’ wishes - something that hasn’t been done since. The decision stopped cases in their tracks.

In states with other outbreaks, free vaccine clinics at universities played a role in slowing the spread of measles at a time when the jab wasn’t always without a cost. Georgia’s Auburn University, Illinois’s University of Chicago and Ohio’s Kent State University offered the shots free of charge.

Cost was the primary hurdle for children in the U.S. not getting vaccinated during the 1989 outbreak, according to the CDC. At the time shots cost over $30, a 1989 New York Times article reported.

Many low-income families also did not have access to primary care physicians who could give children vaccines, Redlener explained.

“[Back then it] was problems of access along with, ‘Oh, is it really serious, anyway?’” he said. More than half of children infected in that outbreak had not been vaccinated.

It took a national effort to pull America out of the crisis. New guidelines for a second dose of the vaccine were released in 1989, giving Americans an added layer of protection from the virus. Two doses of the vaccine are 97 percent effective against infection, whereas one dose is 93 percent effective.

In 1993, President Bill Clinton’s administration launched the federal Vaccines for Children initiative, providing vaccines for kids whose parents who may have not been able to afford them.

By 2000, 76 percent of children in the U.S. had the measles vaccine - which helped stop the continuous spread of the disease for more than a year and brought cases to a record low.

'I think people don't remember measles'

Now, more than 90 percent of children have had their measles shots. But coverage needed to limit spread among kindergarteners is lower than it should be and has been declining since before the pandemic.

So an illness that many doctors thought they had resigned to history has come roaring back and as a far murkier and complex problem to solve.

“Now we have a challenge that none of us have formally been trained for. What do we do with recalcitrant, anti-science ideologues who have bought into the conspiracies being sold by the likes of Bobby Kennedy Jr.?” Redlener asked.

open image in gallery Incoming kindergartener Jeremy Conner, 5, reacts to a measles shot in Santa Ana, California, in August 2002. Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 ( Getty )

While Kennedy denied being anti-vaccine during his confirmation hearings to become health secretary, he’s also touted unconventional treatments for measles and previously falsely claimed that outbreaks were tied to the fact the vaccine didn’t offer lifelong protection. The measles vaccines offers lifelong protection, per the CDC.

“As long as we have a federal government that’s committed to promoting misinformation and conspiracy theories, it’s going to be very difficult to fix anything,” Redlener added.

In response to today's rising cases, HHS says Kennedy has been clear that vaccination is the most effective way to prevent infection and that the department has focused its response on supporting affected communities and strengthening local and state response.

"Under Secretary Kennedy's leadership, HHS has mounted an aggressive outbreak response, providing more than $8.5 million to states and local partners, expanding technical assistance, and surging CDC personnel and resources to support containment efforts where needed most,” Press Secretary Emily Hilliard told The Independent.

Offit believes the measles outbreaks will continue in an era of medical freedom, and as people believe they have the right to make their own health decisions and stop caring about the health of their neighbors.

Part of the problem is that people don’t remember past outbreaks, he said, and some younger doctors working at his hospital had never seen a measles case before.

“I think that not only did we eliminate the disease, we eliminated the memory of the disease. I think people don’t remember measles,” he said.

Stuart Fails to Save the Universe episode two sees the return of a major Big Bang Theory star — but not as fans remember them.

Set after the events of the original sitcom, HBO Max’s new spin-off follows Stuart Bloom (Kevin Sussman), the comic book store owner from The Big Bang Theory, as he accidentally destroys a multiverse device created by Sheldon Cooper and Leonard Hofstadter.

With the help of familiar faces Bert (Brian Posehn), Barry Kripke (John Ross Bowie) and Denise (Lauren Lapkus), Stuart sets off on a mission across alternate realities to restore order to the universe, encountering new versions of characters fans will recognize from The Big Bang Theory along the way.

The latest episode, which aired Thursday night, sees the group enter a reality in which all humans have a device implanted on their necks that delivers an electric shock whenever they argue or get aggressive.

This eventually leads them into a 30-month reeducation facility designed to eliminate conflict. But after completing the program, they are unexpectedly abducted and taken to an abandoned warehouse.

open image in gallery John Ross Bowie, Lauren Lapkus, Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn star in the new ‘Big Bang Theory’ spin-off, ‘Stuart Saves the Universe’ ( HBO Max )

It’s here, once their hoods are removed, that Kaley Cuoco’s Penny reveals herself.

Rather than the blonde, aspiring actress-turned-pharmaceutical sales rep from The Big Bang Theory, this alternate version of Penny has brunette hair and leads a resistance movement against their AI-controlled world alongside her ex-boyfriend Zack (Brian Thomas Smith).

“A big part of it was offering them a challenge to do something entirely different,” co-creator and executive producer Chuck Lorre told Variety of bringing back some original The Big Bang Theory characters in new forms.

open image in gallery Kaley Cuoco reprises her role as Penny in ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ — but with a very different look ( Colin Remas Brown/HBO Max )

open image in gallery In ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe,’ Penny leads a resistance movement against an AI-controlled world ( Colin Remas Brown/HBO Max )

“As you’ve seen in Episode 2, Kaley’s not playing the server in the Cheesecake Factory. It’s still Penny, and now she’s a badass guerrilla leader. That was part of the design from the very beginning. In a multiverse environment, these characters could recur as themselves, but with an entirely different backstory.”

The Big Bang Theory ran from 2007 to 2019 on CBS and made global stars of its core cast members, Cuoco, Jim Parsons (Sheldon), Johnny Galecki (Leonard), Kunal Nayyar (Raj Koothrappali), Mayim Bialik (Amy Farrah Fowler) and Simon Helberg (Howard Wolowitz).

It followed a group of socially awkward scientists and their friends as they navigated relationships, careers and everyday life in Pasadena, California.

The wildly popular show reportedly ended because Parsons turned down $50 million to return for a 13th and 14th season.

Stuart Fails to Save the Universe airs Thursdays at 9 p.m. ET on HBO Max.

News.title: Massage guns vs compression boots: Which is better for muscle recovery?
News.content:
Looking after your body is no longer just about getting a good workout in; it’s ensuring that you’re properly recuperating afterwards, too. Luckily, in 2026, there is a huge range of products designed to aid recovery.

In fact, the recovery tech boom is playing a big role in the growth of the sports technology market overall. Estimates show it’s projected to grow from $39.6 billion in 2026 to $192.3 billion by 2034.

Two of the most popular products in this category are massage guns and compression boots. Both claim to ease muscle soreness and help you bounce back to training sooner, but they sit at very different price points. You can pick up a basic gun from around £40, whereas the cheapest boots we tested were £300. But which method is actually better for improving workout recovery?

Massage guns can help to improve flexibility in older muscles

Massage guns work by delivering repeated percussion and vibration to one specific area, which helps improve the mobility and flexibility of a specific muscle. In turn, this can make your muscles feel less tense and stiff. These gadgets can be used before and after workout sessions.

While useful for all ages, massage guns can be helpful for anyone looking to improve range of movement, ease muscle stiffness and boost blood flow – whether exercising or not.

“It will help temporarily improve your mobility so that you feel like you’ve got a bit more flexibility in that muscle,” explains Jonathan Wreaves, clinical physiologist at preventative health clinic Viavi.

But how do they actually work?

Most massage guns offer a revolutions per minute (RPM) range, which refers to how many times the massage head moves back and forth every minute. This tends to be somewhere between 1200 and 3500. The lower range is ideal for gentle massage and warming up, while a higher RPM is better for targeting bigger muscle groups and more intense tightness.

News.title: Battle rages over access to new ‘miracle’ HIV drug
News.content:
For the first time in the four-decade fight against HIV there is a “miracle” drug that can all but eliminate the risk of infection, but in the Latin American countries where it was tested almost no one can get it.

Trials show that Lenacapavir, made by Gilead Sciences, is almost 100 per cent effective in preventing HIV infection. With just two shots a year, those taking it will avoid contracting the virus even when frequently exposed.

The drug, which many believe could bring an end to the global HIV pandemic, costs $14,000 a dose in the United States. Gilead has agreed to licence generic versions of the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medication at around $40 a dose in 120 low-and middle-income countries, but almost all of Latin America is excluded.

Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Peru are among those with serious HIV epidemics that are shut out, despite having run some of the clinical trials that proved the drug works.

Their status as “upper-middle income countries” means they are too rich to qualify for the cut price generic version and yet they remain too poor to pay the US price.

News.title: Senior dating: a guide to finding love later in life
News.content:
Whether you’re a widow, widower or divorcee, the thought of online dating in later life can feel daunting. However, more and more people are turning to the internet to find romance. Roughly 16 per cent of UK adults are using online dating services to meet a partner, according to Statista. Among them, there are lots of singles over 50 using dating sites.

So here’s how to navigate your senior dating online, with expert advice from psychologist and dating coach Dr Pam Spurr, and sex and relationship coach Angela Vossen.

How do I know if I'm ready to date again as a senior?

Coming out of any relationship is hard. If you’re hoping to date after a divorce, bereavement or break up, it can take a long time to feel ready to date again. Dr Spurr advises taking your time.

“Many people feel bruised, even traumatised, after coming out of a long-term relationship or having been bereaved,” she explains. “Your feelings naturally vary from day to day about whether you're ready to get back out to look for love – or even for fun. A crucial factor is if you've come to the point where you have more good days compared to bad days”.

Dr Spurr explains that good days are the days on which you feel more optimistic about life generally, and you find your thoughts turning to meeting someone new. “That's an important sign that you are healing,” she says. “However, if you're still feeling deeply insecure or are riddled with self-doubt about your worthiness, take your time. When you feel worthy, you will find someone worthy of you”.

Feeling heartbroken? Learn how to get over a break up

How to start senior dating online

If you’re new to online dating, it can feel intimidating at first. The secret is taking things step by step so that you do things at your own pace. The first step, however, should be choosing a senior dating site that will help match you with like-minded people. This will narrow your search and ensure your dating experience is more successful.

Step 1: Create an online profile

Once you’ve decided on a dating site or app and signed up, you’ll be asked to write a dating profile. This should reflect who you are along with your passions, values and what you seek in a partner.

Try to be authentic rather than creating a fantasy version of yourself. If you exaggerate your accomplishments, your date will only feel deceived once they get to know you. Likewise, don’t be tempted to use a photo of yourself from 10 years ago.

What are you waiting for? |  Single and looking to find true love? Sign up today for Telegraph Dating and join more than 220,000 like-minded people. Join today

Step 2: Spark meaningful chats with potential dates

Once you have signed up to a senior dating site and created a profile, you will be free to start looking at other people’s profiles and sending messages to anyone that catches your attention. But how can you initiate a conversation after an introduction?

“When messaging people on dating sites, ask open-ended questions to spark meaningful chats,” says Angela. A good example would be, ‘I can see you enjoy travel. What place have you always wanted to visit but haven’t yet?’ or “tell me more about your love of tennis? Did you watch the US Open?” If things go really well and the chat seems to flow naturally, you may decide to organise a phone chat or ask them out on a date. An initial chat over the phone can help gauge how well you get on and how easily the conversation flows. If this goes well, meeting in person may feel less nerve wracking and a little less ‘blind’.

Step 3: Prioritise your safety

“While most people are well intentioned online, it’s important to protect your safety,” advises Ms Vossen. “Keep personal details private (like where you live or your social media profiles) until you’ve met in person and built trust”. You should also arrange first dates in public places, share your plans with a friend, and trust your instincts if something feels off.

If the first date or two doesn’t quite hit the mark, try not to be too disappointed and remember that you can say no to another date. Ms Vossen says: “Be patient – online dating takes time, but with practice, you’ll gain confidence and enjoy the journey”.

Traditional ways to meet senior singles

Of course, couples continue to meet in a manner that predates online dating sites. If you’re keen to join the older dating scene but find the online world overwhelming, there are plenty of ways to meet people in real life.

1. Holidays and group trips

We are often our best selves on holiday, so it’s the ideal place to find a single senior woman or to meet men if the opportunity presents itself. Why not organise a trip on which you meet new people while doing what you love, whether that’s cycling, walking, sightseeing or just travelling around a new part of the world. There are many escorted tours that cater to specific age groups and interests. They also take away the stress of organising a trip yourself.

“An organised holiday or trip can be a great place to meet someone new and there are many organisations offering these for the over 50s,” says Dr Spur. “A word of caution though, you can spend a lot of money and there's no guarantee that you will meet that special person. However, if it's a place you've wanted to travel to then go with the mindset that you're going to have a great trip. If you meet someone, that's an added bonus”.

2. Activities and social groups

Whether you enjoy walking, reading or volunteering, taking up a new hobby or joining a social group is a great way to enhance your social life and increase your chances of meeting a new romantic interest.

“Joining a club or taking up a hobby can be a fantastic way of meeting singles who enjoy the same pastimes,” says Dr Spur. “You're doing an activity you enjoy knowing that there might also be someone there that will catch your eye”.

If you do meet someone that you’re interested in at a social event, Dr Spur advises starting with a simple ‘hello’ and an easy question such as how long they've been doing that particular activity or hobby. “This can open-up a friendly conversation that might lead to flirting down the line,” she says.

Start online dating for seniors today

Whichever way you decide to start looking for love, approach it in a way that you feel comfortable with. Signing up to an online dating service is a great way to meet other seniors. Remember, it’s never too late to begin a new chapter.

News.title: UK economy to flatline, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Britain’s economy is set to almost grind to a halt for the rest of the year, the Bank of England has warned.

Growth will drop to just 0.1pc per quarter, the Bank predicted, slowing sharply after a strong start to 2026.

Higher petrol prices and energy bills, a weak jobs market and rising mortgage costs are all draining confidence and spending power from the economy.

Inflation, which slowed to a 15-month low of 2.6pc in June, is also expected to rise again to 3.2pc later this year, the Bank warned.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s Governor, said inflation had “fallen faster than we’d expected” but warned that war in the Middle East would lead to a fresh spike.

He added that growth would “weaken slightly further in the near term as the effects of the conflict weigh further on demand”.

The Bank also predicted that unemployment will rise back above 5pc in the coming months, limiting workers’ ability to ask for higher wages to cope with rising living costs.

It presents a challenging backdrop for Andy Burnham and his Chancellor, John Healey, who have pledged to help voters struggling with the cost of living.

The forecasts came as policymakers led by Mr Bailey held interest rates at 3.75pc.

Although three members of the nine-strong Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted for higher rates, up from two at the previous meeting, the Governor dismissed suggestions the Bank is moving towards higher interest rates.

The public should “not… [think] the Bank of England is edging towards a hike,” Mr Bailey said.

“Frankly there is nothing I have said, or any of us have said, along those lines. We took a decision today to leave the Bank Rate unchanged and that is the relevant conclusion.”

Clare Lombardelli, a Deputy Governor, said voting to keep rates at 3.75pc “was not a close judgement”, calling the decision “pretty clear” given slowing inflation in the domestic economy.

Officials are monitoring the economy for any signs that increases in oil, gas and petrol prices caused by the war in Iran are creeping into higher costs and wages in the wider economy.

Mr Bailey said: “The possibility of repeated resumptions of conflict, combined with lower than usual European gas stock levels and a fall in global refining output, mean that risks to energy prices lie to the upside.”

He added: “Reassuringly, there are few signs so far that second-round effects are generating more broad-based inflationary pressures.”

Companies are struggling to pass higher costs on to their customers because of the economy’s weakness, he added.

Workers are typically securing only modest pay rises as the weak jobs market leaves them in a poor position to push for bigger salaries.

Mr Bailey stressed there are still major risks to the outlook given the war and promised to “monitor the situation carefully” and was “ready to adjust our stance”.

“It is our job to ensure that inflation gets back to the 2pc target and stays there, and that is what we will do,” he said.

Borrowing costs dropped in financial markets after the decision.

The Government’s two-year borrowing cost fell from 4.44pc to 4.34pc, the sharpest fall in a month.

The FTSE 250 index of mid-sized UK companies rose 0.8pc to a record high of 24,184.10.

Traders still believe the Bank will raise interest rates twice within a year.

However, Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said rate rises “remain more a threat than a reality”.

He said there was evidence of disinflation in the economy and interest rates could be “cut to 3pc in 2027”, adding: “That’s very different to market pricing for rates to be close to 4.5pc in 2027.”

News.title: Arsonists torch more Ebola clinics as misinformation spirals in DRC
News.content:
Two more Ebola treatment facilities have reportedly been burned down in recent days as health officials struggle to overcome violent public mistrust of medical teams.

At least a dozen facilities have now been attacked since Congo declared its Ebola outbreak amid fear, misinformation and suspicion of outside authorities.

The outbreak is the fastest growing on record and officials said the virus had now killed more than 1,500 people.

The official death toll from the outbreak centred on the north eastern Ituri province of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has risen by 500 in only a week.

Sources told the Telegraph the large jump in deaths was largely caused by a “data harmonisation exercise” between different regions, and the new deaths may not have all happened in the past week.

However, the daily confirmed toll has also continued to climb sharply with the latest government update reporting 50 people dying in the previous 24 hours.

Airfinity, a health analytics firm, said the outbreak “continues to outpace detection and the response” and there is a high chance of it spreading further inside DRC.

News.title: Race for vaccine against new Ebola strain gets $8.5m boost
News.content:
The “most promising” vaccine to tackle the Ebola strain behind an explosive outbreak in the Congo has been given an $8.5 million boost, as researchers race to develop an effective shot.

So far at least 3,360 people have been infected and 1,487 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in an epidemic triggered by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

But unlike past outbreaks of the more common Zaire strain, there are currently no approved vaccines to tackle Bundibugyo.

On Thursday, the Coalition of Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi) revealed up to $8.5 million of funding for the only single-dose inoculation, which was described as the “most promising vaccine candidate” by the World Health Organization (WHO) in an analysis in May.

It is being developed by researchers at Hilleman Laboratories – a unique partnership between the pharmaceutical giant Merck and the British philanthropic powerhouse Wellcome, which is headquartered in Singapore.

The vaccine candidate is a Bundibugyo version of the Ervebo shot, which was created by Merck (MSD in Europe) and has already been approved for Ebola Zaire.

It uses a rVSV platform, where a modified version of VSV virus is used to train the immune system to react to target pathogens – in this instance, the Bundibugyo species replaces Zaire.

News.title: AMR chatbot could prevent drug-resistant infections in African hospitals
News.content:
A phone-based chatbot advising medics how to prescribe antibiotics has helped raise the quality of care in African hospitals and should stop bugs developing dangerous resistance, developers say.

Staff at four hospitals across Zambia and Kenya have been using two digital tools in a pilot project to try to address one of the world’s biggest health threats.

Anti-microbial resistance (AMR) is caused by germs evolving so that medicines such as antibiotics designed to kill them no longer work.

The menace is linked to nearly five million deaths each year and makes it increasingly difficult to treat infections. The annual death toll could nearly double in the next 25 years, according to some forecasts.

The rise in AMR is being significantly driven by the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine and in agriculture.

Using antibiotics when they are not necessary, using the wrong ones, or getting the dosage wrong, all add to the chances that bugs will develop resistance.

With a shortage of new drugs in the development pipeline, one push to defeat AMR has been to get medics to stick to existing prescription, dosage and treatment advice.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Programme through Innovation, Research, and Education (ASPIRE) is trying to give them guidance using technology they already have in their pockets.
