Sports.title: UEFA twist knife into Gianni Infantino with damning vote of no confidence after FIFA U-turn
Sports.content:
UEFA twist knife into Gianni Infantino with damning vote of no confidence after FIFA U-turn

UEFA has released a statement saying it has 'lost confidence' in Gianni Infantino, following his failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FIFA president Infantino had planned to sell off stakes in football governing body's competitions to private investors, but scrapped the idea in the early hours of Saturday morning amid widespread outrage.

4 Gianni Infantino's position as FIFA president is becoming increasingly untenable Credit: Getty

Multiple continental federations were strongly opposed to the project, including UEFA.

European football's governing body warned that its member nations would boycott future FIFA tournaments if the plan went ahead.

Infantino has also seen his inner circle begin to crumble - senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigned on Friday, releasing a strongly worded statement opposing the FFE plans.

And now, after the under-fire football chief was forced to pull the plug on his controversial proposal, UEFA has welcomed the decision.

In a statement, UEFA blasted Infantino's plans, and thanked the 'fans, leagues, clubs, players, individuals, associations and confederations that opposed the scheme'.

The European football authority also said the 'current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family'.

UEFA statement in full “UEFA welcomes FIFA’s decision to withdraw its plan to sell a stake in its competitions – including the World Cup – into private hands. “The proposal was unanimously rejected by UEFA’s national associations and by many other federations and confederations of all sizes around the world, whose job it is to protect football. “UEFA thanks all the fans, leagues, clubs, players, individuals, associations and confederations that opposed the scheme, alongside the many Prime Ministers, Heads of State and commentators who have demonstrated to the FIFA President that football is not for sale. “We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account. “It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again. That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family. “When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of FIFA’s Member Associations to elect him as their President in 2016, he said, “Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in UEFA. You will have to play a part every day in the life of FIFA,” before telling the assembled stakeholders, “The money of FIFA is your money. It’s not the money of the FIFA President. It’s your money. You are the national associations and the money of FIFA has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.” “On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through was anything but transparent. “And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations’ money for the benefit of the game. “UEFA will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing FIFA Forward programme. “We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in FIFA’s bank account to deliver the kick start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of FIFA. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it. “This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.”

No way back?

UEFA's damning statement places even more pressure on Infantino's position in charge of FIFA.

His failed FFE proposal faced almost total opposition across the board, with CONCACAF and the AFC joining UEFA in publicly slamming the plans.

With the proposal reliant on FIFA's 211 Member Federations voting it through, the opposition of three continental federations left Infantino facing 143 votes against his pitch.

The FFE was a plan to roll the World Cup's broadcasting, licensing, ticketing and sponsorship into one big company.

4 Infantino's FFE project had intended to raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling off chunks in the commercial rights of the men's and women's World Cups

4 UEFA are headed up by president Aleksander Ceferin Credit: Getty

20 per cent of it was then going to be sold to private investors, with Infantino in line to make millions.

The private stakeholders would have then got a say in what happened to the World Cup as well, but this will no longer materialise.

Infantino was already under intense scrutiny in his role as FIFA president this summer following the World Cup and the manner of Folarin Balogun's suspended ban.

USA striker Balogun was cleared to play against Belgium in the last 16 after his red card ban was suspended for a year after intervention from US President Donald Trump.

UEFA slammed FIFA's decision at the time, insisting it 'crossed a red line' in a furious statement.

What did Infantino say?

The FIFA president still attempted to defend the project as he climbed down from it in the early hours of Saturday morning.

4 Infantino had already been under pressure for his relationship with the Trump administration Credit: Getty

His statement read: "The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

"And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

"Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

"Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support."

Sports.title: Arsene Wenger called out for silence as Gianni Infantino scraps FIFA’s toxic FFE scheme
Sports.content:
Arsene Wenger has been questioned for failing to speak out on Gianni Infantino's failed FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal.

FIFA president Infantino had planned to sell off stakes in the world football governing body's competitions to private investors but scrapped the idea in the early hours of Saturday morning amid widespread outrage.

3 Infantino's FFE project had intended to raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling off chunks in the commercial rights of the men's and women's World Cups Credit: Getty

Multiple continental federations vehemently rejected the project – with UEFA announcing they would boycott future World Cups if it went ahead.

Infantino has also seen his inner circle begin to crumble: senior advisor Carols Codeiro resigned on Friday, releasing a strongly worded statement opposing the FFE plans.

But one person who has so far stayed silent on the matter is FIFA's Chief of Global Football Development, legendary former Arsenal boss Wenger – much to the surprise of talkSPORT's Tony Cascarino.

Joining Shebahn Aherne on the Weekend Sports Breakfast, the former Chelsea and Republic of Ireland striker said: "The one thing that's really surprised me is Arsene Wenger, who's got a real pivotal role within FIFA and he's obviously been an incredible manager.

"Nothing at all from Arsene Wenger and you'd have felt that he would have [something to say].

"But... the way he's always managed and you always felt he loves the game so much, and what he achieved as a club manager and his role at FIFA – and Arsene's been very, very quiet.

"And it's hard to know exactly where he stands as well – because he'll get questioned, Arsene Wenger."

Aherne suggested Wenger might speak out now Infantino has shelved the highly controversial proposal.

"We don't even know if he might have been against him," Cascarino continued.

"There's certain people... behind the scenes [at FIFA] that have gone, 'Absolutely not, this is not a good idea for football'... selling off the game privately and look, the game makes a lot of money anyway."

3 Burnham has called on Infantino to go Credit: AFP

Infantino's own position in charge of FIFA is bound to come under increased pressure in light of this categorical failure.

And UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Infantino 'the wrong man' for the job.

Burnham, who was critical of the FFE plans from the outset, told reporters on Friday: "My view is strengthening – this was an outrageous suggestion.

"The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [Infantino] is the wrong man to lead the organisation.

"Let me say this very directly: football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine.

"The World Cup is not a product; it is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone's to sell. Dress the deal up however you like; once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.

3 Wenger has a leading role in FIFA but his thoughts on FFE were never vocalised Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

"Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will."

What did Infantino say?

The FIFA president still attempted to defend the project as he climbed down from it in the early hours of Saturday morning.

His statement read: "The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

"And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

"Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place. Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve.

"As a result, this proposal will not proceed. Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support."

Sports.title: Liverpool’s pre-season win over Wrexham has exposed glaring transfer problem
Sports.content:
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola is already being forced to cover for the biggest transfer mistake the club's hierarchy has made.

The Reds ranked Mohamed Salah as the fourth greatest player in Anfield history and yet have little over four weeks to replace him.

7 Mohamed Salah bid an emotional farewell to Liverpool in May, and he is still yet to find a new club Credit: Getty

Two teenagers who haven't played a minute of Premier League football have started at right-wing in each of Iraola's first two games.

That normally wouldn't set any alarm bells ringing in pre-season, especially one that takes place after a World Cup with senior stars on extended breaks.

However, in Liverpool's case, the cavalry won't be belatedly arriving to solve the right-wing issue after Salah's exit at the end of last season.

Against Wrexham, 16-year-old academy talent Joshua Abe was entrusted to start the first half, before Rio Ngumoha took the reins.

The 17-year-old - who made his England debut in June on the right flank - hinted at further developing his game on the opposite side to his favoured left-wing at the start of pre-season.

"Being unpredictable off both sides is key," he said. "Obviously, everyone knows I can play on the left, but on the right I feel like I'm improving and I'm getting better.

"So, yeah, definitely off the left and the right this season."

Ngumoha did indeed score the only goal from the right in the win over Wrexham, with his deflected effort finding the far top corner.

However, the former Cobham starlet is understandably still hugely raw in his new role, having completed just one of his four attempted dribbles while also only managing two touches in the Wrexham box.

Liverpool head coach Iraola said afterwards: "I normally used to try to encourage our wingers to have the ability to play both sides.

7 Liverpool surely had a better plan than to hope Iraola could plug the right wing with a player who favours the left? Credit: AFP

7 Ngumoha showed against Wrexham why he'll need time to develop as a winger who can play both sides Credit: Getty

"I know some of them are more comfortable on one side, but our team is not normally symmetrical," Iraola continued.

"Also, in pre-season, I have to see where they are more comfortable, but in my previous clubs most of the wingers have played both sides."

What was Liverpool's Salah-succession plan before Iraola?

The Reds even surprised Arne Slot when the decision was ultimately made to part ways with the Dutchman at the end of May.

But the club's hierarchy knew months before that Salah's succession plan was being moved up a year after ripping up his contract.

Steven Gerrard told talkSPORT that his dream pick was Michael Olise, but he accepted getting him out of Bayern Munich was fanciful.

Meanwhile, his former Liverpool teammate Michael Owen also suggested Jarrod Bowen prior to the latter remaining at West Ham.

7 Salah is the most notable departure from Liverpool this summer Credit: Getty

Hierarchy shake-up

What Slot's plan would have been for his right side had he stayed at Liverpool is anybody's guess after a myriad of failed experiments.

In games Salah was absent for last season, the Dutchman deployed Jeremie Frimpong and Dominik Szoboszlai at times on the wing - neither of which would have been a long-term solution.

The elephant in the room in terms of Liverpool's transfers is that Michael Edwards, who played a vital role in Salah's arrival under Jurgen Klopp, has stepped down as Fenway Sports Group's (FSG) CEO of football.

Current Reds sporting director Richard Hughes has also been linked with a move to Saudi Pro League club Al Hilal, but remains in charge of incomings and outgoings on Merseyside this summer.

7 Munoz played 18 games for Osasuna last season on the left and made 10 appearances on the right Credit: Getty

Liverpool have indeed been in the market for wingers this summer, having been snubbed in their pursuit of Yan Diomande.

The club then successfully hijacked Newcastle's move for Spain star Victor Munoz in a £34million swoop.

The World Cup winner is predominantly a left winger, but does fit Iraola's bill of being able to operate on the right.

So too is top target Bradley Barcola, for whom talkSPORT understands the Reds are now readying a €100m (around £85m) offer, plus add-ons for the Paris Saint-Germain forward.

The France international has only played on the right flank 37 times in his career and at that price is clearly going to operate in his favoured left position.

7 Over the last two seasons, Barcola has played more than two-thirds of his games on the left wing Credit: Getty

'Square pegs in round holes'

Liverpool explored signing Barcola in 2025 when a price of around €85m (around £73m) was quoted, but reports claimed a desire not to block a pathway for Ngumoha saw their pursuit abandoned.

12 months on, the club may argue that Salah's premature exit has necessitated a rethink, which is why Ngumoha is being tried on the right.

But it would be an almost insurmountable burden for a teenager learning a new role to be expected to replace Salah in only his second full season as a professional, rather than being the chief understudy on both wings to more experienced players.

Peterborough United chairman and Liverpool fan Darragh MacAnthony has admitted he is not enamoured with Barcola's arrival.

He told talkSPORT's Alex Crook: "I'm with Jamie Carragher in the camp. I saw him the other day talking about it. We have like three, four left-wingers already, players who can play there. We need to fill the void left by Salah.

7 Frimpong will be needed at right-back more often than not, with Conor Bradley a long-term absentee Credit: Getty

"Frimpong was meant to help with that, but we know he's had injury issues last year. Not quite what we like to see out wide right when he did play. We need a right winger. It's concerning.

"And we're going out, and we're getting another pacy player who plays on the left the majority of the time.

"So, unless Rio's going to get put on the right, you know, square pegs, round holes, all that kind of thing. I don't know. I don't love it because of the money.

"If he was £60-70 million, and I get it, he's not, you think, okay, it's a no-brainer.

"Then you maybe sell [Cody] Gakpo, and you clear up some space on the left. You still go get a right winger."

MacAnthony added: "Liverpool have got a lot of holes to fill.

"And you've got to start at right wing to fill Mo Salah's departure. So, it does concern me that we're going down this rabbit hole where we might end up paying, I don't know, like the [Florian] Wirtz money; you overpay.

"And then does the player adapt to the Premier League, and is it another bad signing? It's frustrating for me."

Sports.title: Bayern Munich publicly put three players on transfer list including ex-Premier League star
Sports.content:
Joao Palhinha is among three players that Bayern Munich are willing to sell this summer.

Max Eberl, the director of sport at Bayern, has publicly revealed that the players are not part of their plans for the new season.



2 Palhinha is one of three players to be put up for sale by Bayern Credit: Getty

Ismael Saibari was their first summer signing in a reported €50million (£43m) move from PSV Eindhoven.

Bayern then bought Nathaniel Brown, who Manchester United had as a target, in a €55m (£47m) deal with Eintracht Frankfurt.

Players such as Leon Goretzka and Raphael Guerreiro have left at the end of their contracts, and others have gone on loan or permanently.



And according to Eberl, Bayern are keen to let another trio of players depart before the end of the window.

"We have three players we are open to letting go," he explained via @iMiaSanMia on X. "They have no future at Bayern.



"If they want to stay with us, it will be tough because we are not planning with them. Then they won't play a role.

"That's the case with Sacha Boey, Joao Palhinha and Bryan Zaragoza."

Who could Palhinha sign for?

After two solid seasons at Fulham, Palhinha joined Bayern in July 2024 and played a part in their Bundesliga title success that season.



However, he played just 986 minutes across all competitions and then made his way back to the Premier League with Tottenham Hotspur.

The Portuguese midfielder signed on a season-long loan deal, which included an option to buy for £26m.

2 Eberl says the trio do not have a future at the club Credit: Getty

Palhinha played regularly and scored the winner against Everton on the final day to secure the club's status in the top-flight.



Whilst he did impress in north London, the clause that allowed Spurs to sign him permanently has expired.

They have instead signed Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali in deals that cost a combined £185m.

It means Palhinha faces uncertainty over where he will be playing in the new season, although he doesn't seem to be short of interest.

Aston Villa are understood to have been in talks for the 31-year-old, who is keen to stay in England.



Newcastle United are also reportedly keen on Palhinha as a potential replacement for the seemingly Arsenal-bound Bruno Guimaraes.

Sports.title: New FIFA presidential candidate emerges as pressure grows on Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
Victor Montagliani is emerging as a serious contender to rival Gianni Infantino at the next FIFA presidential election, talkSPORT understands.

The potential for the Canadian to become the new FIFA president was exclusively revealed on talkSPORT during the World Cup.

3 Infantino us under increased pressure as FIFA president Credit: Getty

CONCACAF president Montagliani wants to be the top chief at FIFA president one day, as talkSPORT revealed earlier this month, and is now considering whether to put his name forward ahead of the November 18 deadline.

Sources close to the 60-year-old have argued his immediate focus is on being re-elected as CONCACAF president, but it is common knowledge the Canadian has aspirations to be FIFA president one day.

He is now toying with either going head to head with Infantino or pushing for the FIFA president to quit, giving him a more open path.

Sources believe CONCACAF's emphatic rejection of Infantino's plans to sell a stake of FIFA to private investors was in part tactical to align with UEFA and potentially secure votes in the long-run.

It means 96 Member Federations, 41 from CONCACAF and 55 from UEFA, are all against Infantino, and could even block vote against him in the presidential election if a viable candidate emerges.

World Cup chaos

Infantino had already faced scrutiny following the conclusion of the World Cup, including concerns over his relationship with US president Donald Trump, before his controversial plans were revealed.

The FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal would see the football governing body's commercial and operational arms merge as part of an organisation funded by private equity.

All 211 Member Associations were given a $40million (£30m) payment incentive by Infantino to back the project by September 19.

However, there has been stiff opposition to the plans from UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC, and some of Infantino's closest allies at FIFA are understood to also be opposed.

Carlos Cordeiro, the president's senior adviser, has even quit his role in protest of the proposed sale of World Cup stakes.

3 Multiple candidates have been tipped to rival Infantino for the presidency Credit: AFP

It is clear UEFA would welcome a challenger to Infantino if he insists on standing even if FFE fails.

UEFA federations would also welcome Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi standing, but sources close to the Qatari businessman insist he has 'no ambition' to do so.

UEFA President Alexander Ceferin would be the most qualified name, but the Slovenian lawyer is understood to be willing to continue in his current role as UEFA President next Spring.

He had initially ruled out standing for a third full term until 2031, but is now willing to seek re-election if no other candidates step forward.

Ceferin is not looking to go head-to-head with Infantino despite clashing on issues on a number of occasions.

talkSPORT also understands senior officials within Bosnian, Norwegian, Swedish, German and Spanish football have all discussed backing other European candidates, including Legia owner Dariusz Mioduski.

3 The FFE plans have been given little to no support Credit: Getty

Should Al-Khelaifi choose not to stand, which is the current expectation, Poland would favour Mioduski as well.

Confederation of African Football president Patrice Motsepe is another name intent on being FIFA president one day.

The South African administrator is highly unlikely to go head-to-head with close ally Infantino, instead preferring to wait until 2031 in the hope of getting an endorsement during an election Infantino can't stand again in.

When do nominations to be the next FIFA president close?

And there appears to be no appetite to table a vote of no confidence against Infantino either despite it being toyed with at the last FIFA Congress.

Most federations will simply view the election itself as a vote of confidence, which is why a growing number of UEFA members are hoping to back another candidate to avoid Infantino winning a new term without a genuine debate.

Nominations for the next FIFA presidential election can be made up until November 18 with the election taking place on November 18 in Rabat, Morocco.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace star declares parents convinced him to snub summer switch to Saudi Arabia
Sports.content:
Daichi Kamada has revealed how his parents helped to sway him from leaving Crystal Palace for Saudi Arabia.

Kamada looked set to leave Selhurst Park as a free agent this summer at the end of the two-year deal he signed in July 2024.



2 Kamada could have gone to Saudi Arabia, but will remain in London Credit: Getty

However, he has committed his future to the Palace by signing a new one-year deal to keep him at the club until 2027.

The 29-year-old has been a key part of the club's success during the past two seasons with FA Cup and Conference League triumphs.

Kamada did enough to attract interest from Saudi Arabia, where he could have been in line for a huge payday amid its lucrative finances.



But, after consultation with his parents, the midfielder opted not to move there and remain in south London.

Staying put

Speaking to TV Asahi Sports, via @Fooootest on X, he said: "Up until last winter, I had an offer from Saudi Arabia and was thinking about going there to secure my future.



"I thought my parents would be thrilled, but they told me, 'At this timing, absolutely do not go.'

"It was an enormous amount of money, so I figured they'd be delighted, but that was not the case at all."



Palace chairman Steve Parish was delighted to see Kamada extend his stay as he commented: "This is fantastic news for Crystal Palace. Over the last two years Daichi has made a great impact in the centre of midfield, as well as becoming a fans’ favourite on and off the pitch.

"I am delighted that he has turned down the many options he had to extend his stay in South London.

"Daichi will now have a well-earned break after his excellent World Cup and join us later in pre-season as we enter a busy Premier League and European season."

2 Kamada will stay at Palace for at least another season Credit: Getty



A new dawn at Selhurst

Palace are set to begin their first season under Pierre Sage, who has replaced Oliver Glasner as manager.

They will also make their Europa League debut, having qualified with their Conference League success in May.

Oscar Mingueza is their only summer signing so far following his free transfer from Celta Vigo.

However, they have banked £52million by selling Maxence Lacroix to Premier League rivals Chelsea.



Palace's pre-season schedule got underway with a 5-1 victory over Swindon Town before defeats to Bromley and Lens.

A 0-0 draw with Famalicao followed, with the Eagles then beating Al Ula 3-1 on Friday night.

Sports.title: UEFA declares loss of confidence in Gianni Infantino's FIFA presidency: Pressure mounts on under-fire boss after disastrous World Cup plot as football chiefs look to overthrow him
Sports.content:
UEFA have called for shamed FIFA president Gianni Infantino to go after he scrapped the ‘shabby, back-room deal’ to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Pressure is mounting on the under-fire boss after his controversial plan to sell a £3.1billion stake in football's most coveted tournament to a group of private investors led by Josh Kushner - an extended relation of US President Donald Trump - collapsed on Friday night.

The scheme, which received wholesale opposition from football nations around the world, has seen scrutiny on Infantino's presidency intensify.

UEFA, European football's governing body, led the charge against Infantino's plot and, in a lengthy statement released on Saturday morning, declared they had lost trust in his leadership.

UEFA said: 'UEFA welcomes FIFA’s decision to withdraw its plan to sell a stake in its competitions – including the World Cup – into private hands.

'The proposal was unanimously rejected by UEFA’s national associations and by many other federations and confederations of all sizes around the world, whose job it is to protect football.

'UEFA thanks all the fans, leagues, clubs, players, individuals, associations and confederations that opposed the scheme, alongside the many Prime Ministers, Heads of State and commentators who have demonstrated to the FIFA President that football is not for sale.

UEFA have lost confidence in shamed FIFA president Gianni Infantino after ‘shabby, back-room deal’ to sell stakes in the World Cup.

Gianni Infantino waves goodbye to his unilateral plans for private investment in FIFA with his presidency in jeopardy

Carlos Cordeiro (left) quit as an advisor to Gianni Infantino (centre) on Friday

'We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account,' the UEFA statement continued.

'It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again. That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.

'When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of FIFA’s Member Associations to elect him as their President in 2016, he said, “Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in UEFA. You will have to play a part every day in the life of FIFA", before telling the assembled stakeholders, “The money of FIFA is your money. It’s not the money of the FIFA President. It’s your money. You are the national associations and the money of FIFA has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else".

'On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back-room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through was anything but transparent.

'And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations' money for the benefit of the game.

'UEFA will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing FIFA Forward programme.

'We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in FIFA’s bank account to deliver the kick-start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of FIFA. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it.

'This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.’

FIFA member nations could trigger a vote of no confidence to oust Infantino, who is seeking a fourth term in next year's elections. The threshold to initiate the process is 46 FIFA member associations; UEFA have 55 members.

In the early hours of Saturday morning, Infantino abandoned his proposals to inject private equity into the operational and commercial aspects of FIFA tournaments.

His humiliating backtrack came thanks to the heroics of UEFA, CONCACAF, the AFC and two members of the FIFA hierarchy, who all took a stand against his divisive plans

The AFC, Asia's governing body, were the third and final confederation to reject Gianni Infantino's proposal. Their resistance made it clear he did not have the support to proceed, as opposing nations rose to a staggering 135 - 64 per cent of the FIFA membership.

With the controversy surrounding Infantino, member nations could trigger a vote of no confidence. The threshold to initiate the process is 46 FIFA member associations

The commendation followed CONCACAF's rejection on Thursday and came after UEFA announced a boycott of FIFA competitions. New Zealand Football also objected to the plans, despite the OFC delaying a continent-wide response.

Infantino said: 'The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

'And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

'Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

'Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

'Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, and particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.'

The statement marked an embarrassing U-turn, less than 24 hours after he attempted to clarify his plans - blaming the media for misconstruing them.

One international football insider told Daily Mail Sport: 'UEFA's response is at the nuclear button end of the spectrum, which is impressive. We thought Infantino would survive the Trump refereeing intervention - but he has overreached this time.'

The proposal reached a terminal stage when Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to Gianni Infantino, announced his resignation from FIFA - becoming the first internal dissident.

Six hours later, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour turned against the president - risking his job by criticising the plans and calling on nations to dethrone Infantino. Lamour admitted FIFA Forward Enterprise was the brainchild of 'one person' as he landed a critical blow to the FIFA president.

Infantino had hoped to create a new enterprise with significant investment from Joshua Kushner - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law. Meanwhile, investment bank J.P. Morgan were advising on potential investors.

Democratic senator Ron Wyden, who leads an investigation into Jared Kushner, said on Friday: 'Soccer fans around the world are rightfully outraged by this scheme from Infantino and Joshua Kushner to turn the World Cup into just another commodity for private equity to buy up.

'It seems clear from the global backlash that this corrupt plan is unlikely to succeed, but it is just one of dozens of shady deals by Trump's family and close associates to get rich from the presidency.'

A significant number of FIFA members raised concerns from the initial leak of the plan, questioning how such thorough ideas could be developed unilaterally without prior consultation.

Despite FIFA maintaining throughout that there would be a proper consultation period, there were major questions about how that could be achieved when potential investors were already lined up.

UEFA accused FIFA of trying to bribe members with a £30million ($40million) incentive to approve Infantino's plan, with a September 19 deadline to respond to the offer.

Alongside UEFA's protest, sources told the Daily Mail Sport that CONCACAF nations believe he is losing or has already lost their confidence.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham believes Infantino's position is untenable and he is not alone.

Speaking to reporters in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham said: 'This was an outrageous suggestion. The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation.'

Sepp Blatter, Infantino's predecessor, took to social media to renew his attacks on his successor by writing on Friday evening: 'FIFA is not a private equity fund. It is an association with statutes, regulations, and a fiduciary responsibility to protect the global game.

'If you sell football's crown jewels to private investors, you also sell part of the game – especially its soul. Money matters, but it must never become everything.'

Sports.title: 'Some **** from doping is here': How expletive-ridden text messages and a dog walk led to former Wimbledon champion landing a FOUR-YEAR drugs ban
Sports.content:
'Some **** from doping is here': How expletive-ridden text messages and a dog walk led to former Wimbledon champion landing a FOUR-YEAR drugs ban

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Former Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova referred to a doping control officer (DCO) as a '****' and took her dog for a walk after refusing a drugs test which led to a four-year ban from tennis, the tribunal's full written decision on the case has revealed.

Shockwaves were sent through the sport in late June when the 2023 champion was handed the jaw-dropping sanction for barring the DCO from administering a test at her home in Prague at 8pm in December 2025.

Vondrousova claimed that she had been concerned for her safety and suffered 'an acute stress reaction' which had hampered her decision-making, prompting her to sign a document offered by the DCO confirming her refusal.

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) stressed in their decision to sanction the Czech star to the fullest extent came from wanting to ensure the length of a ban refusing a test is the same as testing positive.

'This is to ensure that anyone who is doping cannot serve a shorter ban simply by refusing to be tested,' The ITIA's initial statement confirmed.

The release of Friday's written decisions in full has revealed that the extent to which Vondrousova was deemed to have deliberately refused the test by the independent tribunal.

The full written reasons as to why Marketa Vondrousova received a four-year ban from tennis have been published

'This is a very unfortunate manner in which the player made a decision in the heat of the moment to refuse doping control, in a state of stress and anxiety, with significant consequences,' the tribunal said on Friday, adding that she had not offered 'compelling justification' for refusing the test.

The 26-year-old's defence was threefold: that she had felt unsafe by the arrival of a DCO outside of her dedicated testing window; that the DCO had not followed procedure and had not identified herself to Vondrousova, adding to the threat she felt; and that her decision-making had been impaired by her anxiety and the 'acute stress reaction' which overcame her.

But findings from Vondrousova's WhatsApp messages showed that she had been quick to understand that the DCO was here to test her outside of her requested window when the officer first rang her doorbell and announced herself.

'So like here is ringing some **** from the doping,' Vondrousova messaged her boyfriend, fellow Czech player Andrew Paulson, after first refusing the DCO entry to her apartment, and speaking on the phone to her agent Enric Molina.

Vondrousova and the DCO gave differing accounts as to what happened next, with the former suggesting that they had one more exchange via intercom, and the latter two.

10 minutes after their conversation, Vondrousova left her building to find the DCO still waiting to administer the test as she took her Italian greyhound for a walk.

Vondrousova was then prompted a final time by the DCO that her refusal to take a test would have serious consequences, and signed a form which confirmed her decision before continuing on her dog walk.

'She left,' Vondrousova messaged Molina, before sending him a picture of her completed form. '(T)his is completely f***ed up.' She later posted a statement about the incident, including a picture of the DCO and tagging the ITIA and World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) on her Instagram Story.

Both Vondrousova and Molina claimed to have no knowledge that players could be tested outside of their specified window.

All players in the ITIA testing pool must share a time and location where they are available for testing every day, updating it as necessary, with Vondrousova's scheduled for the morning.

But the organisation consistently stressed that out-of-competition and out-of-hours testing is imperative to ensure clean sport, with the ITIA regularly sharing information on their 'any time, any place' guidelines - which was cited during the tribunal.

Molina had spoken to the organisation that evening at around 9pm, sharing that he had never had a client tested outside of their window and querying whether it was a 'new' initiative.

The ITIA argued that Vondrousova, who has taken 83 tests over the last eight years, could not 'credibly' say that she was not aware of the rules.

After the incident, Vondrousova briefly shared her first account of refusing the test on her Instagram Story

While Vondrousova was deemed to have been aware that she was dealing with a DCO despite her claim that she had not identified her properly, allegations that she had been unsafe were also unpicked.

Vondrousova had cited the horrifying 2016 incident which saw her compatriot Petra Kvitova stabbed after a man pretending to be boiler repairman assaulted her at her home in Prostejov as her reasoning for why she had felt unsafe.

But despite Vondrousova's argument that her apartment was in an area of Prague with high crime rates, the tribunal disagreed, citing that the city was consistently ranked one of the safest in Europe.

Vondrousova had simultaneously admitted that she lived in a 'nice area', and the tribunal found her to have 'exaggerated' similarities to Kvitova's ordeal.

The tribunal also saw her account of feeling unsafe as being at odds with her decision to take her dog for a walk and come face-to-face with the DCO, with Vondrousova describing the small dog as 'not much of a scary dog'.

The player's claim that her 'acute stress reaction' had hampered her decision-making also faltered as neither of the two doctors who had given evidence on Vondrousova's mental wellbeing made themselves available for cross examination.

The ITIA admitted to understanding that the situation would cause some anxiety, but rejected that she had not been able to maintain a high level of cognitive function throughout the incident.

The organisation's own expert added that 'the retrospective nature of the diagnoses made by the experts which the Player relied upon (and their lack of any contemporaneous evidence to support them) presented inherent clinical risks which needed to be treated with caution'.

Vondrousova has the right to appeal the decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), but her sanction began on 22 June of this year, and if served in totality, will see her return to the WTA tour at the age of 30.

Sports.title: England refuse to rule out Ben Stokes retirement U-turn ahead of next summer's Ashes: 'Anything is possible'
Sports.content:
Rob Key has refused to rule out an Ashes return for Ben Stokes next summer, claiming: ‘Anything is possible.’

It was typical of Stokes’ show-stealing ability that on the morning that England director of cricket Key was at Lord’s explaining his decision to reappoint Joe Root as Test captain under new coach Stephen Fleming that a sensational international retirement u-turn was being floated.

Since calling time on his international career at the end of June, Stokes has slipped back into life with Durham and been the subject of an approach by Sydney Sixers to play in Australia’s Big Bash League.

Suspicion remains down under, however, that despite Stokes insisting he will be watching England v Australia matches from hospitality boxes next summer, he will at the age of 36 be back for one last hurrah against the old enemy. Even Australia coach Andrew McDonald spoke of the ‘fairytale’ of ‘one more Ashes’ earlier this week.

Asked if there had been a change of heart, Key said: ‘It would be a brilliant story if he does. He hasn't, but I wouldn't be surprised. Anything is possible with Ben.’

It will potentially be a future conversation for Fleming, whose first involvement with England will be in selection for the first Test against Pakistan on August 19, but whose work on the ground here will not commence until the following month.

Ben Stokes could reverse his decision to retire from international cricket ahead of the Ashes

England's director of cricket Rob Key has stressed that 'anything is possible' for the ex-captain

Identified by England director of cricket Rob Key as the man to haul the Test team out of its current malaise, Fleming was appointed in the knowledge that pre-existing family commitments prevented him from being in place immediately, meaning his first direct involvement will not be for several weeks.

A firm arrival date is yet to be confirmed, but it will coincide with the third Test at Edgbaston between September 9-13 at the earliest. If his first Test in charge is in South Africa next winter, he will have only one on home soil - against Bangladesh next May - ahead of Australia’s arrival.

‘My job, I believe, is to get the best person to do the job. And it wasn't a stipulation for any of the candidates that you had to be there for Pakistan. Had that been the case, that would have limited the field drastically,’ Key said.

‘It was about trying to get the best person to do that. A month ago, this was probably not on a lot of people's radar, certainly myself, Stephen Fleming, as well. In life, you have a lot of things that you have to do that have been planned a long way in advance.’

Fleming, 53, has never coached in first-class cricket before, having spent 18 months with Chennai Super Kings, and their spin-off franchises in South Africa and the United States, in addition to two seasons with Southern Brave in the Hundred.

‘He has worked with the best players in the world. We’ve seen he's up to speed with where the game's at. You don't lose that experience that you have in Test cricket, that you gain as a player, and, more importantly, as a captain,’ argued Key.

‘I've never met anyone who said a bad word about his leadership in Test cricket. I think all of those things put into the mix. I'm as optimistic as ever, really, that we've got the best people to take English cricket forward.’

Key also dismissed any notion that after four years of Fleming’s fellow New Zealander Brendon McCullum in charge, this was a juncture for an English coach to be appointed, saying: ‘I think it’s preferable to have the best coach.’

Adding of Fleming: ‘He knows English cricket really well. He's been close to it. He's obviously played in it. He has a huge amount of love and respect for the county game, in particular, what it did for him as a player, and for his development.

‘So as much as he'll be over in September, he's already sort of very much in the weeds of it all.’

Root quit the captaincy four years ago saying the job had impacted negatively on his life away from the game, particularly through the Covid period of 2020-22, but enjoyed deputising for Stokes in the second Test against New Zealand this summer and was keen to add to his England record 65 caps in charge.

‘Those two, Fleming and Root will be a great complementary pairing to take English cricket forward. He's our best ever batter. Our great cricketer, that can actually now have a chance to captain the side without any of the stuff he had to deal with last time. I'm just so glad that he gets that chance,’ Key reflected, adding that Harry Brook’s time would come further down the line.

Former New Zealand cricketer Stephen Fleming has been named Brendon McCullum's successor, with Joe Root as his captain

‘He's still developing as a player and as a person, to be honest. The Test match captaincy is the biggest job in cricket in England, and I think that it's perfect now with Joe who gets the chance to do it where he can now take this ship forward as the most senior player by a long, long way and Harry can now continue on the project he's done in the white-ball job and continue learning how to become an outstanding leader of a cricket team.

‘You've got the 2027 World Cup, all of those things, and at some stage Harry Brook will be an outstanding Test captain of England cricket. I just didn't feel the time was right now.’

Whether Key will still be around to make the appointment remains to be seen, having survived a post-Ashes review in January.

So, after losing 4-1 to Australia, did he feel lucky to keep his job? Did he fear the sack? Consider his own position?

‘I think all of the above. This is a job where you're constantly under pressure all the time. There's uncertainty in it all the time. That's part of being in this role. How close I came (to being sacked), I don't know. How close I came myself, what I was thinking, I obviously know. But it's been a good few months – and even before that – where you're constantly thinking: are you the right person? What is the thing you’ve got to do? Are you the person to put that in place? I believe I am, but that's for the people above me to decide all the time.’

Sports.title: 'Clicky Ponting' is just the tip of the iceberg. I've played club cricket for decades and these are the wildest stories of cheating, from vaseline to elastic bands and fattening up umpires to a trail of sawdust
Sports.content:
At the snap of a finger, Brian Devine became English cricket's Public Enemy No 1 - and 'Clicky Ponting' was born.

An investigation is underway in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League after several videos appeared to show Saltburn CC slip fielder Devine clicking his fingers as the ball passed the batsman to mimic the sound of an edge.

Devine’s aim is as clear as it is shocking – to con the umpire into giving his team a wicket. The spirit of cricket this most definitely is not, and Devine and his team’s actions have shocked the cricketing world (and his now former sponsor, the local curry house).

But Saltburn are hardly the only team over the years to bend the rules – and in some cases, openly break them.

The 2018 scandal which saw three Australian cricketers receive long bans for their part in a sandpaper ball tampering plot and Alex Carey’s controversial 2023 Ashes run out of Jonny Bairstow are high-profile recent examples in international cricket.

And similar incidents to Saltburn’s have taken place regularly at grassroots level, too. We've gathered together the best (or worst, depending on your view) from decades' worth of experience in the glory, and shame, of club cricket.

Brian Devine, the man at the centre of the 'Clicky Ponting' club cricket scandal

Devine (circled) is being investigated by his local league, with allegations he clicked his fingers when the ball passed an opposition player's bat to simulate the sound of an edge

Vaseline assistance

Sunny Agnihotri played for West Blatchington Cricket Club between 2002 and 2008, and won the Sussex Invitation League Division 1 twice.

When they met Crawley Eagles, the opposition would put Vaseline on their bats ahead of the match. The idea was that when the ball nicked the outside edge, it wouldn’t make so much noise.

‘We asked the umpires about it and they said it’s not against the rules,' said Agnihotri. 'They were also definitely rummaging in their pockets between balls, so we knew something untoward was going on. They made it so obvious. The dark arts happen a lot.’

Local rivals Brighton Insurance would waste time when they batted first to use up the daylight.

Between a dismissed batsman walking off and a new one replacing him, you had three minutes. But on the field of play, you could still get padded up. Brighton players would throw all their equipment on the pitch and take longer than three minutes without punishment.

‘They would take double the time so that when it was our turn to bat, it would be gloomier,’ Agnihotri said.

Izzy Martin

But similar incidents to Saltburn’s have taken place regularly at grassroots level too

It’s not always the players…

There was an umpire in the Leicestershire leagues during the late 1990s renowned for getting a twitchy trigger finger the closer it got to opening time at the bar.

When he started to get really thirsty, he would whisper under his breath: ‘Next one that hits the pads… give it a big appeal’ and, when the fielding side did, he duly obliged.

A trick of one former Leicestershire Premier Division champion team was to send beers to the umpires' room and offer them sweets while in the field in a bid to get them on-side so decisions would fall in their favour.

‘Where there’s a will, there’s a way,’ said one member of the side. Their wicketkeeper was also known for trying to kick the stumps down and appealing that the batter had been bowled.

I remember playing in a county age-group match in which one fielder on the team, who went on to become a professional, took a catch on the half-volley and celebrated as though it was clean.

Another team in the Leicestershire leagues was once accused of sending the same batsman in twice in different kit, until their plan was foiled when the star man was spotted by the home team scorer through her binoculars.

Anonymous

No matter the spread of the 'spirit of cricket', the laws are always open to a little bending

Let's all band together

I played in a match many, many years ago where three of our batsmen were given out caught behind, all of them swearing blind they never got a nick on the ball.

After some brief research, we realised the wicketkeeper had an elastic band attached to his glove, which he snapped against it to make the noise of a nick, fooling the umpire into giving it out in a similar trick to Saltburn's.

Anonymous

Saltburn CC, which has now come under international scrutiny after Devine was caught on camera

Questionable declaration

In 2017, Pembrokeshire rivals Carew and Cresselly took on each other in the final game of that year’s West Wales league season. Carew were top, Cresselly second.

Cresselly faced a difficult task that day, but not an impossible one. Carew’s lead was 21 points and a win was worth 20, but then you had the bonuses to consider – a point for every 40 runs up to 200 and a point for every two wickets.

In short, it boiled down to this: if Cresselly could win and take two more bonus points than Carew, they’d snatch the title. But Carew had a devilish plan.

As far as I’ve been told in my retracing of the steps, they even checked the rules with the umpire before the game, found their read of the situation was accurate, and set about putting it in action.

Batting first, they declared on just 18 for one. First there was shock, then revulsion. It was filthy and entirely legal.

Cresselly were welcome to the 20 points, which they achieved by knocking off the chase in just a few overs, but the opportunity for any bonuses had been snatched clean off the table. It was Carew’s title by a single point.

Riath Al-Samarrai

Saltburn weren't the first side to mimick an edge - one of our contributors played against a team whose wicketkeeper used an elastic band!

Bailout

One day, while in action for Saffron Plantationers – a village side in Quendon near Saffron Walden in Essex – I was at the crease with my team needing four runs to win.

My plan was to charge the bowler and hit the ball down the ground. I was still deep in my crease as the bowler ran in. But his delivery was short of a length, so I stepped back and pulled it for four. As I did so, however, I trod gently on my own stumps and off came the bails.

But instead of me being given out hit wicket, as I should have been, everyone at the ground watched the ball disappear to the boundary. Not seeing the bails were off, the umpire signalled four and the end of the game.

After a while, the opposition wicketkeeper noticed something off and questioned why the bails were no longer on the stumps. But I just kept walking off the pitch as technically, the game was now over.

It was one I got away with but I’m not proud of my actions – I got caught up in the moment and should have fessed up. I do seem to remember sleeping OK that night though!

Matt Gatward

Australia captain Steve Smith breaks down at a press conference in light of his side's Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal in 2018

Another cheat bites the dust

I remember playing for Eynsford at Chislehurst and West Kent one year in the Kent leagues.

Eynsford were interrupted in their victory charge by a short, sharp shower. After 20 minutes off the field to allow the pitch to dry, the umpires suggested a restart and asked Chislehurst to put out some sawdust for the bowlers to allow for better grip.

The response from the Chislehurst captain was: ‘Sorry, we haven’t got any.’

Unfortunately for him, a visiting member had seen him put a bag from the club shed into his car boot, leaving a trail of sawdust between the two locations. When called out, he had the front to say he knew nothing about it!

Anonymous

No age allowances

Not cheating as such, though by way of intimidation it comes close to the line.

I distinctly remember my senior debut in the adult leagues. As someone who had a modicum of talent and was playing Northamptonshire junior cricket at the time, I was chucked in alongside grown men aged just 13 in a bid to speed up my development.

Cricket is meant to be a sport played by gentlemen - but don't be surprised if you hear a few expletives at a village game, no matter how young the person on the receiving end is

Playing for South Northamptonshire village side Marston St Lawrence, I faced a tough task against experienced cricketers. Unsurprisingly given my youth, I struggled with the bat, playing and missing repeatedly.

I was as frustrated as anyone on the field, but my tender years didn’t stop me getting both barrels from the bowler who I couldn’t lay a bat on. I’ll never forget his words.

‘Just hit it, you c***!’ he shouted at me, his words starting off an unpleasant exchange with my more senior partner at the other end.

I was so shocked to be verbally abused at that age, I could not muster a reply. However, in the years since I've thought regularly about what I should have said.

If I had my time again, the response would have been: ‘I’m f***ing trying!’

Alex Bywater

Sports.title: Spain's 'down to earth' World Cup hero Marc Cucurella praised for wholesome interaction with postman as he lets him wear his winner's medal
Sports.content:
Spain star Marc Cucurella thrilled his local postman after the World Cup winner offered him the medal he won Stateside last month to wear after dropping off his deliveries.

The former Chelsea defender has been a Horsham resident for some years, moving there after a previous home was targeted by burglars shortly after his 2023 transfer to the west London club.

The West Sussex enclave provided a peaceful sanctuary for Cucurella and his young family, with locals frequently sharing their positive experiences on social media if they crossed the defender's path.

But few can claim the experience his postman Gary enjoyed during one of his last rounds for the departing Real Madrid star.

Sharing his story with Horsham's social media account, the postman said: 'Had the pleasure of chatting to local World Cup winner Marc Cucurella while delivering his post today.

'Very nice, down-to-earth guy. Let me hold his winners' medal.

Marc Cucurella was praised for his thoughtful interaction with his local postman in Horsham

Gary the postman was allowed to try on Cucurella's gold World Cup winners' medal

'I reckon I am the first Englishman to hold a World Cup winners' medal in 60 years.'

Fans were quick to show their support for Cucurella's once-in-a-lifetime gesture, with one commenting: 'The biggest and greatest accolade for any football player. And he was kind enough to share that.'

Another added: 'Amazing stuff. He sounds like a really nice guy.'

One chronicler of life in Horsham wrote: 'Amazing. We keep hearing great things and sorry to be losing him. Wishing him the best of luck in his new adventures'.

In the photograph, Cucurella showed off his new braided hairstyle, a notable departure from his iconic curls.

Switching up his look has been just one piece of the 28-year-old's post-World Cup celebrations, with the player also making good on his promise to ink the face of his manager Luis de la Fuente on his body.

Horsham's social media account has previously shared snapshots of Cucurella's life in the south of England, and cheered on their 'local boy' in Spain's World Cup final against Argentina.

Since becoming a resident in the market town, Cucurella and his family have slotted in seamlessly to local life, interacting with other parents at their children's schools and even becoming regular visitors to Indian restaurant Hen & Chicken.

Life in Horsham is likely one of the reasons that Cucurella's partner Claudia Rodriguez admitted that she was feeling mixed emotions about his move back to Spain to join Real Madrid.

Posting on Instagram after the £47.4m deal was announced, she wrote: 'I don't know how to say goodbye to my home.'

'Thank you to everyone who has been a part of this experience; I feel so lucky for everything we've shared these past years. I arrived with two babies and I'm leaving with two little boys and a British girl, and I don't know how I'm going to explain to them that Chelsea is no longer part of our lives.

'Everything we've experienced these past years has been a pure learning experience; we've lived through it all, but above all, we've enjoyed this journey. Thank you to everyone who has been a part of this chapter of our lives, thank you to my girls, whom I'm going to miss a lot, and thank you to every Blue I've met. I wish you all the best; London will always be Blue.'

Cucurella's partner Claudia Rodriguez spoke last month about her sadness at leaving England

Rodriguez's comments come in stark contrast to how she felt before the family moved into their latest house in England.

In the wake of the traumatising burglary, the influencer told Daily Mail Sport that she had been afraid to go to sleep.

'The security is one of things I'm more worried about,' Rodriguez admitted. 'It's very hard when you are not comfortable at your home.

'I'm scared to sleep alone with my kids, for example. So for today, the most important thing for me, I think, is the security of me and my family.'

Sports.title: Manchester United keeping tabs on Newcastle defender Lewis Hall ahead of potential summer move - plus latest on Marcus Rashford's Old Trafford future
Sports.content:
Manchester United keeping tabs on Newcastle defender Lewis Hall ahead of potential summer move - plus latest on Marcus Rashford's Old Trafford future

Manchester United remain appreciative of Newcastle United left back Lewis Hall but acknowledge it would be a difficult transfer to pull off.

The club are still assessing market movements, checking who is available at the right price, before deciding on their next priority position.

Another midfielder has been at the forefront of their thinking while another forward still hinges on Marcus Rashford departing. Despite interest from other clubs, as it stands, he remains likely to start the season at United.

Cover at left back is required as United are going into the new season with Luke Shaw, who has one year left on contract, as their only recognised senior option in that position.

Harry Amass can cover but has been told he would be better seeking first team opportunities elsewhere.

Manchester United admire Newcastle and England left back Lewis Hall

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise once Matthias Jaissle is in place.

Though midfielder Bruno Guimaraes may yet join Arsenal, if they make a formal offer over £80million, the club want to add players to ensure they are competitive.

Sports.title: Humiliated FIFA president Gianni Infantino accepts defeat in controversial plot to sell the World Cup in embarrassing U-turn - now he is in a fight to save his job
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Gianni Infantino has been humiliated after his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup died thanks to the heroics of UEFA, CONCACAF, the AFC and two members of the FIFA hierarchy.

While it appears the FIFA president will fight on to save his job, the Swiss football administrator has abandoned his proposal to sell £3.1billion ($4.1bn) in shares in FIFA tournaments to private investors.

Infantino said: 'The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

'And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders.

Join the discussion Should football's biggest tournaments ever be open to private investment and ownership?

Gianni Infantino waves goodbye to his unilateral plans for private investment in FIFA

Infantino had hoped to create a new enterprise with significant investment from Joshua Kushner (pictured) - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law

Carlos Cordeiro, senior adviser to Infantino and member of the White House World Cup task force 'As a Senior Advisor to the FIFA President, a former banker, and a lifelong football fan, I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup. 'Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game. 'Selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification. 'Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions. Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football? 'It has been the privilege of a lifetime to serve FIFA for more than five years and to work alongside dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game. I hope they, too, will speak up, because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it.'

'Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place.

'Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

'Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, and particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.'

The statement marks an embarrassing u-turn for Infantino, less than 24 hours after he attempted to clarify his plans - blaming the media for misconstruing them.

On Friday, the AFC became the third confederation to reject Gianni Infantino's proposal to raise private capital for the commercial and operational management of FIFA tournaments.

The decision followed CONCACAF's rejection on Thursday and came after UEFA announced a boycott of FIFA competitions. New Zealand Football also objected to the plans, despite the OFC delaying a continent-wide response.

One international football insider told Daily Mail Sport: 'UEFA's response is at the nuclear button end of the spectrum, which is impressive. We thought Infantino would survive the Trump refereeing intervention - but he has overreached this time.'

According to Sky News, UEFA are also thought to have asked for binding assurances that 'FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership' to end their boycott.

It became clear on Friday afternoon that Infantino did not have the support to proceed with his plans, with the opposing nations rising to a staggering 135 - 64 per cent of the FIFA membership.

The proposal appeared to reach a terminal stage when Carlos Cordeiro, senior advisor to Gianni Infantino, announced his resignation from FIFA - becoming the first internal dissident.

Six hours later, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour turned against the president - risking his job by criticising the plans and calling on nations to dethrone Infantino. Lamour admitted FIFA Forward Enterprise was the brainchild of 'one person' as he landed a critical blow to the FIFA president.

Carlos Cordeiro (left) quit as an advisor to Gianni Infantino (centre) on Friday

Kevin Lamour, FIFA's Chief Operating Officer 'What has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination. 'To put it very clearly and directly: the project that has sparked so much controversy and debate is not a FIFA project. It is even less a project of FIFA's administration. It is the project of one person. FIFA's own administration was deceived. 'Not only must this project not go ahead but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions. Everyone must take responsibility. Because it is becoming increasingly difficult for FIFA's administration to work under these conditions. 'Our mission is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service. A president must bring people together, unite them, and inspire them. Today, we are experiencing the opposite. 'I have no authority to speak on behalf of my colleagues, and perhaps I am mistaken. But my feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for FIFA, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us. That saddens me. The ball is now in the court of those who have the power to change things. 'I know I have a duty of loyalty to my employer. But I also, and above all, have a duty of loyalty to certain values and to the upbringing I have received, and a duty to support my colleagues. And if that means I lose my job, then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight.'

Infantino had hoped to create a new enterprise with significant investment from Joshua Kushner - brother of Jared, Donald Trump's son-in-law. Meanwhile, investment bank J.P. Morgan were advising on potential investors.

Democratic senator Ron Wyden, who leads an investigation into Jared Kushner, said on Friday: 'Soccer fans around the world are rightfully outraged by this scheme from Infantino and Joshua Kushner to turn the World Cup into just another commodity for private equity to buy up.

'It seems clear from the global backlash that this corrupt plan is unlikely to succeed, but it is just one of dozens of shady deals by Trump's family and close associates to get rich from the presidency.'

A significant number of FIFA members raised concerns from the initial leak of the plan, questioning how such thorough ideas could be developed unilaterally without prior consultation.

Despite FIFA maintaining throughout that there would be a proper consultation period, there were major questions about how that could be achieved when potential investors were already lined up.

UEFA accused FIFA of trying to bribe members with a £30million ($40m) incentive to approve Infantino's plan, with a September 19 deadline to respond to the offer.

Those plans, though, are now dead in the water after Infantino scrapped them at half past midnight (UK) on Saturday.

There is growing opposition to Infantino's presidency, with sources telling Daily Mail Sport that CONCACAF nations believe he is losing or has already lost their confidence.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham believes Infantino's position is untenable and he is not alone.

Speaking to reporters in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham said: 'This was an outrageous suggestion. The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation.'

With the controversy surrounding Infantino, member nations could still trigger a vote of no confidence. The threshold to initiate the process is 46 FIFA member associations.

UEFA and their member associations are yet to be drawn on that matter. Infantino is seeking a fourth term in next year's elections.

Sepp Blatter, Infantino's predecessor, took to social media to renew his attacks on his successor by writing on Friday evening: 'FIFA is not a private equity fund. It is an association with statutes, regulations, and a fiduciary responsibility to protect the global game.

'If you sell football's crown jewels to private investors, you also sell part of the game – especially its soul. Money matters, but it must never become everything.'

Sports.title: Leandro Paredes facing minimum nine-game ban – but could avoid FIFA's Argentina punishment
Sports.content:
Leandro Paredes facing minimum nine-game ban – but could avoid FIFA's Argentina punishment

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes is facing a nine-game ban for violent conduct in the aftermath of the World Cup final - but could avoid punishment altogether after a surprise admission

View 2 Images Leandro Paredes could get off scot-free (Image: Image Photo Agency, Getty Images)

Leandro Paredes could avoid serving any suspension despite facing multiple FIFA disciplinary charges following Argentina's explosive World Cup final defeat to Spain. The Boca Juniors midfielder is under investigation for three separate counts of violent conduct after tempers erupted in the aftermath of last month's showpiece.

‌



While the charges leave him facing the prospect of a lengthy international ban, comments made after the final have opened up the possibility of an unexpected escape route. The incidents involving Paredes unfolded after the final whistle, with the Argentina international repeatedly confronting Spain players as emotions spilt over.

‌



TV footage appeared to show him kick and shove Eric Garcia before jabbing the defender in the throat. Moments later, he allegedly targeted Gavi, grabbing the midfielder before throwing him to the ground during another heated exchange.

‌



Article 14 of the FIFA Disciplinary Code states that every individual act of aggression carries a minimum three-match suspension. If Paredes is found guilty on all three charges, he could therefore receive a ban totalling nine matches.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

FIFA open disciplinary proceedings after Argentina's Falklands banner vs England READ MORE :

FIFA come down hard on Argentina stars as charges handed out after World Cup final brawl READ MORE :

However, the 32-year-old recently hinted that he could retire from international football, potentially allowing him to sidestep any immediate punishment.

‌



When asked about his future with the national team a few days after the final, Paredes replied: "I don't know. It's a process: you have to digest it, think it through, avoid making rushed decisions, and it's certainly something that needs to be discussed."

Although international retirement would initially help Paredes circumvent a prospective punishment for violent conduct, FIFA can invoke Article 70 to extend the sanction worldwide - as it did when Luis Suarez was banned from all football-related activities for four months after biting Giorgio Chiellini at the 2014 World Cup.

That type of intervention is generally reserved for the game's most severe disciplinary offences, meaning Paredes is unlikely to fall into the same category.

‌



View 2 Images Paredes (centre) has been charged with three counts of assault by FIFA

FIFA has not yet delivered its final ruling and, although a nine-match suspension remains possible under the disciplinary regulations and previous precedents, a ban of five or six games is widely viewed as the more probable outcome.

Paredes is not the only Argentina figure facing disciplinary action. Nahuel Molina has also been charged with two acts of aggression following the final - one completed and one attempted - while assistant coach Roberto Ayala is the subject of a separate aggression charge that could likewise result in a suspension.

‌



FIFA has also launched proceedings against the Argentine Football Association (AFA) over alleged discriminatory chants and gestures, breaches of match and security regulations, delays to kick-off, inappropriate messages displayed by players and supporters, and the throwing of objects.

Should those allegations be upheld, the AFA could receive a significant financial punishment and, in the most serious circumstances, face partial or complete stadium closures for future home fixtures.
