The Vessel: Engineering ‘Abundance’

The Errea Wittu is not just another ship; it is a sprawling industrial facility built to operate in the deep waters off Guyana’s coast. Constructed by MODEC, a global leader in floating production systems, the vessel is purpose-built for the Uaru field. Its name, ‘Errea Wittu,’ was chosen to reflect the prosperity the project is expected to bring, translating to ‘abundance’ in the local Warrau language.

The Uaru Project and the 250,000 Bpd Milestone

The Uaru project represents the fifth major development within the prolific Stabroek Block. ExxonMobil and its co-venturers, Hess Corporation and CNOOC, officially sanctioned the project with a final investment decision on April 27, 2023. From the outset, the consortium targeted a 2026 startup date, a timeline that the vessel’s departure now appears to be meeting.

Transforming Guyana’s National Output

The arrival of the Errea Wittu marks a pivotal moment for Guyana’s economy. On November 12, 2025, ExxonMobil announced that production across its existing three operating FPSOs had reached a combined milestone of 900,000 barrels of oil daily. This figure already placed Guyana among the world’s fastest-growing oil producers.

A Fleet of Giants in the Stabroek Block

To understand the significance of the Errea Wittu, it is essential to view it within the context of ExxonMobil’s broader Guyanese armada. The first vessel, Liza Destiny, began production in 2019, proving the viability of the basin. It was followed by Liza Unity, Payara, and Yellowtail, each progressively larger and more complex.

Economic Implications for Guyana

The sheer volume of oil flowing from vessels like the Errea Wittu is rewriting Guyana’s fiscal destiny. The country’s GDP has experienced explosive growth, and oil revenues are funding massive infrastructure projects, from new hospitals and schools to highways and a deep-water port. The production sharing agreement with the consortium ensures that the government receives a significant share of the profits, alongside royalties.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the name 'Errea Wittu' mean?

The name ‘Errea Wittu’ translates to ‘abundance’ in the Warrau language, an indigenous language of Guyana. The name was chosen to reflect the significant oil resources the FPSO is designed to unlock.

How much oil will the Guyana FPSO Errea Wittu produce?

The Errea Wittu is designed with a production capacity of approximately 250,000 barrels of oil per day. It also has the capacity to treat 540 million cubic feet of gas per day and inject 350,000 barrels of water per day.

When will the Errea Wittu start producing oil?

ExxonMobil sanctioned the Uaru project in April 2023 with a target for first oil in 2026. The vessel is currently in transit or nearing deployment, consistent with that startup timeline.

World.title: Jamaica Holness Appeal Dismissed as Court Lifts Case Stay
World.content:
Jamaica

Key Facts —Ruling Date The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on July 31, 2026, considered on paper by a panel of Justices Frank Williams, Marcia Dunbar-Green and Frank Brown, with Justice Paulette Williams delivering the decision. —Legal Grounds The appellate court found the Supreme Court judge made no error of fact, law, or principle in refusing to strike out portions of an Integrity Commission affidavit. —Case Status The stay of proceedings was lifted, allowing the judicial review to proceed in the Supreme Court. —Core Dispute The case concerns the Integrity Commission’s 2024 investigation report into Prime Minister Holness’ financial affairs. —Legal Team Response Holness’ legal team said the appeal primarily concerned his requests for un-redacted documents from the Integrity Commission, that the ruling does not adversely affect the case, and that they will continue to pursue disclosure. The commission was unable to certify his 2021 declarations and referred matters onward; no charge has been laid and the allegations remain unproven.

The Jamaica Holness appeal against a procedural ruling in his ongoing legal battle with the Integrity Commission was dismissed by the nation’s Court of Appeal on Friday, July 31, 2026. The appellate court lifted a stay that had paused proceedings, clearing the way for a judicial review of an investigation into the Prime Minister’s financial affairs to advance in the Supreme Court.

Jamaicas Court of Appeal ruled on Prime Minister Andrew Holness appeal. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Court of Appeal Ruling

The Court of Appeal dismissed Prime Minister Andrew Holness’ challenge to a lower court’s decision that refused to strike out portions of an affidavit filed by Integrity Commission official Craig Beresford. Justice Paulette Williams delivered the ruling on the morning of July 31, 2026, according to Nationwide Radio reports.

The appellate panel determined that the Supreme Court judge had handled the procedural issues correctly and committed no error of fact, law, or principle. The judgment stated that the lower court correctly treated the affidavit evidence as relevant, applied the right legal principles, and acted within her case-management powers when she struck out parts of an amended fixed-date claim form. Those struck-out portions were seen as an attempt to re-litigate matters that had already been decided.

As an immediate consequence, the stay of proceedings that had been in place was lifted. This procedural move allows the substantive judicial review to move forward in the Supreme Court without further delay on this specific interlocutory issue.

Background of the Integrity Commission Probe

The legal dispute originates from an Integrity Commission investigation into Prime Minister Holness’ financial affairs. The probe culminated in a 2024 investigation report that has been the subject of intense political scrutiny. The Integrity Commission is a statutory anti-corruption body in Jamaica tasked with monitoring the financial conduct of public officials.

The Commission’s report has been linked to broader questions around illicit enrichment and the handling of Holness’ statutory declarations. However, it is critical to note that the July 31, 2026, appeal decision was strictly an interlocutory ruling on an affidavit-striking application. It was not a final finding on the substantive allegations of illicit enrichment or any other misconduct. No confirmed report indicates that Holness has been found guilty of illicit enrichment or charged with any crime in relation to this probe.

A separate Supreme Court record exists under the case number SU2024CV03844, titled Andrew Holness et al v Beresford Graig et al. The Integrity Commission’s official court-matters page lists that matter as ‘On Appeal,’ highlighting the multi-layered nature of the litigation.

Timeline of the Litigation

The legal battle has unfolded over several key dates. On December 6, 2024, Holness was granted leave for judicial review in the underlying case, according to a Supreme Court judgment cited by the Integrity Commission. This initial step allowed him to challenge the Commission’s processes in court.

Nearly a year later, on July 31, 2025, Justice Althea Jarrett gave oral reasons in the interlocutory applications and granted leave to appeal, with a stay pending that appeal. This set the stage for the appellate review exactly one year later, on July 31, 2026, when the Court of Appeal dismissed Holness’ appeal and lifted the stay, allowing the core judicial review to resume.

Political Consequences and Next Steps

The dismissal of the appeal represents a procedural setback for Prime Minister Holness, keeping the Integrity Commission’s scrutiny in the public eye. While the ruling does not equate to a finding of wrongdoing, it ensures that the judicial review of the investigation will proceed, potentially prolonging a politically sensitive narrative.

Holness’ legal team moved quickly to manage the political fallout, stating that the ruling does not adversely affect the overall case. They emphasized that they have already obtained a wide set of documents from the respondents through the discovery process. The team maintains that it is still entitled to the unredacted documents that were the subject of the appeal and will now focus on the substantive legal issues still before the court.

The continuation of the case ensures that questions around transparency and the Prime Minister’s financial declarations will remain a focal point for opposition parties and civil society groups as the judicial review moves toward a hearing on its merits.

Understanding the Legal Stakes

The distinction between an interlocutory appeal and a final merits ruling is crucial for understanding the current state of the case. An interlocutory appeal challenges a judge’s decision on a procedural or evidentiary matter before the main trial concludes. The Court of Appeal’s decision solely affirmed that the lower court judge managed the pre-trial process correctly.

The substantive judicial review will now examine the legality of the Integrity Commission’s actions and processes, not necessarily the truth of the allegations in its report. The Prime Minister’s legal strategy appears focused on challenging the Commission’s procedures and seeking full disclosure of unredacted documents, which his team argues are necessary for a fair hearing. The lifting of the stay means these arguments will now be litigated on their merits in the Supreme Court.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Court of Appeal rule in the Jamaica Holness appeal?

The Court of Appeal dismissed Prime Minister Andrew Holness’ appeal on July 31, 2026. The court found the Supreme Court judge made no error in refusing to strike out parts of an Integrity Commission affidavit, and it lifted the stay that had paused the judicial review proceedings.

Does this ruling mean Andrew Holness was found guilty of illicit enrichment?

No. The July 31, 2026, ruling was an interlocutory decision on a procedural matter regarding affidavit evidence. It was not a final ruling on the substantive allegations of illicit enrichment or any other misconduct. No confirmed report indicates Holness has been found guilty or charged.

What happens next in the Integrity Commission case against the Prime Minister?

With the stay of proceedings lifted, the judicial review will now move forward in the Supreme Court. Holness’ legal team says it will focus on the substantive legal issues and continues to seek unredacted documents from the Integrity Commission.

World.title: Bahamas Blackout Hits Nassau as Grid Failures Mount
World.content:
Bahamas

Key Facts —New Providence Cause An electrical fire at the Blue Hills Power Station, caused by a suspected underground cable fault, led to the explosion of a 15MVA transformer on July 30, 2026. —Restoration Status Bahamas Power and Light restored electricity to approximately 50% of consumers on New Providence by 7:18 a.m., though the final full-restoration time remains unconfirmed. —Cat Island Outage A turbocharger failure and subsequent oil leak caused a fire on the Cat Island 1 engine on June 6, 2026, causing an outage restored in stages over about 22 hours on June 6-7, eight weeks before the Nassau failure. —Tourism Impact The Cat Island outage forced the cancellation of the closing night of the Rake & Scrape Festival, directly impacting cultural tourism on the island. —Other Islands Affected These were separate, unrelated failures rather than one national blackout; further outages were reported in 2026 across Eleuthera, Exuma, Abaco, and Grand Bahama due to causes ranging from lightning to a bomb threat.

A severe Bahamas blackout plunged the entire island of New Providence into darkness on July 30, 2026, after an electrical fire at the Blue Hills Power Station caused a transformer to explode. The incident was the most dramatic in a series of island-wide power failures across the archipelago, exposing vulnerabilities in the nation’s electrical grid and disrupting life for residents and tourists alike.

Power infrastructure in the Bahamas after repeated grid failures. (Photo internet reproduction)

New Providence Plunged Into Darkness

The complete loss of power supply across New Providence, the nation’s most populous island, was triggered by a suspected underground cable fault. According to a report from Tribune242, this fault caused the explosion of a 15MVA transformer at the Blue Hills Power Station. Bahamas Power and Light (BPL) crews responded to the emergency, and by 7:18 a.m., the utility confirmed that electricity had been restored to approximately 50% of consumers. The staged restoration brought power back to areas including Bonita Bay, Winton, Yellow Elder, Stapleton Gardens, Paradise Island, East Street South, South Beach Estates, Pinewood, Marshall Road, Bamboo Town, Fox Hill Road, Gladstone Road, Firetrail Road, Carmichael Road, and Sears Road. The final full-restoration time for the entire island was not immediately available in public reports.

Government and Utility Response

The government responded to the New Providence crisis by stating that the Prime Minister’s office was working directly with BPL to manage the situation. Officials reported that all engines were back up and running and that technical teams were systematically bringing remaining areas online as the system was carefully calibrated. The incident highlighted the fragility of the aging power infrastructure, with separate 2026 reports noting that outages had previously affected critical facilities like Princess Margaret Hospital and forced some businesses to close, implying significant economic and public service disruptions beyond the immediate loss of electricity.

Cat Island Fire Cancels Cultural Festival

A separate island-wide Bahamas blackout struck Cat Island on June 6, 2026, with a direct and quantifiable impact on tourism. BPL reported that a fire involving the Cat Island 1 (CI 1) engine began at about 8:30 p.m. after the turbocharger failed and leaked oil onto the exhaust manifold. The resulting blaze caused a total power loss across the island. BPL explicitly stated that the outage affected the closing night of the Rake & Scrape Festival, a significant cultural event, leading to its cancellation. Full power was not restored until 6:14 p.m. on June 7, 2026, meaning residents and visitors were without electricity for approximately 21 hours and 46 minutes.

A Wave of Island-Wide Outages

The incidents in New Providence and Cat Island were not isolated. A pattern of widespread power failures affected multiple Bahamian islands throughout 2026. On March 30, BPL reported successive outages across Eleuthera caused by system faults, with severe weather including lightning and a pole fire in South Eleuthera contributing to the problems. In June, Eyewitness News reported an outage on Exuma affecting about 1,500 customers from Hermitage to Williams Town, alongside a smaller outage for about 40 customers in Farmer’s Cay and a brief disruption for roughly 190 customers on Mayaguana.

Abaco, Grand Bahama, and Systemic Strain

The strain on the electrical grid continued into July. Tribune242 reported weekend outages across both Abaco and New Providence, with parts of Abaco experiencing an 18-hour power loss. The causes cited for these disruptions included lightning, cable faults, damaged equipment, transformer problems, and heavy electricity demand. In a separate and unusual incident on Grand Bahama, the Grand Bahama Power Company was forced to conduct an emergency shutdown after a bomb threat, cutting power across large parts of that island for hours. While no quantified tourism losses in US dollars are available for these events, the repeated disruptions to businesses, hospitals, and cultural festivals paint a clear picture of a utility struggling to maintain reliable service.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the major Bahamas blackout on New Providence?

The island-wide blackout on New Providence on July 30, 2026, was caused by an electrical fire at the Blue Hills Power Station. A suspected underground cable fault triggered the explosion of a 15MVA transformer, leading to a complete loss of power supply across the island.

How did the Bahamas blackout affect tourism?

The most directly confirmed tourism impact was on Cat Island, where an island-wide outage forced the cancellation of the closing night of the Rake & Scrape Festival. While no specific US dollar losses are quantified for other islands, widespread outages forced business closures and disrupted services, implying a broader negative impact on the visitor economy.

Which islands were affected by power outages in 2026?

Confirmed widespread or island-wide outages occurred on New Providence, Cat Island, Eleuthera, Exuma, Abaco, and Grand Bahama. Smaller outages were also reported on Mayaguana and Farmer’s Cay, with causes ranging from equipment fires and lightning to a bomb threat.

World.title: Brazil Air Force Interception Downs Suspect Plane From Bolivia
World.content:
Brazil

Key Facts —Date of incident Friday, 31 July 2026 —Intercepting aircraft Two A-29 Super Tucano fighters deployed by the Brazilian Aerospace Operations Command (COMAE) —Origin of suspect aircraft Bolivia; entered Brazilian airspace without a flight plan, radio contact, or identified registration —Outcome The aircraft performed a forced landing on an unprepared strip in Mato Grosso do Sul, roughly 200 km north of Campo Grande —Post-landing status After detention shots (tiro de detencao) under Brazils airspace-policing rules, the aircraft was found abandoned; no crew was located and no drugs or illicit cargo were found, with no arrests made

In a decisive Brazil Air Force interception on Friday, 31 July 2026, two A-29 Super Tucano fighters forced a suspect aircraft arriving from Bolivia to make an emergency landing on an improvised airstrip in the interior of Mato Grosso do Sul. The operation, coordinated by the Brazilian Aerospace Operations Command (COMAE), underscores the nation’s intensifying crackdown on unauthorized cross-border air traffic, though the occupants of the abandoned plane remain at large.

Brazilian Air Force A-29 Super Tucanos intercepted a suspect aircraft. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Interception Operation

The Brazilian Air Force (FAB) scrambled two A-29 Super Tucano light attack and advanced training aircraft after a suspicious plane was detected entering Brazilian airspace from the south of Bolivia. According to official reports published on the day of the incident, the aircraft had no filed flight plan, maintained no radio communication with air traffic control, and was operating with an unidentified registration.

Under the coordination of COMAE, the FAB pilots followed standard airspace policing protocols. After the suspect aircraft repeatedly failed to comply with orders to identify itself and alter course, the fighter pilots escalated the situation, compelling the plane to descend. The aircraft ultimately executed a forced landing on an unprepared or improvised strip in a remote area of Mato Grosso do Sul, approximately 200 kilometers (about 124 miles) north of the state capital, Campo Grande.

Aircraft Found Abandoned

When authorities reached the landing site, the aircraft was found abandoned. Reports available from the day of the incident do not confirm that any crew members or occupants were located or detained. The immediate area was searched, but no arrests were reported in connection with this specific event.

Crucially, the available reports do not confirm the presence of any cargo, drugs, or contraband aboard the abandoned plane. While the forced landing is a confirmed outcome of the Brazil Air Force interception, the final legal disposition of the aircraft – whether it was formally seized or destroyed – was not stated in the coverage. The reports only confirm it was found deserted after the unscheduled landing.

Brazil’s Border-Airspace Crackdown Framework

This 31 July incident is part of a broader, ongoing effort by Brazilian authorities to police the nation’s vast and porous borders, particularly against unsanctioned flights from neighboring drug-producing countries. While the July 2026 reports explicitly describe the action as an “operation of airspace policing” under COMAE, they do not explicitly name the well-known “Operation Ostium” (Operação Ostium) in connection with this specific event.

Operation Ostium is a long-running joint operation involving the FAB and other security forces, specifically designed to strengthen the shield along Brazil’s frontiers. The operation routinely uses A-29 Super Tucanos for interception missions. The lack of an explicit mention of Ostium in the 31 July reports does not preclude its involvement, but the available facts do not confirm the link.

A Pattern of Interceptions: The April 2026 Case

By contrast, a fully documented Brazil Air Force interception from earlier in the year provides a clearer picture of the typical operational cycle and outcome. On 10 April 2026, the FAB intercepted an EMB-810D Seneca aircraft with registration PT-RQY near Rondônia. That plane, also arriving from Bolivia, was forced to land near Rondolândia in Mato Grosso state.

In that incident, which was explicitly linked to Operation Ostium, the suspects set the aircraft on fire and fled the scene before authorities could apprehend them. This pattern of abandonment and flight is a common tactic used to destroy evidence and evade capture, a scenario that may parallel the unknown circumstances of the 31 July forced landing.

The A-29 Super Tucano: A Key Asset

The Embraer A-29 Super Tucano is the workhorse of the FAB’s border policing fleet. A turboprop aircraft designed for light attack, counter-insurgency, and advanced training, it is ideally suited for intercepting slow, low-flying aircraft that typically attempt to evade radar detection along the Amazon frontier. Its ability to operate from rudimentary airstrips and its long loiter time make it a critical asset for COMAE’s persistent surveillance and interception missions over the vast, often roadless, expanses of the Brazilian interior.

The deployment of two Super Tucanos for the 31 July mission highlights the FAB’s standard procedure of establishing air superiority and presenting an overwhelming show of force to compel non-compliant aircraft to follow instructions, minimizing the risk to populated areas.

Unanswered Questions in the July Incident

The lack of confirmed information regarding cargo, arrests, or the aircraft’s final fate leaves key questions open. It remains unconfirmed whether the plane was empty upon landing or if cargo was removed by the fleeing occupants. The absence of a confirmed link to a named operation like Ostium in the immediate reporting also leaves a procedural gap in the public record, even though the action falls squarely within the mandate of Brazil’s airspace policing doctrine.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened during the Brazil Air Force interception on 31 July 2026?

Two Brazilian A-29 Super Tucano fighters intercepted a suspect aircraft that had entered Brazilian airspace from Bolivia without a flight plan or radio contact. After the plane failed to comply with orders, it was forced to make an emergency landing on an improvised strip in Mato Grosso do Sul, about 200 km north of Campo Grande.

Were any drugs or arrests made in the 31 July 2026 interception?

No. Available reports from the incident do not confirm any cargo, drugs, or seizures. The aircraft was found abandoned, with no drugs or illicit cargo found and no arrests made, and no crew members or occupants were located or reported as arrested.

What is Operation Ostium and was it involved in this interception?

Operation Ostium is a joint Brazilian operation focused on frontier security and airspace policing, often using A-29 Super Tucanos to intercept suspect aircraft. While the 31 July 2026 interception was an airspace policing mission under COMAE, the available reports do not explicitly name Operation Ostium in connection with this specific event, unlike a similar interception in April 2026.

World.title: Nicaragua Presidential Term Reform Moves to Seven Years
World.content:
Nicaragua

Key Facts —Proposed Term A draft reform presented to the National Assembly on July 28, 2026, proposes extending the presidential term from six to seven renewable years. —Expected Approval A first vote is expected in early September 2026, but the reform must pass two separate legislatures, so final ratification would not come until the first half of 2027. —Co-Presidency The reform builds on a constitutional overhaul approved in November 2024 and in force since February 2025 that established a co-presidency for Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo. —Opposition Bar The 2026 proposal includes provisions to bar opposition figures labeled as ‘traitors’ or ‘coup-plotting’ from future elections. —International Condemnation The OAS, UN experts, and the IACHR have strongly condemned the constitutional changes as institutionalizing an authoritarian regime.

The Nicaragua presidential term is poised to be extended to seven years under a new constitutional reform proposal sent to the country’s National Assembly, a move that would further cement the joint rule of President Daniel Ortega and co-President Rosario Murillo while drawing fresh international criticism.

Nicaraguas National Assembly is weighing a seven-year presidential term. (Photo internet reproduction)

The 2026 Reform Proposal

On July 29, 2026, Reuters reported that a draft constitutional reform had been submitted to Nicaragua’s Congress to extend the presidential term from six to seven “renewable” years. The proposal, sent on a Tuesday evening, is expected to be approved in September 2026, according to the same report. Vatican News also confirmed the National Assembly’s plan to approve the amendment in September, though it noted the change was from five to seven years, reflecting some confusion over the baseline term following previous reforms.

The Ortega-Murillo Co-Presidency

The 2026 proposal builds directly on a sweeping constitutional overhaul approved by the National Assembly on November 22, 2024. That reform, which entered into force on February 18, 2025, according to the U.S. Library of Congress, extended the presidential term from five to six years and, most notably, elevated Vice President Rosario Murillo to the position of “co-president” alongside her husband, Daniel Ortega.

Election Uncertainty

The timeline for future elections remains deeply conflicted. Before the 2025 term extension, some election-tracking sources pointed to a general election in November 2026, while others had already shifted the expected presidential vote to November 2027. However, in July 2026, President Ortega declared there would be “no more elections,” a statement widely interpreted as a cancellation of any future electoral process.

International Reaction

The international community has responded with strong condemnation. The General Secretariat of the Organization of American States (OAS) condemned the 2024 reform package as illegitimate and an “aberrant” institutionalization of dictatorship. The UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua stated the 2024 reform gave Ortega virtually unlimited power and deepened repression.

Consolidation of Power

The sequence of constitutional changes – from the 2025 co-presidency and six-year term to the proposed 2026 seven-year term – represents a systematic consolidation of power by the Ortega-Murillo family. The reforms have progressively eliminated term limits in practice by making terms “renewable,” removed institutional oversight, and now seek to legally bar any meaningful opposition from participating in elections, should any even be held.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the proposed change to the Nicaragua presidential term?

A draft constitutional reform presented to the National Assembly on July 28, 2026, proposes extending the presidential term from six to seven renewable years. The National Assembly is expected to approve the amendment in September 2026.

Who are the current co-presidents of Nicaragua?

Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo, serve as co-presidents following a constitutional reform approved in November 2024 that entered into force on February 18, 2025. The reform elevated Murillo from vice president to co-president.

What has been the international reaction to Nicaragua's constitutional changes?

International bodies including the OAS, UN human rights experts, the UN High Commissioner, and the IACHR have strongly condemned the reforms. They describe the changes as institutionalizing a dictatorship, eliminating democratic checks and balances, and deepening repression.

World.title: Novak Djokovic Returns to Cincinnati With US Open History at Stake
World.content:
Novak Djokovic will return to the Cincinnati Open in August, choosing one final hard-court tournament before resuming his pursuit of a record 25th Grand Slam singles title at the US Open. The 39-year-old Serbian is part of the Cincinnati field after withdrawing from the Canadian Open in Montreal to manage his workload. His decision gives him additional recovery time following Wimbledon while still providing an opportunity to test his form before the season’s final major.



The Cincinnati Open runs from August 8 through August 23. The US Open begins August 23, with the singles main draws starting August 30 in New York. Djokovic’s appearance will mark his return to a tournament where he has produced some of the most memorable tennis of his career.

He is a three-time Cincinnati champion, winning the event in 2018, 2020 and 2023. His most recent title came after a remarkable final against Carlos Alcaraz that lasted three hours and 49 minutes. Djokovic saved a championship point before defeating Alcaraz 5-7, 7-6(7), 7-6(4). The match remains the longest best-of-three-set final in ATP Tour history.

Cincinnati now carries a different kind of importance for Djokovic. He remains capable of reaching the closing stages of the sport’s biggest tournaments, but winning them has become increasingly difficult as Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner have taken control of the men’s game.

Djokovic reached the Australian Open final in February after defeating Sinner in a five-set semifinal. Alcaraz then denied him the title in four sets, becoming the first player to defeat Djokovic in an Australian Open final.

At Wimbledon, Djokovic survived a five-hour, 15-minute quarterfinal against Félix Auger-Aliassime before losing to Sinner in the semifinals. It was another strong Grand Slam run, but it also illustrated the physical challenge facing Djokovic when he must defeat several leading players over two weeks.

“It’s good, but not good enough,” Djokovic said after his Wimbledon exit. His reduced schedule reflects that reality. Djokovic has increasingly avoided tournaments that might leave him physically depleted before the Grand Slams, preferring longer training periods and carefully selected appearances.

That strategy allows him to arrive rested, but it can also leave him short of competitive matches. Cincinnati offers a compromise. It gives Djokovic a high-level hard-court test against many of the same players he could face in New York, while leaving time to recover before the US Open singles competition begins.

The tournament will feature a deep men’s field led by Sinner, Alcaraz and several other leading contenders. Alcaraz won the Cincinnati title in 2025, while Sinner captured the championship in 2024. Djokovic enters the event ranked No. 5, meaning his path could include an earlier meeting with one of the tournament’s leading seeds.

The expanded Cincinnati format also makes recovery between matches and management of the summer heat important parts of any title run. The immediate objective will be finding his timing on outdoor hard courts. The larger question is whether he can still defeat Sinner or Alcaraz late in a major after navigating several demanding rounds.

Djokovic has not won a Grand Slam singles title since the 2023 US Open, when he collected his 24th major. He has continued reaching finals and semifinals since then, but the record-breaking 25th title has remained out of reach. Cincinnati will not settle that pursuit. It will, however, provide the clearest indication yet of whether Djokovic is ready for another serious challenge in New York.

World.title: Boston Scientific Confirms Costa Rica Layoffs in $800M Plan
World.content:
Boston Scientific has confirmed that its Costa Rican operation forms part of a global restructuring program that sets aside as much as $300 million for employee termination benefits, though the company has not disclosed how many workers it will cut in Costa Rica, in which of its local sites, or on what timeline.

The medical device manufacturer’s board of directors approved the plan, which the company calls its 2026 Restructuring Plan, on July 21. It was disclosed publicly six days later in a Form 8-K filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing estimates total pre-tax charges of between $700 million and $800 million, broken down into $300 million to $350 million to move production lines between facilities, $275 million to $300 million in employee termination benefits, and $125 million to $150 million in other costs including consulting fees, contract cancellations, program management and asset write-offs.

Between $600 million and $700 million of the total is expected to result in cash outlays. The company projects the program will reduce gross annual pre-tax expenses by roughly $500 million once its benefits are realized, and says those savings will be reinvested into growth initiatives. The plan began this year and is expected to be substantially complete by the end of 2029.

In the filing, Boston Scientific stated that it anticipates some headcount reductions while continuing to create positions in areas of growth. It provided no figures for total job losses and no country-level breakdown. Asked afterward about the Costa Rican operation, the company confirmed that the country is included in the reorganization but declined to specify numbers or the areas affected. In a written position, Boston Scientific said Costa Rica has been an important part of its global organization for more than 25 years and that it maintains a commitment to its long-term future in the country.

The scale of that operation is substantial by any measure, though the company’s own public figures for its Costa Rican workforce have not been consistent. Boston Scientific has previously stated through its vice president of operations that it employs 10,000 people in Costa Rica, a figure it has also characterized as 16.9 percent of a global workforce of 59,000. In a separate response to questions this week, the company put its local payroll at approximately 12,000 across San José, Alajuela, Cartago and Heredia. The two figures have not been reconciled by the company, and no explanation has been offered for the difference.

Against those numbers stand the commitments Boston Scientific filed with the state. The record of free trade zone benefits granted to the company, published in La Gaceta, shows a projected investment of more than $850 million together with 9,531 direct jobs beginning in January of this year and a further 200 positions by September 2029. Boston Scientific has not confirmed whether it will maintain those projections following the restructuring announcement. Those figures are the terms on which the company received its tax and tariff exemptions, and they represent the clearest public benchmark against which the plan’s local effect can eventually be measured.

Evidence that the cuts have already begun in Costa Rica comes from workers themselves. A research and development engineer who was let go and spoke on condition of anonymity described being notified without warning after three years supporting product review work for one of the company’s local divisions. The engineer said reductions of one to two people had occurred across several different teams and that layoffs of this kind had not previously been seen at the Costa Rican operation, in contrast to the United States. That account has not been independently confirmed by the company or by labor authorities.

The government has acknowledged it does not yet know the domestic impact. Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos said information on Boston Scientific remains in development and that the global plan has not specified its effects in Costa Rica. The administration of President Laura Fernández has announced preliminary measures in response.

The announcement lands on a free trade zone regime already under strain. More than 600 companies operate under the regime, and together they generated 67 percent of the $11.722 billion in goods Costa Rica exported in the first half of 2026. Medical device manufacturers accounted for $5.382 billion of that total, with the United States as the principal destination. Costa Rican exports to the United States now face a 12.5 percent tariff imposed on July 24 following a Section 301 investigation into the enforcement of prohibitions on goods produced with forced labor, a rate higher than the 10 percent applied to Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

Boston Scientific has operated in Costa Rica since 2004, manufactures more than 1,800 types of medical devices in the country and opened an additional plant in Cartago earlier this year. It ranked as the country’s leading medical device exporter in 2024 and the first half of 2025. What remains unknown is the only question that matters locally: how many of those jobs, and which of those plants, fall inside the $300 million the company has now set aside to pay people to leave.

World.title: Krismar Espinosa found guilty of executing Wilbert Banks Jr. in jealousy-fuelled execution
World.content:
Krismar Espinosa found guilty of executing Wilbert Banks Jr. in jealousy-fuelled execution

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-six-year-old Krismar Espinosa was found guilty on Friday afternoon of the April 2024 murder of bicycle technician and cycling enthusiast Wilbert E. Banks Jr., who was shot seven times after being lured to the Lake Garden area of Ladyville by a woman at the center of the feud.

Justice Nigel Pilgrim delivered the verdict shortly after 1 p.m. in a courtroom filled with relatives of both men. The decision brought an emotional moment for Banks’ family, who had waited more than two years for the case to be concluded.

After reviewing the evidence, Justice Pilgrim said the court was satisfied that Espinosa shot and killed Banks without legal justification in what he described as an execution-style killing. The judge rejected Espinosa’s defence as untrue and found the prosecution’s main witness—Espinosa’s former girlfriend and Banks’ former partner—to be truthful, credible and reliable.

The woman testified by video link that Espinosa became jealous after finding a photograph of Banks and accused her of continuing a relationship with him. She said Espinosa threatened to kill her and her son unless she helped lure Banks to Lake Garden Road.

According to her testimony, Espinosa borrowed his employer’s vehicle and dropped her off in Belize City. Banks later encountered her and offered to drive her back to Ladyville. When they reached Lake Garden, she exited Banks’ vehicle and Espinosa emerged and opened fire from the passenger side.

Banks attempted to escape but was struck by additional gunfire, lost control of his vehicle and crashed. The witness said she ran from the scene, but Espinosa chased her, forced her into his vehicle and threatened her against speaking about the killing.

Police recovered her cellphone near the murder scene, leading investigators to the Lords Bank home where she and Espinosa were found. Officers had also recovered nine expended 9mm shells at the scene. Public reporting at the time stated that Banks was found mortally wounded inside his crashed vehicle shortly after 11:30 p.m. on April 5, 2024.

Justice Pilgrim acknowledged that the woman’s evidence had to be treated cautiously because she had participated in luring Banks to the location. However, he concluded that she acted under threats of violence and that her account was strongly supported by the gunshot damage to Banks’ vehicle, the medical evidence and the physical evidence recovered by police.

The court also questioned Espinosa’s credibility, particularly the conflicting explanations he gave for borrowing his employer’s vehicle. Espinosa claimed he had taken the vehicle to run an errand, later said he went to purchase food and also alleged that the vehicle ran out of fuel. The judge found that those explanations did not correspond with his employer’s testimony.

Espinosa had denied the allegations, claiming he was home between approximately 8:50 and 11 p.m. on the night of the murder and that the case against him had been fabricated.

Banks, 38, worked for several years at Ordonez Bike Shop and was well known within Belize’s cycling community. Friends and relatives publicly remembered him as a quiet, humble and helpful man who was passionate about bicycles and cycling.

Crown Counsels Maria Santana-Nembhard and Joseph Perez prosecuted the case, while Espinosa was represented by attorney Michael Peyrefitte.

Sentencing has been scheduled for September 7, 2026. Justice Pilgrim ordered the preparation of a Social Inquiry Report, a prison report and a Victim Impact Statement ahead of the sentencing hearing.

World.title: Belize Rural North Area Representative rejects voter transfer “incentives”, says resources should benefit community
World.content:
Belize Rural North Area Representative rejects voter transfer “incentives”, says resources should benefit community

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Today, Belize Rural North Area Representative Marconi Leal publicly rejected the practice of offering incentives to encourage voters to transfer into a constituency, saying he will not compromise his principles or divert resources away from community development to increase the voters list.

Leal described the voter transfer period as a “stressful season” for area representatives and said he has faced direct requests from individuals seeking payment in exchange for transferring and voting for him.

“As much as I want to increase my voters list, I will not do it at the expense of having to give ‘something’ before you have even had the opportunity to vote for me,” Leal wrote.

He questioned the commitment of individuals who transfer into the constituency for incentives and later move their registration elsewhere, describing them as “jumpers” who, in his view, have little interest in the long-term development of the communities he serves.

Leal said he has been receiving messages from people asking, “What are you willing to give me to transfer and vote for you!?” He criticized what he described as a transactional approach to voter transfers, arguing that some individuals are more concerned about what they can receive than the development of the constituency.

The area representative said he remains focused on serving the 24 villages in Belize Rural North and responding to their development priorities. “If I were to lose the next elections because of not doing so then so be it,” Leal said adding that he would rather use available resources to support residents and communities than pay individuals to transfer their votes.

Leal said he welcomes eligible voters who seek guidance on polling locations, electoral boundaries or limited transportation assistance, saying such requests demonstrate concern for their communities and country.

World.title: International News: Heat wave scorches U.S. as millions face alerts and temperatures near 120°F
World.content:
International News: Heat wave scorches U.S. as millions face alerts and temperatures near 120°F

By Zoila Palma: A dangerous heat wave is gripping large parts of the United States, with more than 39 million people under heat alerts as temperatures soar across the South and Southwest.

Temperatures have climbed above 100°F in several cities, while highs of 119°F were recorded Thursday near Topock, Arizona, and Tecopa, California, according to the National Weather Service.

The heat dome that previously brought extreme temperatures to central and eastern parts of the country has shifted west and is expected to intensify before spreading into the Intermountain West and northern High Plains.

Parts of the Southwest could see temperatures between 110°F and 120°F through early next week, with some areas potentially experiencing one of their 10 hottest days on record, Yahoo reports.

Extreme heat warnings are in effect across parts of Arizona, California, Nevada, Utah, Oklahoma and western Arkansas, including major population centers and popular national parks. Heat index values could reach 120°F in parts of southern Arizona and South Texas, while overnight temperatures are expected to remain dangerously high, offering little relief from the heat.

World.title: International News: Fast- fashion giant Shein reports $99 million quarterly loss as US tariffs weigh on sales
World.content:
International News: Fast- fashion giant Shein reports $99 million quarterly loss as US tariffs weigh on sales

By Zoila Palma: Fast-fashion giant Shein has reported a $99 million loss for the first three months of 2026, a sharp reversal from the $395 million net income recorded during the same period a year earlier.

The company attributed part of the decline to slower US sales following the removal of a tariff exemption on low-value packages, while ongoing uncertainty over US-China trade tensions has also affected its business.

Shein said the elimination of the US “de minimis” exemption, which previously allowed goods valued at $800 or less to enter the country without tariffs, has negatively affected sales and overall revenue growth.

In response to higher duties and taxes, the company said it is considering several measures, including raising prices in the US to offset some of the increased costs, BBC reports.

The company also reported that the conflict involving Iran had weakened demand, raised operating costs and caused delivery delays in some markets. However, the first-quarter loss included a $328 million paper loss linked to an accounting change involving special investor shares, meaning the underlying financial performance was affected by factors beyond direct operating results.

The latest financial disclosure comes as Shein prepares for a potential stock market debut in Hong Kong after receiving approval from China’s securities regulator.

World.title: Consumer confidence dips slightly in June as Belizeans remain cautious about major purchases
World.content:
Consumer confidence dips slightly in June as Belizeans remain cautious about major purchases

By Zoila Palma: Consumer confidence in Belize edged lower in June 2026, with the national Consumer Confidence Index (CCI) falling marginally by 0.4 percent to 41.1, down from 41.3 in May, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB). The decline continues a downward trend seen in recent months, although at a slower pace than the sharper decreases recorded earlier in the year.

The SIB said the decline was mainly driven by weaker sentiment toward major household purchases and current economic conditions. The Durable Goods component fell by 8.5 percent, from 37.6 to 34.4, indicating increased pessimism about purchasing items such as homes, vehicles, furniture and appliances. The Present component also declined by 0.9 percent, from 37.9 to 37.6, as consumers became slightly more pessimistic about current economic conditions and their household finances.

However, consumers were more optimistic about the year ahead. The Expectations component rose by 6.4 percent, moving from a pessimistic 48.3 in May to an optimistic 51.4 in June, reflecting improved views of future economic conditions and household finances. By district, Orange Walk recorded the largest decline in confidence, falling 8.9 percent to 36.0, while Cayo saw the biggest improvement, with confidence rising 6.5 percent from 38.5 to 41.0.

The CCI, which ranges from zero to 100, measures consumer sentiment about the economy, household finances and major purchases, with a score above 50 generally indicating optimism. The index is considered an early indicator of future household spending, saving and investment, and therefore can provide insight into potential economic growth.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture conclude Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture conclude Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Stann Creek Department of Agriculture, through the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), successfully conducted a Value-Added Beekeeping Products Training for members of the Maya Mopan Bee Cooperative.

The training was funded through the Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project (CRESAP).

The training was designed to strengthen the capacity of beekeepers by introducing value-added processing techniques that enable participants to diversify their enterprises and maximize the economic potential of hive products.

CRESAP noted that by expanding beyond honey production, beekeepers can explore new market opportunities, increase the value of their products, and improve the sustainability of their operations.

World.title: UNICEF, Caribbean Climate Change Centre strengthen partnership on child-focused climate action
World.content:
UNICEF, Caribbean Climate Change Centre strengthen partnership on child-focused climate action

By Zoila Palma: UNICEF and the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) have signed a five-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at strengthening efforts to protect children’s rights and well-being from the growing impacts of climate change across the Caribbean.

The partnership will promote child-sensitive climate policies, resilient social services, climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction, while giving young people greater opportunities to participate in climate action and decision-making.

Children across the region are increasingly exposed to hurricanes, flooding, droughts, extreme heat and environmental degradation, threatening access to education, healthcare, nutrition, clean water and sanitation.

UNICEF Representative Sajid Ali said climate change is not only an environmental issue but also a child rights challenge, noting that children are among those least responsible for the climate crisis while facing some of its greatest consequences.

CCCCC Executive Director Dr. Colin Young welcomed the agreement, saying children and youth have not traditionally been a central focus of climate resilience programming and that the partnership will help place them at the heart of regional climate action.

A key area of collaboration will focus on climate-resilient sanitation services, alongside efforts to strengthen education, health, nutrition, water and sanitation systems and disaster preparedness.

World.title: Wheatley granted injunction barring IC charges until judicial review
World.content:
Andrew Wheatley

The Supreme Court has granted an injunction preventing the Integrity Commission (IC) from charging Cabinet Minister Dr Andrew Wheatley until the hearing and determination of an application by his lawyers for judicial review.

Wheatley had applied for leave to pursue judicial review against the IC’s recommendation that he be charged with illicit enrichment.

Observer Online understands that the Supreme Court on Friday granted Wheatley’s application, recommending that the judicial review be heard by a panel of three judges.

Before granting the injunction, presiding Judge Justice David Batts had suggested that the IC consider an undertaking not to charge Dr Wheatley until the hearing and determination of the judicial review.

The commission said it could not give an undertaking at this time. The judge then granted the injunction.

It is understood that the IC’s application for leave to appeal the ruling was denied.

The Integrity Commission had alleged that there is a disproportionality in Wheatley’s assets when compared to his income to the tune of $164 million.

Wheatley rejected the allegation and accused the IC of failing to take into consideration $168 million in rental income accumulated over a decade.

He is being represented by a high powered legal team including King’s Counsel Ransford Braham, Abe Dabdoub and Neco Pagon.

The Integrity Commission is being represented by King’s Counsel Kevin Powell.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.
