World.title: More for MSMEs
World.content:
WILLIAMS... it is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica.

ONLY about one per cent of the Government’s annual procurement spending currently reaches micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), a disparity Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the upgraded Government of Jamaica Electronic Procurement portal (GOJEP 2.0) is intended to address. The platform will increase MSME access to public contracts.

Speaking during Thursday’s launch of the updated digital procurement portal, Williams said the modernised system eliminates outdated technical requirements, and creates more opportunities for local businesses to access a share of the Government’s roughly $470-billion annual procurement spend.

“Let me put the scale in perspective. Each year, the Government of Jamaica spends roughly US$3 billion — translated into Jamaican dollars, that’s about $470 billion, depending on the currency at any point in time – and this procures goods, services, and works from the private sector. This is close to, I think, about 13 per cent of our GDP (gross domestic product). And yet, of that enormous sum, only about one per cent reaches our micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises,” the minister pointed out.

“That imbalance is exactly what we are determined to correct so that more Jamaican businesses can share in the billions that Government spends each year, particularly as we rebuild in the wake of Hurricane Melissa. So every procurement decision carries real responsibility. It must inspire public confidence, deliver value for money, create economic opportunity, and make certain that every dollar entrusted to Government works harder for the people we serve,” she said during the event held at AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Williams, GOJEP 2.0 is an upgraded version of the Government’s online system for buying goods, works and services from the private sector. She explained that the remodelling of the digital portal will see the removal of outdated barriers, put in place stronger record keeping aimed at making the process faster and more transparent.

“It’s easier to use. You no longer need to install extra software just to submit a bid. You log in from any ordinary web browser on any device, including your phone. It’s better connected. The system now talks to other government systems, so the same information doesn’t have to be entered twice, it keeps a proper record digitally,” explained the minister.

“Every key decision made during evaluation is captured and tracked automatically instead of living in a paper file or in someone’s memory. It cuts duplicate paperwork for government staff, and it collects far better data on how long procurements take, how much competition is there, and how well our small business set-asides are working,” Williams added.

She also pointed out that bidders and buyers will now be able to follow opportunities that the government brings to market, and see who ultimately wins the work. Furthermore, she assured that GOJEP 2.0 was not the finished product, noting that upgrades will continue overtime.

“It is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica. And, over the next years, we will build a fully integrated end-to-end digital procurement system, one that connects planning, tendering, evaluation, contract management, supplier performance, and payment.

“Imagine in a year or two being able to open GOJEP and see the goods, works, and services that government intends to buy over the coming years. A business could then prepare, assess its capacity, build partnerships, secure certification, arrange financing, and position itself to compete. For our MSMEs especially, that advanced visibility can be the difference between watching from the sidelines and winning the work,” said the finance minister.

Meanwhile, Chief Public Procurement Policy Officer Jovell Barrett also highlighted the gap that exists for MSMEs, pointing out that of the 300,000 active businesses registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica, less than 10,000 unique people and entities are awarded government contracts each year.

“Government is one of the largest purchasers of goods, works and services. And so, the question that we have asked ourselves at the Office of Public Procurement Policy is how many Jamaican businesses see government as a potential customer? How many entrepreneurs look to the public procurement system as an opportunity? And perhaps most importantly, how many do not see public procurement as an opportunity — and if they don’t, why?” said Barrett.

He hailed Thursday’s launch of GOJEP 2.0 as an opportunity to ensure that every taxpaying Jamaican has a fair chance to participate in the public procurement process.

“That’s the vision that I have and that’s what I want to see as a Jamaican. Why? I want to see more Jamaicans participating in public procurement. When public procurement operates as I want to see it happen… small businesses, hundreds and thousands of them in each community, [will] become a mechanism through which public procurement will work best and will be able to develop our economy more. It becomes the instrument of change that Government really wants it to be. That is the power of public procurement,” he said.

World.title: Dexta Daps stays true
World.content:
Dexta Daps.

As thousands of patrons prepare to descend on Montego Bay for Dream Wknd, few performers arrive with the kind of anticipation that surrounds Dexta Daps.

Over the past decade the dancehall star has built one of the genre’s most devoted followings by staying true to the soulful, emotionally driven sound that first set him apart.

“Staying true to the vibe that started my career and keeping the music honest and relatable,” he says when asked about the secret to his longevity. “I evolve with the production sounds, but I don’t chase trends; solid melodies, real emotion, and a performance that connects with the audience is always the goal.”

In a genre that constantly reinvents itself, Dexta Daps has remained relevant by refining his craft rather than reinventing his identity. As production styles and audience tastes have evolved, he has focused on strengthening the qualities that first resonated with listeners.

His creative process, however, has never stood still.

“It’s ever-evolving,” he explains. “I’ve continued to sharpen my sense of arrangement and storytelling while balancing intimate, soulful moments with the dancehall energy.”

That balance has become one of his defining trademarks. Whether delivering emotionally charged ballads or high-energy dancehall records, he has demonstrated an ability to connect with audiences on multiple levels, creating music that feels both deeply personal and widely relatable.

As with any artiste whose career has spanned several years, thoughts inevitably turn to legacy. For Dexta Daps, the impact he leaves extends far beyond chart success or hit records.

“If fans only remembered one thing about my career years from now,” he says, “I’d want it to be that I gave people real, heartfelt music that resonated beyond the dance songs, music that felt honest and performances that stayed with them.”

That same commitment to delivering memorable performances is what fans can expect when he takes the stage at Dream Wknd, one of the Caribbean’s premier entertainment festivals, which runs from July 30-August 3 this year.

Sharing the stage with Dexta Daps at Dream’s Montego Bay debut are some of the biggest names in dancehall, including Alkaline, Tommy Lee, Govana, Shaneil Muir, Tifa, Elephant Man, General B, Jamal, Skeng, and Armanii, alongside a number of international acts.

“It’s always great to share the stage with so much talent,” he says. “It’s about representing the culture well and keeping the energy high for the crowd. I don’t take that for granted.”

While he remains tight-lipped about exactly what fans can expect, he hints that patrons should be prepared for something special.

“Always a few surprises,” he says with a laugh. “However, I can’t reveal them because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

Looking beyond the summer, Dexta Daps’s focus remains firmly on creating new music while continuing to expand his reach internationally.

“More music, working on an album,” he responds.

So, with new music, an album in the works, and another Dream Wknd appearance on the horizon, Dexta Daps is continuing to build a career rooted in authenticity, one heartfelt performance at a time.

World.title: DOLPHIN COVE’S US$2.5-M LIFT
World.content:
Visitors interact with dolphins at one of Dolphin Cove Limited’s Jamaican attractions. The company has added approximately US$2.53 million to its net book value following a revaluation of its Jamaican properties

DOLPHIN Cove Limited has added approximately US$2.533 million to its net book value after revaluing its Jamaican properties, an adjustment disclosed while its majority shareholder has agreed to sell its controlling stake and is seeking to add four directors.

Property Consultants Limited valued the group’s Jamaican land and buildings as at March 31, but its report reached Dolphin Cove’s board after the company had published its first-quarter financial statements.

The appraisal increases the carrying value of property, plant and equipment by approximately US$2.576 million. After adjustments to deferred taxation, the net increase in Dolphin Cove’s book value is approximately US$2.533 million.

Applied to the previously reported March figures, the adjustment would lift property, plant and equipment from approximately US$26.65 million to US$29.23 million and shareholders’ equity from US$27.39 million to approximately US$29.92 million, before any other second-quarter movements.

The increase is equivalent to approximately nine per cent of the equity Dolphin Cove reported at the end of March.

It is an accounting adjustment rather than new income or cash. Dolphin Cove said the revaluation has no effect on revenue, operating results or cash flow for the period.

The revised values will be reflected in the company’s financial statements for the six months ended June 30.

Dolphin Cove did not identify the individual Jamaican properties covered by the appraisal, disclose their separate values or say whether the updated figures were considered in the proposed sale of the company’s controlling stake.

The transaction under way is a sale of shares in Dolphin Cove rather than a direct sale of the properties.

World of Dolphins Inc agreed on July 9 to sell all 313,901,858 Dolphin Cove shares it owns to Global Attractions Limited, a Saint Lucia company incorporated in March. The shares represent 79.99 per cent of Dolphin Cove.

Neither the purchase price nor the expected completion date has been disclosed. Completion is subject to conditions, including arrangements for the refinancing and discharge of Dolphin Cove’s existing credit facility with Sagicor Bank Jamaica Limited. The beneficial owners of Global Attractions, its financing arrangements and its plans for Dolphin Cove also remain unknown.

The property adjustment has now been announced as World of Dolphins seeks to add four directors to the listed company’s board.

The majority shareholder has nominated Colin Kerr, Darys Estrella, Alberto Bergés González and Sylvain Dominici for election, according to a notice signed by World of Dolphins representative and Dolphin Cove director Steven Strom.

Dolphin Cove has not published biographies of the nominees, explained their connections to World of Dolphins or said whether any of them is associated with Global Attractions.

It also has not explained why the selling shareholder is seeking to expand the board before the ownership transaction is completed.

The nominations were scheduled for consideration at Dolphin Cove’s annual general meeting on Thursday, July 30, at The Courtleigh Hotel & Suites.

However, the chairman was expected to seek shareholders’ consent to adjourn the meeting to allow investors at least 14 days’ notice of the proposed appointments. The outcome was unavailable at press time.

If shareholders approve the adjournment, the resumed meeting would be held between August 13 and August 28. The exact date has not been announced.

Based on Dolphin Cove’s latest public disclosures, electing all four nominees would expand its five-member board to nine if the present directors remain in office.

World of Dolphins currently holds enough shares to determine the outcome of the elections if it votes its 79.99 per cent stake. That could change if the sale is completed or the voting rights are transferred before the adjourned meeting.

Once completed, the acquisition will trigger a mandatory offer allowing minority shareholders to sell their shares to the new controlling owner. The price and other terms have not been published.

Dolphin Cove said its properties in Saint Lucia and the Turks and Caicos Islands will also be revalued. It did not say when those appraisals would be completed or whether it expects them to increase or reduce the assets’ carrying values.

World.title: ‘He who has the gold’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

Veteran administrator Tony James says FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal to privatise world football is “underhanded”, but cautions that developing nations under severe financial stress will find the promised US$40-million payout nearly impossible to resist.

James, who led the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) from 1985 to 1992 and has spent over 50 years working in football, offered a sharp critique of Infantino’s proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Under the plan, FIFA aims to create a private commercial entity valued at US$20 billion (over $3 billion) to handle broadcasting, ticketing, sponsorship, and hospitality rights for competitions like the World Cup. Developed alongside JP Morgan, the strategy involves selling up to 21 per cent to private equity investors — led by Joshua Kushner’s firm, Thrive Eternal — to raise US$4.2 billion (roughly $665 billion) in upfront capital. Kushner is the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

To win over member nations, FIFA offered a substantial payout of increasing baseline development funding from US$10 million (over $1.5 billion) to US$20 million (over $3 billion) per nation for the 2027-2030 cycle. Associations could also access an additional US$20 million upfront through a new FIFA Fast Forward Programme for infrastructure, putting up to US$40 million on the table per country ahead of a September 19 deadline. Infantino, however, warned that member nations declining support would continue to receive the baseline.

While continental governing bodies have moved to block the move, James says that for smaller member associations, the financial reality takes precedence.

“It is underhanded, and the cynical view is being reinforced by the way it is being proposed now,” James told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. “He who has the gold makes the rule. That’s how people perceive of it; that it’s the current way of the world. You’re trumping (pardon the pun) institutionalised good governance structures, integrity, etcetera. That’s what’s being put out in the public now.”

Despite the governance concerns, James says smaller associations operate in a vastly different financial reality than European giants.

“This US$40 million for each affiliate will have traction in all the poorer and developing countries,” he said. “The focus will be on CAF [Confederation of African Football], and Concacaf, which includes the Caribbean, but it’s also the poorer countries in Asia and UEFA.

“UEFA’s principled position is understandable, but it’s fortunate in having three financial platforms. One is the World Cup, like everybody else, and their teams are the top of the heap. Let us call them Category A teams because they’re the ones who are going to get most of the money. All of the rest of us are Category B and C teams that should get money, but not like the A teams.”

James’s comments come as global opposition to Infantino’s scheme reaches a boiling point. After an emergency meeting, Concacaf — the governing body for North America, Central America, and the Caribbean — unanimously voted down the proposed enterprise plan, joining European governing body UEFA in open revolt. Concacaf made its announcement moments after the Observer’s interview with James.

In its official statement, Concacaf mentioned severe procedural failures surrounding the proposal.

“During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies,” Concacaf said on its website. “In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programmes following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.”

Concacaf confirmed all 41 member associations rejected the deal after UEFA’s warning that it would pull its teams from FIFA competitions entirely.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said on its website on Thursday.

Despite Concacaf’s joint rejection, local sentiments reflect exactly what James described.

JFF President Michael Ricketts rejected all of the Observer’s calls to him seeking a comment, and declined to respond to questions posed on WhatsApp.

However, while speaking to Nationwide Sports, he struck a far more open tone regarding the commercial structure.

“I have not discussed it with my directors, but my personal feeling is that, on the face of it, I really don’t think that anything is wrong with it,” Ricketts said. “It’s workable. But the big problem I’m having is the — for want of a better word — non-transparent way in which it was done. We would’ve spent so much time together with the leadership of FIFA before, during, and after the World Cup, and we were never apprised of these discussions, and this would bring to the fore some level of non-transparency.”

Ricketts’s pragmatic view is tied directly to local circumstances. He told the Observer in an interview on July 14 that the JFF is strapped for cash after a costly, unsuccessful World Cup qualifying campaign. He also said in that interview that he would fully support Infantino’s plan to expand the World Cup to 64 teams as early as the 2030 tournament as it would provide a greater chance of qualification for Jamaica.

A US$40-million windfall would completely alter local operations. Furthermore, with Jamaica actively bidding to co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup with the US, Mexico, and Costa Rica, maintaining good relations with FIFA ahead of Infantino’s re-election bid in March remains a practical priority.

While acknowledging the lifelines that FIFA funds provide, James warned that dumping millions into unprepared administrative set-ups brings serious risks.

“Regrettably, I don’t think most developing countries have an administrative structure to deal with this kind of money. They don’t,” he said. “You also have to ask, given our system, how much of this US$40 million would actually reach football development, because human nature says when you have money, it’s about a source of power, greed, corruption, football politics, and that syphons off the money.”

And on whether Infantino’s tactics amount to using FIFA’s massive wealth to secure political survival ahead of the upcoming presidential vote, James gave a blunt assessment of how the global game operates.

“He has been a disgrace,” James said. “But in a new world where the golden rule applies, when he hits FIFA and hits the politics, what do you think they’re going to say to him? When he tells them how much he has earned off this World Cup, that the vision was his, the planning was his, what he has had to do, ‘Listen, we had problems here and there, but at the end of the day, look at what I have done for you. Look at what FIFA has done for you. Who are you going to vote for?’ What do you think is going to be the response? It’s all about performance. Let’s face it, he has performed.”

World.title: 2026 Isuzu D-MAX: Built to last
World.content:
The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the Isuzu D-MAX pickup continues in 2026. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Isuzu has long been one of the darlings of the commercial vehicle sector, having built a reputation for durability, reliability, and longevity over its long history.

The D-MAX pickup is endowed with these characteristics, and for 2026 continues to be so.

EXTERIOR

The four-door cab pickup is based mostly on function rather than form. Redesigned from the ground up, Isuzu calls it their ‘Spirit of Truck’ DNA, giving the D-MAX a masculine and no-nonsense look from its wide stance and wedge-shaped body lines. However, function over form still rules, and the D-MAX uses aerodynamic integration of the lower body to boost fuel efficiency and reduce wind noise. For those wanting style, up to 18-inch wheels can be had.

INTERIOR

Inside the new spacious cabin it reflects the working nature of the D-MAX. There’s a quality impression and the presence of durability to the cabin. There’s a mixture of hard-wearing plastics, with soft-touch materials at the main points of user contact. Ergonomics is a key word, with simple large buttons for the main functions to be accessed with ease under all conditions, and feel like they’ll be working for years to come.

Storage is plentiful for those who have to work. The deep centre console will swallow important gear, as will the dual gloveboxes. Cup holders and door pockets that all can hold a 1.5-litre bottle further contribute to the ability to hold personal cargo. The D-MAX has redesigned seats with improved internal materials for higher comfort, and better lateral support to increase occupant, especially driver, comfort.

The infotainment is similarly focused, using USB-C for smartphone-run connectivity and services.

ON THE ROAD

Powered by a 3-litre turbodiesel, the D-MAX is not lacking in this area. With 190bhp and 332lb/ft of torque, it manages to be both frugal and powerful. This is because there is tons of low-end torque to effortlessly pull the D-MAX along in the situations it’s built to operate in.

Boost response is good, and it rarely has to be taken into the higher rpms for more power. On road, this keeps engine noise and vibration low so as not to upset passengers in the cabin, meaning a strong case for prolonged on-road use.

But the D-MAX didn’t get its reputation for its on-road manners. Off-road, it has the ability to match the class leaders, because it’s all under the skin with a chassis boasting greater torsional and longitudinal rigidity. The same suspension that smooths out rough roads and can deal with highway travel can easily handle tough terrain with or without payload.

Rookie or professional, the D-MAX gives confidence in challenging situations, delivering up to 800 millimetres of wading depth, 30 degrees of approach angle, 22.9 degrees of breakover, and 24.2 degrees of departure angle. Being equipped with 2WD, 4WD, and 4WD Low, plus a rear differential, few things can slow, even stop, the D-MAX on a trail.

VERDICT

The D-MAX retains the ethos of the Isuzu brand. There’s a reason the company is a commercial equipment manufacturing powerhouse, and that all is installed into their flagship pickup. The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the D-MAX pickup continue without question. 2026 adds some key updates and refinements to keep it a top contender.

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by

coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies

that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of

irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.

World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Northern Ireland misses a deadline to fix its budget crisis
World.content:
Bryant, a former Anglican priest who’s never held a Cabinet post before, held his first press conference as Northern Ireland secretary shortly before meeting delegations from the region’s two main government parties, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionists.

Bryant emphasized that the U.K. government expects Stormont to get more bang for its buck by reforming the delivery of local services, most crucially hospital care, where Northern Ireland suffers the worst waiting lists in the entire National Health Service.

“Look, we need to get to a budget,” Bryant said. “And I understand the financial pressures. I know everybody expects me to come with a checkbook. I’m actually coming with a checklist of things that I want to get sorted.”

Sinn Féin, which holds the key finance and economy ministries, has shied from taking any significant decisions on raising local taxes—not that the DUP wouldn’t immediately veto such moves. Nothing much can happen in Northern Ireland’s system of cross-community government unless the largest parties on each side of the divide can agree.

The two parties blame each other for delivering so little and agree that it’s up to the U.K. Treasury to break the budgetary impasse by providing them much more annually to spend. An independent budgetary watchdog, the Northern Ireland Fiscal Council, recently concluded that the region wasn’t being subsidized by English taxpayers to the same levels as in Scotland and Wales — and if it was, Northern Ireland could gain an extra £1 billion to £3.5 billion annually.

While few expect the Burnham administration to come anywhere close to that, both sides in Belfast do expect Bryant to take charge of key budget decisions — which is what his predecessors did when the Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in 2017 from a Sinn Féin walkout, and again in 2022 from a Democratic Unionist walkout.

World.title: London mayor Sadiq Khan accuses Palantir of bypassing procurement rules
World.content:
Palantir claims that Khan’s office blocked the contract unlawfully and “irrationally,” citing comments attributed to the mayor’s spokesperson which referred to the company’s unspecified “values and ethics.”

Louis Mosley, Palantir’s U.K. CEO, has argued that Khan’s decision puts politics above Londoners’ safety, while Met Police Commissioner Mark Rowley has said that the force’s inability to access Palantir’s technology would worsen the impact of cuts to the force’s budget.

In a pre-trial defense statement filed last Thursday and seen by POLITICO, lawyers for MOPAC said Palantir’s claim is “without merit and should be dismissed,” stating that the Met Police “conducted an award process that was unlawful.”

It says the Met Police and Palantir designed a pilot of the technology in 2025 so that the value remained below a £500,000 threshold at which it would have required MOPAC approval. MOPAC, led by Khan’s deputy mayor for policing and crime, oversees the Met Police.

Prior to the conclusion of that pilot in April 2026, the Met Police and Palantir started discussions on directly awarding Palantir a much larger contract to extend the pilot, according to the statement.

The Met Police intended “at each stage” to award the larger contract to Palantir, the statement says, adding that the approach that was “supported/encouraged/assisted” by the company.

World.title: UK to hold budget on Oct. 28, chancellor announces
World.content:
“Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security,” said the chancellor in the letter. “That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East.”

Healey also pledged the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.”

Burnham announced today that local English mayors will be given powers to retain and spend business rate taxes to boost growth in their regions.

The prime minister said mayors will soon have power over income taxes, but Healey will unveil a whitepaper and a “roadmap” on the topic at the autumn budget.

World.title: Sánchez slams Europe's lack of solidarity over Ceuta in letter to von der Leyen
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has lamented what he describes as a lack of European solidarity over the Ceuta crisis in a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, in which he points to misinformation, prejudice and petty politics.

 

The letter, sent on Saturday and seen by Euronews, comes after Sánchez described the arrival of 50,000 migrants from Morocco in Ceuta in a single day, after the double-fenced border was breached, as an "attack" and a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity".

Pedro Sánchez's letter to Von der Leyen over the Ceuta crisis Pedro Sánchez

In the strongly worded letter, Sánchez describes the response from some EU partners as "rather asymmetric".

While breaches of national borders are often swiftly condemned by member states and often portrayed as hybrid attacks, several EU countries instead called for tighter controls on Spain, urging Madrid to restore order rather than expressing solidarity.

"Most have shown us their support and solidarity, and have offered their assistance," the Spanish premier writes in the letter.

"Others, however, have chosen to attack Spain and to call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen Area," he continued, in an apparent reference to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government, which on Friday announced it would suspend freedom of movement with Spain, even as migrants were returning to Morocco.

It remains unclear what the measure would mean in practice.

Sánchez also appeared to hit back at Italy, arguing in the letter that Spain has "one of the least porous external borders of the European Union," citing Frontex data.

"In the current international context, the European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," he added.

Madrid defends track record

Sánchez has come under scrutiny from conservative and right-wing governments over plans to regularise the status of 500,000 people living in Spain without legal permits.

Madrid has defended the decision, which was not consulted with the EU, arguing that these are people who already live and work in Spain and should be granted social rights. The European right has criticised the move as reckless, arguing that it could lead to a surge in irregular arrivals.

Still, Spanish sources say that conflating the regularisation process with the irregular crossings into Ceuta is short-sighted, arguing that the two episodes are unrelated. Madrid described the events in the enclave as an attack on its territorial integrity, rather than as a migrant crisis.

In his letter, Sánchez also defended the government's response to the crisis.

He said border control had been restored within 48 hours, humanitarian assistance had been provided to those who crossed, and almost all those who entered irregularly had been returned. On Friday, the EU said no illegal crossings had been recorded out of Ceuta into mainland Spain, and therefore the rest of member states.

Sánchez said these measures were carried out in coordination with the Moroccan authorities, with limited assistance from other European countries. The EU said Friday it was ready to deploy more means through Frontex, although this was not requested.

He added that Spain's had shown solidarity to EU countries facing similar challenges, including during the 2021 border crisis involving Belarus and several Eastern European countries, and the surge in migrant arrivals on the Italian island of Lampedusa in 2023.

It remains unclear what prompted the mass crossing of around 50,000 people from Morocco into Ceuta on Thursday, as border controls collapsed. Rabat has denied any instrumentalisation of migration for political reasons, although similar incidents have occurred in the past during periods of diplomatic tension between the two.

Even as border checks became overwhelmed, the EU praised Morocco's cooperation in managing migration flows. Spain said it had agreed with Rabat to accelerate returns. Footage from Ceuta showed many young Moroccans returning voluntarily on foot, as the city was practically put on locked down and the Spanish army patrolled the streets.

Emergency meeting

Sánchez has formally asked the European Council to urgently convene a video conference of EU interior ministers. He said the meeting should aim to establish a common European response and to reaffirm the protection of the EU's external borders.

He said that is a shared responsibility, not just those on the front line in the south.

The Spanish prime minister ends the letter by calling on European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to show leadership and ensure that the European Union responds to the situation in Ceuta "swiftly, effectively and in a coordinated manner."

While European Council chief Costa expressed solidarity with Spain, von der Leyen focused on returns, calling the scenes in Ceuta "unacceptable" and blaming human traffickers.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | August 1st, 2026 – Midday
World.content:

World.title: Ceuta migrant crisis sparks strong reactions from all over Europe
World.content:
Italy caused a stir when it called to shut Spain out of the EU's visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in Morocco was overwhelmed this week by more than 60,000 migrant arrivals.

 

This crisis, during which 67 people died, is the largest surge of irregular arrivals ever recorded on a single day in EU territory. Although Ceuta is located in North Africa, this crisis has sparked vivid concerns among European governments.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Thursday said Spain should be suspended from the Schengen area, as she described the images from Ceuta showing the migrants arriving as "shocking" and calling for "extraordinary measures" to be taken.

Spain blasted Italy's "demagoguery" and summoned the country's ambassador to Madrid to lodge a protest.

Finland and Denmark backed Italy's request while France, Portugal and Germany have been less offensive, calling for the "protection of the EU's borders".

'Suspension of Schengen cooperation'

"On illegal immigration, we will not yield an inch: defending the borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriations will continue to be the line of this Government," Meloni wrote on X.

The hard-right Brothers of Italy party proposed the suspension of the Schengen area with Spain, and announced extraordinary measures to defend Italy's border. Statements that soon were backed by Denmark and Finland.

"It goes without saying that the EU must immediately take all necessary measures and consider all options, including a suspension of Schengen cooperation," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said.

"Countries that do not fulfil their obligation to protect the external border cannot be members of Schengen," Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said.

Abundant right-wing reactions

"The images coming from Ceuta show how the Madrid Government's decision to grant Spanish, and therefore European, citizenship to over 500,000 irregular immigrants is profoundly wrong and encourages human trafficking," Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani wrote on X.

The call was also echoed by leading right-of-centre figures across Europe.

"Appalling situation at the Spanish border. The devastating images are the direct consequence of the pull factor of massive regularisation doubled with instrumentalisation of illegal migration," Manfred Weber, German leader of the centre-right European People's Party (EPP), wrote on X.

Germany is likely the destination for most of these migrants. Alice Weidel Leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany

"Spanish authorities have recorded 50,000 illegal border crossings [latest figures show it's 60,000] in Ceuta so far, with Germany likely the destination for most of these migrants," Alice Weidel, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany, wrote on X. "Germany must prepare itself: borders must be secured and rejections rigorously enforced."

Jordan Bardella, France’s radical right leader who is the president of the Patriots for Europe Group in the European Parliament, sent a letter on Friday, seen by Euronews, asking President Roberta Metsola “to hold an urgent debate on the developments in Ceuta and on the failure of the European Union's migration policies.”

'Italy's position is unworthy'

For left-wing politicians in Spain and abroad, these attacks are opportunistic. The Ceuta crisis, they say, has simply given critics an excuse to target migrants and paint them as a threat.

"In Europe, right-wing attitudes have prevailed in picturing migrants as a threat," said Spanish left-wing S&D MEP Juan Fernando López Aguilar, a former justice minister under the Zapatero government.

This is right-wing propaganda at its worst. Cecilia Strada Italian left-wing S&D MEP

"Italy’s position is unworthy of a European partner," S&D Spanish MEP Javi Lopez said on X. "When migration is weaponised, Europe answers with solidarity, not selfishness. After 700,000+ arrivals from Libya, Italy received European support, not lectures. Solidarity is not a one-way street."

"This is right-wing propaganda at its worst," Italian S&D MEP Cecilia Strada told Euronews. "Before a humanitarian emergency with tens of deaths and an unknown number of missing people, one would expect European solidarity rather than instrumental attacks aimed at political profiteering."

Milder reactions from France and Germany

Other countries chose not to call for a suspension of Spain from the EU visa-free zone. France reinforced its border controls with Spain but reminded that Ceuta has a particular status.

"Ceuta does not benefit from free movement to the rest of the Schengen Area," French President Emmanuel Macron said. "However, I asked the Interior Minister yesterday to step up checks at our border with Spain should this prove necessary: four mobile police units, aircraft and drones have been deployed."

French diplomatic source also says, "France is closely monitoring the situation in Ceuta [...] and will continue to coordinate with all of its European partners, first and foremost Spain, to which it expresses its support."

Ceuta does not benefit from free movement to the rest of the Schengen Area. Emmanuel Macron French President

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz reacted on Friday to the crisis, calling for implementation "without delay" of the EU Return Regulation.

"Protecting the EU’s external borders is crucial to combating illegal migration," German Chancellor said on X. "I support Spain’s intention not to allow illegal migrants onto the European mainland."

The Portuguese Government reaffirmed that "the integrity of the Schengen system depends on strict border control and a determined fight against all forms of illegal immigration," without calling for Spain to be temporarily removed from the Schengen area.

Dutch Foreign Minister also reacted implicating Morocco saying "we count on Spain to do what is necessary to protect the EU's external borders and on Morocco to take the necessary steps as well."

EU rejects Italy's call

EU chief Ursula von der Leyen described the scenes in Ceuta as "unacceptable", and her executive team is in contact with Spain and Morocco.

A European official said the EU understood "some governments are concerned" but stressed the priority was "securing our external borders" while rejecting Italy's call to suspend Spain from the Schengen free-travel zone.

Brussels also noted the current crisis concerned the enclave of Ceuta, located on the African continent, and that additional checks are necessary for entry into mainland Europe, where no movement has been detected so far.

"It's not like they're landing in Spain and moving onto France," the official, seeking anonymity to speak openly, said.

World.title: Two reported attacks on tankers near Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Two tankers have reported coming under attack near the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime agency said on Saturday, as tensions between Washington and Tehran over the region continue to build.

 

According to UKMTO, one vessel said it had been "struck by an unknown projectile" while northeast off the coast of Lima, Oman, causing damage to the engine room.

No injuries have been reported so far, per the agency.

Around three hours later, UKMTO said it had received a report of a second incident, this time northeast of Khasab in Oman.

"The Master of a tanker reports seeing a large splash and explosion in close proximity to the vessel," it said in a warning, adding that no damage to the ship had been reported at the time.

The agency advised vessels in the region to proceed with caution and to dial in any suspicious activity.

Authorities are investigating the incidents.

The Strait of Hormuz

The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, is one of the world's most crucial oil and gas transit chokepoints, carrying roughly a quarter of the global seaborne oil trade.

Tehran effectively closed the waterway following US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, and it has since become a key factor in the ongoing US-Iranian conflict - despite the "memorandum of understanding" agreed between the two sides in June.

On Friday, the US military rejected claims that Iran had reclosed the Strait, saying it remained "open for commercial vessel transit."

"Iran does not control it. Thousands of ships have sailed through the international waterway over the past four months," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said.

The statement came as US President Donald Trump said he was "losing faith" in the prospect of a peace deal and threatened to hit Iran "very hard."

"At some point, they're going to say, 'we just can't take it anymore,'" he added.

A man sits on a surfboard as a container ship and other commercial vessels appear anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 27, 2026. AP photo

US forces renewed strikes on Iran earlier this week after a brief pause, targeting what CENTCOM said were Iranian Revolutionary Guard command centers, maritime capabilities, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defence sites.

"The strikes aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries," CENTCOM said.

The US had carried out 13 consecutive days of strikes on Iran earlier in July in an effort to "degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz."

In response, Tehran launched strikes on American military bases across the Middle East, targeting facilities in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar.

World.title: Could the EU kick Spain out of the Schengen area over the Ceuta crisis?
World.content:
As around 60,000 migrants irregularly entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Several EU countries are asking for Spain to be temporarily excluded from the free-movement Schengen area, a last-resort measure that could only be used in exceptional circumstances.

 

The largest surge of irregular arrivals ever recorded on EU territory in a single day sparked concerns among European governments, despite the fact that Ceuta is located on the African continent, offering migrants no easy route to mainland Europe.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was the first to raise the possibility on Thursday, announcing “extraordinary measures” to defend Italy’s borders.

Italy subsequently reintroduced air and maritime border controls with Spain on Friday, after a meeting chaired by Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi.

Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen backed Italy’s request, calling on other European countries to follow suit, and Denmark Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen suggested considering the option. The call was alsoechoed by leading right-of-centre figures across Europe.

Can Spain be suspended from Schengen?

According to the Schengen Borders Code, the EU could recommend suspending a country’s participation in Schengen as a last-resort measure, to be used only in cases of “persistent serious deficiencies relating to external border control.”

In such a case, the European Commission would need to propose the suspension, which would then have to be approved by the other EU member states.

The concerned country would then be recommended to reinstall controls at its internal borders with other member states.

There is no indication that this procedure will happen anytime soon.

“There are regular evaluations and in case there are serious deficiencies detected at the border crossing point, we issue a report which is then discussed with the member state [concerned] first,” a EU official said, without further speculation.

The Commission also signaled that special rules apply to Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla under the Schengen system, which make them de facto external territories when it comes to free movement.

"There is already border control between Ceuta and Melilla and the rest of the Schengen area," a EU official said.

Any EU country can temporarily reintroduce checks at its internal borders with Spain, for renewable periods of up to six months, as Italy just did for one month.

France already has controls in place at all its land borders, with a decision predating the Ceuta crisis and based on different reasons, including persistent jihadist threats, a rise in antisemitic attacks and rising violence among migrants.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced increased controls at the border after the outbreak of the crisis.

Portugal, the other EU country sharing a land-border with Spain, has not adopted this measure so far, while it said in a press release that "integrity of the Schengen system depends on tight external border controls."

World.title: FIFA bins controversial private investment plan after backlash
World.content:
FIFA has announced it is dropping plans to allow private investors to purchase stakes in major competitions following fierce pushback.

 

In a statement, FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the project had "created divisions" that were "no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."

"Our purpose has always been - and will always be - to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed," he added.

The football world governing body had outlined a proposal in late July that it said would increase funding to its 211 member associations through a new subsidiary running its commercial operations and events, including World Cups.

Dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), the venture aimed to cash in on what Infantino described as the sport's "remarkable commercial value" by inviting third parties to take minority, non-controlling investments in the new entity.

FIFA said FFE could raise up to $4.2 billion based on an initial equity valuation of $20 billion.

UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin, right, and FIFA President Gianni Infantino pose during the 48th UEFA congress in Paris, Thursday, Feb. 8, 2024. Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

In a statement on Saturday, European governing body UEFA said it welcomed FIFA's decision to shelve the proposal, adding that it would now work with its associations and other confederations to "devise a plan" to ensure such a situation did not occur again in the future.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game. We must identify those responsible and hold them to account," UEFA said. "The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family".

Backlash

FIFA's proposal had been widely condemned across the footballing world and beyond, with many accusing Infantino and FIFA of attempting to sell the sport.

UEFA and its 55 member associations threatened to boycott FIFA events over the plan, saying "the World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product."

"No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership," it said on Thursday.

CONCACAF, or the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, also rejected the plan and called for "greater transparency and proper governance" in the wake of the controversy.

The Asian Football Confederation has said it "stands in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF in expressing serious concerns over FIFA’s proposal."

The saga has put Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016, under huge pressure in his role, and prompted the resignation of one of his senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro.

Kevin Lamour, FIFA's chief operating officer, also slammed the investment plan as "the project of one person."

“Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions," he said in a statement to the Associated Press earlier this week.

Infantino had already been facing a wave of criticism over FIFA's handling of a number of incidents in the 2026 World Cup, which was held across the United States, Mexico and Canada - most notably the decision to suspend a ban for USA striker Folarin Balogun.

World.title: Mysterious DNA: two unknown ancestors found in human genome
World.content:
Researchers at the prestigious University of California, Berkeley, have made a spectacular discovery: they identified stretches of DNA in the genomes of modern humans (source in German) that come from previously unknown ancestors. The scientists talk about so-called "ghost ancestors," because nothing is yet known about these extinct human groups.

 

Homo sapiens is today the only human species still alive. In the distant past, however, it shared the Earth with numerous other hominins.

Earlier studies had already shown that modern humans interbred with Neanderthals and the so-called Denisovans and had joint offspring. Many people still carry the genetic traces of these encounters in their DNA today. A new study now suggests that there were at least two further, previously unknown human groups that also passed on DNA to our ancestors.

One of these previously unknown ancestors interbred in Africa with the forebears of modern humans more than 50,000 years ago. This happened before the last major migration wave of Homo sapiens to Europe and Asia. The genes inherited at that time now account for around 1% of the DNA of all humans, roughly as much as the share of Neanderthal DNA.

According to the researchers' calculations, this mysterious human lineage had split from the evolutionary line leading to modern humans around 800,000 years ago, roughly at the time when Neanderthals and Denisovans also diverged from one another.

"Earlier studies had already hypothesised that there is a so-called ghost lineage, meaning genetic traces of unknown extinct human lineages in the genomes of modern humans," explains Berkeley doctoral student Yulin Zhang, one of the study's lead authors. "However, it was previously unclear whether this unknown lineage occurs only in Africans and when this admixture happened. We have now been able to identify and map the relevant DNA segments in the genomes of modern humans and show that this ghost lineage is found in all people living today, not just in Africans."

Timeline: 1.8 million years

Even more enigmatic is the second ancestor, which the researchers describe as a "super-archaic ancestor". This human lineage had already branched off from other hominins around 1.8 million years ago. More than 200,000 years ago, it probably interbred in Eurasia with the Denisovans, and via this detour fragments of the ancient DNA finally found their way into the genome of modern humans.

"The evidence for this super-archaic ancestor is particularly exciting because it reveals genetic contributions from a human lineage that lived more than a million years ago, even though no DNA from this population has yet been decoded," says Arjun Biddanda, a postdoctoral researcher at Johns Hopkins University and co-lead author of the study.

"Thanks to ancient DNA from Neanderthals and Denisovans and new genealogical methods, we are increasingly realising that human populations have repeatedly mixed with one another in the course of evolution," says Priya Moorjani, professor of molecular and cell biology at the University of California, Berkeley. "Human evolution therefore resembles less a branching family tree and more a complex network in which different populations were linked by repeated migrations and admixture."

Difference between Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA

Most people outside Africa today carry about 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA in their genomes. More precisely, on average around 1 to 2% of the genome of present-day Europeans and Asians comes from Neanderthals. This is the result of interbreeding between Neanderthals and early modern humans around 50,000 to 60,000 years ago, shortly after Homo sapiens left Africa.

The inherited DNA segments still influence humans today. Some variants are associated with the immune system, skin and hair traits or adaptation to environmental conditions. Others increase the risk of certain diseases or affect the response to infections.

Population groups in Asia and Oceania also carry, in addition to Neanderthal DNA, genetic contributions from Denisovans. Corresponding remains of Denisovans have mainly been sequenced from the Eurasian region:

The genome of the oldest human fossil yet discovered in Mongolia provided new insights into early human history around six years ago. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig and the Mongolian Academy of Sciences showed that around 25% of the DNA in the approximately 34,000-year-old remains of a woman came from West Eurasian ancestors. The team also found in the woman's genome, as in that of a roughly 40,000-year-old individual from China, DNA traces of Denisovans, the extinct human form that lived in Asia before modern humans arrived there.

It is also interesting that Neanderthals and Denisovans interbred with each other as well. From a fossil from Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains in southern Siberia, near the borders with Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China, it is known that it belonged to a woman with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father, direct evidence that the two human forms had joint offspring.

The skullcap found in the Salkhit Valley in eastern Mongolia comes from a woman who lived around 34,000 years ago. Institut für Archäologie, Mongolische Akademie der Wissenschaften

Exactly who these "ghost ancestors" and the "super-archaic ancestor" were is still unclear. However, the calculated dates of their divergence fit known human forms. The ghost ancestors could have belonged to Homo groups of the Middle Pleistocene that lived in Africa around 800,000 years ago. The super-archaic ancestor, by contrast, could be identical with or closely related to Homo erectus, which populated Eurasia as early as about 1.8 million years ago.

World.title: Tongue tied: Humans once spoke tens of thousands of languages, so what happened?
World.content:
A new study has found that linguistic diversity in human history peaked much later than previously thought and then rapidly declined with the rise of empires.

 

According to the study, published in the journal Science, the languages spoken today are the legacy of the small number of tongues that survived a major 'language bottleneck' in the past.

To reach this conclusion, researchers analysed the linguistic diversity of 171 hunter-gatherer communities living today and used the data to estimate how many languages were spoken on Earth roughly 12,000 years ago, after the last Ice Age.

On that basis, when the global population was still below 7 million, around 4,500 to 6,200 different languages were spoken worldwide.

The number of languages grew for thousands of years

The research suggests that as the world's population grew, so too did linguistic diversity. Between roughly 1,000 and 3,000 years ago – in other words, relatively recently – tens of thousands of different languages were spoken around the globe. The scientists describe this period as the 'golden age' of linguistic diversity.

However, this period did not last long. The study finds that linguistic diversity then entered a rapid and largely irreversible decline.

Claire Bowern, one of the authors of the study, said the most surprising finding was that the peak of linguistic diversity occurred so recently, adding: "The highest level of linguistic diversity may not have occurred in the distant Palaeolithic, as is often assumed, but in the period when states grew and the first empires emerged."

The researchers found that the Age of Empires, which began around 4,000 years ago, did not initially reduce linguistic diversity, but that about 2,000 years ago the number of languages worldwide started to drop 'as if falling off a cliff'.

According to the study, the main driver of this decline was the expansion of multi-ethnic states and large empires.

Strengthening political structures absorbed smaller communities and imposed their own languages, while local tongues gradually disappeared.

Related First Kodavere song festival aims to revive Estonian dialect

Only 7,500 languages remain today

Today, around 7,500 languages are spoken across the world. Although this is higher than the estimated figure 12,000 years ago, it is far lower than the tens of thousands of languages believed to have existed at the peak of diversity.

Data from the Endangered Languages Project suggests that around 3,300 of the languages currently spoken are under serious threat. Of these, 437 are considered critically endangered.

The researchers say that more than 400 languages have vanished completely over the past 50 years. Colonialism stands out as one of the key factors in this process.

For instance, the division of areas inhabited by indigenous communities in Africa's Kalahari Desert by national borders has fractured the communities that speak N|uu. Today, it is thought that only one person is still able to speak this language fluently.

Bans and economic pressure played a role

According to the study, legal prohibitions, violence and forced assimilation have all played an important part in the disappearance of many languages.

In addition, pressure to switch to dominant languages such as English and Spanish has also contributed to the decline in linguistic diversity.

Scientists note that although the current pace of language loss is very high, the new study indicates that extinctions in the past occurred even more rapidly than they do today.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
World.content:
In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.

Are hormones making heatwaves more dangerous for women?

Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up.

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider , an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.

Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."

How to survive heat waves in the city To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A research gap, not a biological difference

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.

The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.

Why does the data suggest otherwise?

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"

Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.

In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.

In scorching Taipei, locals seek ways to survive urban heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The real risk is exposure for women, not biology

If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?

Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studieshow heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

Long working hours, limited breaks, and repeated exposure to heat - women often face greater burdens under these conditions Image: Aaron Favila/AP/dpa

Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.

Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.

For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."

Edited by Ben Knight

World.title: Greece battles wildfires, including near Athens
World.content:
Firefighters were battling blazes in over 70 locations across Greece. Strong winds continue to fan the flames, adding to the firefighters' struggles.

A raging wildfire has continued to engulf a popular coastal resort in Greece, even as hundreds of firefighters battle to put it out amid gusty winds.

The fire broke out on Friday near the coastal village of Agios Vasileios.

More than 300 firefighters have been deployed to control the wildfire, in an effort to prevent it from spreading to the area of Porto Germeno, some 70 kilometres (45 miles) northwest of Athens in the region of Viotia.

"The fire has reached the sea... homes have certainly been damaged," a fire department spokesman told the French AFP news agency.

The Greek fire brigade said it was at the maximum level of alert Image: Costas Baltas/Anadolu

"The winds are very strong. Aircraft are trying to operate as best they can, but some are unable to and have been transferred to another fire (in the Peloponnese) where conditions are milder," he added.

Winds up to 130 kilometres per hour, recorded on Saturday by the weather service of the National Observatory of Athens, have made the fire department's efforts more difficult.

"The environmental damage is huge," the mayor of Thebes, Giorgos Anastasiou, told Open TV.

Fire breaks out in several places across Greece

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, with more than 70 locations in Greece affected by Friday.

The Greek fire brigade said it was at the maximum level of alert, warning that the fire risk was particularly high in the Attica peninsula and in Evia, an island east ‌of Athens where fires are frequent.

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, including on the popular island of Crete Image: Costas Baltas/Anadolu

"The fire has reached the sea... homes have certainly been damaged," a fire department spokesman told AFP.

Theodore Giannaros, a wildfire meteorologist and senior researcher at the National Observatory of Athens on Saturday said the damage to the Porto Germeno area was "inconceivable."

Wildfires have raged in several parts of Greece this week, including the popular island of Crete, affecting some 5,000 hectares on the island. Three firefighters have lost their lives so far.

Several European countries have been battling savage wildfires this summer, amid extreme heatwaves and little rain.
