World.title: War in Ukraine: Why Crimea has become a strategic target
World.content:
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian logistics centers and energy facilities in Crimea. What are the consequences for local supplies, and how does Kyiv hope this strategy will affect the course of the war?

In an attempt to isolate Crimea from the mainland, the Ukrainian armed forces have intensified their attacks on the peninsula, which was invaded and annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine is using long-range drones to attack transports on the M14 highway between the Russian city of Rostov-on-Don and Melitopol in occupied southern Ukraine. It is also targeting Russian shadow fleet ships in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, as well as energy facilities that supply the Russian military.

Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of the Ukrainian forces for unmanned systems, says 196 Russian ships and more than 100 energy facilities have been hit in the past month alone. His figures cannot be independently verified.

Russia appears to be struggling to supply both its military and the civilian population in Crimea. Fuel coupons were issued at the end of May, but ran out after 24 hours, after which gasoline was being traded on the black market. A state of emergency was declared in Crimea, especially Sevastopol, in response to repeated disruption of the electricity and water supply, and of the internet and cellphone networks.

What are residents in Crimea experiencing?

Nina, a pensioner who lives in a village near Feodosiya, southeastern Crimea, told DW about the difficulties people there are facing: Residents there can't cook because of power cuts, and fuel shortages mean public transport only runs intermittently. Nina's worst fear, though, is not having electricity in winter.

Russian-occupied Crimea hit by fuel shortages and power cuts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The longest power cuts have been in the north of Crimea. This is where Ivan lives [name changed]. He tells DW that for some time, people were unable to get hold of fuel with either coupons or cash. The only exceptions, he says, were police officers, state officials, and doctors. For several days, everything collapsed: Cars ran out of fuel and simply came to a stop; people didn't know how they were supposed to get to where they were going.

Ivan said that most shops no longer stock perishable goods, because they can't run their fridges and freezers: "There are no milk products, or fish, or meat," he said. "There are only a few shops with electricity generators, but the prices there are much higher than before."

Some small, private, volunteer initiatives are trying to help. The blogger Olena Gerasimenko works with companies in Simferopol to bring drinking water to people suffering from power cuts, and to hospitals and kindergartens. In her blog, she reports that people are complaining about the lack of help from the Russian-installed "authorities" in Crimea.

On social media, people say that, because of the power cuts and having no means of communication, residents of northern Crimea are sending post by public bus. But the buses aren't running regularly either.

What are Ukraine's tactics?

Ukraine's efforts to block supply routes both in and to Crimea are directed primarily against the small Russian tankers and tugboats that transport oil to larger ships and fuel to the Crimean mainland. Parallel to this, it is also destroying transformer substations. But Commander Brovdi says Ukraine is deliberately sparing the Kerch Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, connecting the peninsula with the Russian region of Krasnodar.

In a recent interview with the Irish journalist Caolan Robertson , Brovdi said the road and rail bridge should be maintained as a corridor for people to escape from Crimea. The aim is not to destroy it, Brovdi says, but to cut off Russian troops from supplies and reinforcements. "We want to make it impossible for the Russian military machine to remain and continue to operate there."

Satellite photo of the Henichesk Bridge, damaged by Ukrainian attacks, and a new, alternative bridge connecting Russian-occupied southern Ukraine to northern Crimea Image: Vantor/REUTERS

The military expert Ivan Kyrychevskyi serves in a Ukrainian drone unit. Speaking to DW he emphasized how important the air attacks on Crimea are for the frontline on the ground. "To stop the Russians getting anywhere near Zaporizhzhia, they have to put pressure on their lines of communication in the occupied south of Ukraine. This applies above all to Crimea. The blockade of shipping traffic in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea essentially has the same objective," says Kyrychevskyi. "For far too long, Crimea has served the Russians as a tranquil harbor and unsinkable aircraft carrier from which to carry out their offensives in southern Ukraine."

Pavlo Narozhnyi, a Ukrainian military expert and founder of the charitable organization Reactive Post, describes Crimea as a massive military base. Russian troops in the regions of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia are heavily dependent on it. Narozhnyi says that for a long time Russian logistics primarily ran through the peninsula, but this supply source is now being cut off on two sides: On land by attacks on the M14 highway, and at sea by attacks on transport vessels near the Crimea Bridge. "This way we are not isolating only Crimea but also the Russian troops in the south of Ukraine," Narozhnyi told DW. His organization supplies life-saving equipment to Ukrainian artillery divisions on the frontline.

Situation 'no worse' than in Ukrainian cities3

Narozhnyi explains that, at present, up to three million people in Crimea depend on Russia for their supplies. "A thermal power station that provided up to 60% of Crimea's entire electricity supply has been destroyed. The supply of oil products has been interrupted. The population is already experiencing problems, even with everyday things." The military expert also warned that these problems will get even worse in the fall, when the weather turns colder and people want to heat their homes. "Putin will then have to deal not only with military problems, but also the problems of the population," Narozhnyi says.

People use flashlights to navigate a dark street during a power outage in Yevpatoriya, Crimea, in July 2026. Image: Alexey Pavlishak/REUTERS

According to Sidharth Kaushal of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London, attacks on power stations do not automatically contravene international law, particularly if the facilities have military significance and the attacks comply with the rule of proportionality.

Ukrainian experts confirm that the targeted facilities primarily supply electricity for military facilities. Kaushal told DW that he assumed a large-scale blockade strategy by Ukraine could ultimately compel Moscow to negotiate a ceasefire.

Commander Brovdi is asking people to be patient. "I apologize to the residents of Crimea, the Ukrainians, for the current difficulties. They are experiencing restrictions of advantages they have enjoyed all their lives – the supply of energy, water, and communications. But they are in a situation no worse than that of people in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Nikopol, Kherson, and hundreds of other cities that are targeted on a daily basis."

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

World.title: How crypto miners are stealing power in Southeast Asia
World.content:
Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids, and exposing links to organized crime.

A raid in Malaysia last week exposed how cryptocurrency mining is becoming entangled with electricity theft and organized crime across Southeast Asia.

In Malaysia's southern state of Johor, 71 cryptocurrency-mining machines had been running around the clock across four rented premises for about a month before police moved in.

During the raids on July 22 and 23, officers arrested three suspects and seized computers, routers and vehicles alongside equipment used to illegally mine Bitcoin.

Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said the syndicate bypassed electricity meters, leading to an estimated €14,500 ($16,600) in losses in about a month, according to local media reports. The machines were thought to be generating between €17,200 and €21,500 in monthly revenue.

The case was relatively small by Malaysian standards. Between 2020 and 2025, national utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) identified almost 14,000 premises linked to electricity theft for cryptocurrency mining. Its cumulative losses reached around €1.1 billion.

Recorded cases of such theft increased from 610 in 2018 to 2,397 in 2024, according to Malaysia's Energy Ministry, which has described illegal mining as a serious threat to public safety, economic stability, and the national electricity system.

"In Malaysia, thousands of incidents have triggered investigations into illegal mining for cryptocurrency purposes," said Sonny Zulhuda, associate professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

"This poses a huge problem for the security of electricity resources, economic sustainability, competition, and revenue loss," Zulhuda told DW. "Enforcement has been lagging behind, due to a lack of legislative preparedness and limited agency capability in enforcement and investigation. This is unfortunate because Malaysia is fast developing its digital infrastructure."

Where crypto mining meets organized crime

Cryptocurrency mining is not inherently criminal, but authorities are increasingly finding links between illegal crypto mining, online gambling, money laundering, and Southeast Asia's industrial-scale cyber scam networks.

Last October, the United States and the UK sanctioned the Cambodia-based Prince Group and associated companies, alleging that the network operated forced-labor scam compounds and laundered proceeds through cryptocurrencies and other assets.

US authorities also seized Bitcoin worth around $15 billion at the time from wallets whose private keys were held by Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi, describing the cryptocurrency as proceeds and instruments of fraud and money laundering.

Inside Cambodia's scam industry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thailand's Department of Special Investigation has made the clearest connection between stolen electricity and transnational crime.

In 2025, investigators dismantled three major illegal crypto mining networks, seized more than 6,390 machines and estimated losses to the Provincial Electricity Authority at more than €24.9 million.

In one operation, authorities found around 1,900 mining machines at warehouse sites. The electricity authority estimated that the network was consuming power worth around €575,000 each month while paying only a fraction of the amount due.

Indonesia battles crypto mining crimes as well

Indonesia has seen similar cases. In December 2023, police in the province of North Sumatra raided ten sites and seized more than 1,100 Bitcoin-mining machines. State utility PLN estimated losses over six months at around €700,000.

Governments have responded with raids, tougher penalties and cooperation between police, utilities, regulators and anti-corruption agencies. Malaysia has created a multi-agency committee and deployed smart meters at substations to identify abnormal consumption.

But enforcement remains difficult. Equipment can be moved quickly, premises can be rented through intermediaries and meter tampering may involve organized networks or insider assistance.

Saaidal Razalli Azzuhri, a telecommunications expert at the University of Malaya, told DW that raids should be supported by transformer-level monitoring, mandatory licensing, disclosure of companies' beneficial owners, and investigations tracing bank transfers and cryptocurrency wallets.

"The objective should not be to prohibit blockchain technology, but to ensure that miners pay the full economic cost of their electricity and do not transfer their costs and infrastructure risks to the public," he said.

Zulhuda said that Southeast Asian governments need to deal with this issue properly so they don't send the wrong message to companies that want to invest in the region's growing digital sectors.

Malaysia has several laws to curb illegal cyber activities, including the Cyber Security Act 2024 to protect its National Critical Information Infrastructure and the recently enacted Cybercrimes Act 2026 to address digital system misuse and abuse, he added.

Laos pulls the plug

Laos shows that even legal, state-backed cryptocurrency mining can struggle to deliver the promised benefits.

Scam factory: Behind Asia's cyber slavery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In mid-2021, the government authorized six companies to mine and trade cryptocurrencies. The plan appeared suited to a country that had invested heavily in hydropower and sometimes produced more electricity than its economy could absorb. Mining offered a way to monetize surplus energy.

At its peak in 2021 and 2022, the industry consumed around 500 megawatts. But the surplus proved unreliable.

Some miners accumulated unpaid bills. More importantly, officials concluded that the industry created few jobs and little demand for domestic suppliers compared with manufacturing or other commercial activities.

Deputy Energy Minister Chanthaboun Soukaloun said last October that the government intended to end electricity supplies to miners.

Laos wants to redirect the power towards metals processing, electric-vehicle manufacturing and artificial intelligence data centers, while increasing electricity exports to neighboring countries.

The experiment offered a broader warning. Cheap electricity can attract crypto miners, but it does not guarantee lasting investment or wider development. When operators steal power, or consume subsidized electricity without creating much value, the public is left carrying the cost.

Edited by Keith Walker

World.title: Germany weighs the future of minijobs
World.content:
Germany's popular minijob system allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions. But a reform is on the cards that may soon end this advantage.

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests. The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.

Abdollahi says she likes "almost everything" about her job at the University of Cologne's physics library — the only exception is the occasional tedious task, such as taking inventory of the library's collection. But even that doesn't bother her too much — after all, she only works twice a week for around five hours at a time.

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob", whichthe country's government is considering eliminating in its current form.

Minijobs popular with women and students

A minijob is a form of part-time employment in Germany which pays a maximum of €603 (around $685) per month. As long as employees don't earn more than this amount, they don't have to pay social insurance contributions or income tax.

Minijobbers can also opt out of paying their share of pension contributions — and most of them do just that.

A minijobber typically works around 10 hours per week to reach the €603 cap, making it an ideal job for those with other commitments, such as students or stay-at-home parents. Women make up around 57% of all minijobbers, according to Germany's central agency for minijobs.

The agency also estimates that nearly 7 million of Germany's 45 million employees have a minijob. Some of them have it in addition to another job, while others have a minijob as their only form of employment.

Minijobs were introduced in the 1960s to facilitate low-level employment with little bureaucracy and to combat moonlighting. In 2003, they were redesigned as part of a comprehensive labor market reform.

They have long been criticized for reinforcing gender inequality in the job market, as minijobs are held disproportionately often by women, preventing them from building up substantial pensions.

Are Germany's 'mini-jobs' being scrapped? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What are the benefits for employers?

Employers typically pay a flat tax of 2% on minijobbers' wages, as well as social contributions amounting to around 30% of gross pay. Despite these additional costs, many businesses rely on minijobbers because they offer flexibility.

"There are operational situations where hiring someone only makes sense if the number of hours is truly minimal," Holger Schäfer, a senior economist specializing in labor market economics at the German Economic Institute (IW), told DW.

Supermarkets, for example, need more cashiers on Saturday afternoons than they do on Monday mornings, making minijobs an easy way to fill the staffing gap. The extra weekend work is also why retail and hospitality are the two industries that employ the most minijobbers.

How could minijobs change?

In early July, Germany's governing coalition announced its plans to raise the flat tax rate for minijobs from 2% to 5%. The government also stated its intention to fully implement the Pension Commission's proposals, which were presented in late June and aim to ensure the sustainability of Germany's pension system in the future.

One of these proposals focuses specifically on minijobs, and would eliminate the opt-out option for pension contributions and abolish the special status of minijobs. This would make minijobbers subject to regular social security contributions, effectively bringing an end to minijobs in their current form. According to the commission, this would strengthen social security systems, reduce the risk of poverty in old age, and address gender inequalities.

For Abdollahi, it could mean earning up to €130 less per month. The 26-year-old says she would probably try to increase her work hours to make up for the loss.

She could also get a research job that would require her to work for up to 20 hours per week, but this would considerably slow down the pace of her studies. "Even with my admittedly very chill job here, on the days I work, I usually don't study," Abdollahi explained.

What Germans young and old think about the pension system To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How is the proposal being received?

Many labor unions have welcomed the proposal, including Nahrung-Genuss-Gaststätten (NGG), a trade union representing workers in the food, beverage, catering, and hospitality industries.

"Minijobs have not proven to be a bridge to good employment; rather, they cement precarious working conditions for millions of people," the NGG cited their chairman Guido Zeitler in a press statement.

Enzo Weber, a labor market expert from the Institute for Employment Research (IAB), believes the reform may encourage people to work more or pursue different career paths. It would "prevent people from getting stuck in the minijob trap" and "ensure that women's career development doesn't stall during child-rearing years, since they simply remain in low-paying jobs due to misguided tax incentives," Weber told DW.

Business representatives, however, have pushed back against the proposed changes. "Abolishing minijobs would be a mistake," argued Rainer Dulger, president of the Federal Association of German Employers' Organizations, adding that minijobs help businesses remain flexible and tap into additional labor potential.

IW economist Schäfer, meanwhile, doubts that abolishing minijobs would encourage people to work significantly more hours. He also notes that a €600 job fully subject to social security contributions would generate rather small additional benefits. "It's simply not worth it to set the entire social security machinery in motion for such employment relationships," Schäfer said.

Still, he sees room for reform when it comes to people who take on a minijob alongside their primary employment. "We have an economic misallocation of resources when a skilled worker would rather deliver pizza after work than work overtime in their actual main job," he explained. "But that doesn't mean we have to abolish minijobs altogether."

German pension plans draw praise, criticism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Exemptions for university students?

The Pension Commission's proposals also include an exemption for school students, which would allow them to continue working minijobs in their current form. Now, the Social Democratic Party (SPD) is considering whether this exemption could be extended to university students.

Abdollahi believes that would be the right decision. "They are one of the groups that need it the most, especially students from outside the EU," she said.

Abdollahi's own minijob at the library allowed her to enter the German labor market more easily and helped her improve her language skills. "It gives me a chance to practice German in a low-pressure environment," she noted.

But Abdollahi and other students in Germany now have to wait to learn what will happen to minijobs, as the government is expected to debate the proposed changes later this year.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Sami Behbehani contributed to this report.

World.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy says Patriot missile shortage costs lives
World.content:
At least nine people died, and more than 20 were injured after Russia struck Ukraine's capital with ballistic missiles. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blames a lack of interceptor missiles for the deaths.

At least nine people died and 23 were injured after Russia struck Ukraine's capital city Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on Saturday morning.

The missiles struck several homes and a five-storey residential building, while cars were also set alight.

Several buildings in Kyiv caught fire during the onslaught Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

What else do we know about the damage from the attack?

Four children were among the 23 injured, the emergency service said.

In a post on his Telegram account, Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said that several people were trapped in a damaged residential building during the attack.

The first and second floors of the building had partially collapsed, he said, while some warehouses in the city were also on fire.

'Fire and destruction' affected 5 Kyiv districts, emergency services said Image: Sergei Supinsky/AFP

Zelenskyy stresses need for defense systems

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched 35 missiles overnight, including 27 ballistic missiles, as well as 185 attack drones. He said only one ballistic missile was intercepted, blaming a shortage of interceptors for Ukraine's Patriot air defense systems.

"As usual, the Russians struck ordinary residential buildings," Zelenskyy said, adding that 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy and infrastructure facilities were damaged.

"Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people," he said. "And every night without them results in more casualties."

The attacks come as Moscow has intensified its bombing campaigns in recent weeks and months.

Last week,Zelenskyy met with his US counterpart Donald Trump and the UK's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham as he seeks increased support to boost Ukraine's air defences.

World.title: Sánchez afea la actitud “egoísta” de algunos gobiernos europeos por la crisis de Ceuta y pide una reunión urgente de la UE
World.content:
El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, en la Asamblea de Ceuta, este viernes.

El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

“La Unión Europea no puede permitirse este tipo de reacción egoísta, polarizadora e ilegal”, dice Sanchez por carta. Italia, Alemania y otros 22 países piden a Bruselas coordinación para el control de la frontera

El presidente del Gobierno de España, Pedro Sánchez, ha acusado a varios gobiernos europeos de actuar en la crisis de Ceuta movidos por el “prejuicio, las noticias falsas, la ignorancia o el interés político” y calificó su respuesta a la situación migratoria en la ciudad autónoma española de “egoísta, polarizadora e ilegal”. En una carta remitida a la cúpula de las instituciones comunitarias, Sánchez carga contra la reacción de algunos de sus socios de la UE (sin poner nombres) y pide una reunión urgente de ministros del Interior, después de que Italia suspendiera su cooperación Schengen con España y Finlandia y Dinamarca plantearan abiertamente la posibilidad de excluir temporalmente su cooperación de libre circulación con Madrid. España estima que más de 48.000 de las alrededor de 50.000 que entraron en Ceuta desde Marruecos ya han regresado.

“La reacción de los Gobiernos europeos ha sido bastante asimétrica”, dice el presidente español en su misiva, remitida a la presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, al presidente del Consejo Europeo, Antonio Costa, y a Micheál Martin, primer ministro de Irlanda, el país que tiene este semestre la presidencia semestral del Consejo de la UE. “La mayoría nos ha mostrado su apoyo y solidaridad y nos ha ofrecido su ayuda. Otros, sin embargo, han optado por atacar a España y pedir su exclusión temporal del espacio Schengen”, ha criticado Sánchez en el texto, en el que muestra su “profunda preocupación” por esa reacción de “algunos Gobiernos europeos”.

Carta de Pedro Sánchez a Bruselas.

El gobierno español reclama que la actitud de esos socios es “contraria al derecho europeo, al derecho humanitario y a los principios de solidaridad” que sustentan la Unión. Una acusación de incumplimiento legal, no solo político. Sánchez recuerda en su afilada carta que Ceuta no forma parte del espacio Schengen —lo que resta sentido jurídico, según su argumento, a cualquier amenaza de suspensión— y cita datos de Frontex, la agencia de fronteras europea, para asegurar que España registra la mitad de entradas irregulares que Italia entre 2021 y 2026, pese a ser el único Estado miembro con frontera terrestre con África.

Asegura que España restableció “plenamente” el control fronterizo en menos de 48 horas, devolvió a “prácticamente la totalidad” de los migrantes llegados de forma irregular y evitó cualquier movimiento no autorizado hacia el resto de Europa. Todo ello, según la carta, “con muy poco apoyo de otros Estados europeos”.

El ministro del Interior irlandés, Jim O’Callaghan, habló el viernes con su homólogo español, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, sobre la crisis de Ceuta. Además, Irlanda, como presidencia de turno del Consejo de la UE, ha convocado para este sábado una reunión del Mecanismo Integrado de Respuesta a la Crisis Política, activado en relación a la migración desde 2015, en la que los expertos de los Estados miembros analizarán la situación. Los representantes de los países ante la UE también mantendrán una reunión el lunes sobre este asunto.

Policías y militares españoles trasladan a un amplio grupo de migrantes hasta la frontera después de las entradas masivas desde Marruecos por vía terrestre y marítima hacia Ceuta este sábado. Falta de solidaridad

Sánchez plasma la falta de solidaridad y de reciprocidad de algunos de sus socios —que han aprovechado para cargar contra su política migratoria y contra la regularización masiva que llevó a cabo España hace unos meses— en episodios concretos y afirma que España acogió a migrantes llegados a Europa del Este a través de Bielorrusia en 2021, cuando el dictador Aleksandr Lukashenko utilizó a solicitantes de asilo para lanzar un ataque híbrido contra la UE, y a la isla italiana de Lampedusa en 2023.

La actitud de esos gobiernos europeos, sostiene Sánchez, “resulta contraria a los intereses a largo plazo de Europa y al sentido común más básico, ya que Ceuta no forma parte del espacio Schengen, prácticamente no quedan migrantes sin devolver y, según Frontex, España es una de las fronteras menos permeables de la UE”.

Sánchez ya había respondido públicamente y por separado a las críticas de Italia, citando en redes sociales las mismas cifras de Frontex y afirmando que “la solidaridad y la empatía son opcionales; el respeto a los tratados europeos y a los hechos, no”. La ministra finlandesa de Interior, Mari Rantanen, había acusado a España de haber “fracasado por completo” en la protección de la frontera exterior de la Unión, mientras la primera ministra danesa, Mette Frederiksen, pedía valorar “todas las posibilidades, incluida la suspensión de la cooperación de Schengen”.

La Comisión Europea ha sostenido que la expulsión de un Estado miembro de Schengen no puede decidirse unilateralmente y corresponde, en su caso, al Consejo; el presidente del Consejo Europeo, António Costa, había respaldado ya públicamente la respuesta del Gobierno español a la crisis.

World.title: Las mejores playas en los alrededores de Santander
World.content:
Los Tranquilos. La preciosa y relajada playa de Los Tranquilos –por algo su nombre– es, en realidad, la prolongación del arenal que a lo largo de seis kilómetros se extiende desde el Puntal, que penetra en plena bahía de Santander, hasta la localidad de Loredo después de pasar por el paraíso surfista de Somo. Los Tanquilos se encuentra, pues, al final de esta increíble franja de arena que permite el baño, bien en las calmadas aguas de la bahía o, hacia el otro lado, entre las agitadas olas del mar abierto, donde se ubica Los Tanquilos. La mejor manera de venir es también en una de las embarcaciones que comunican Santander con Somo y desde allí en un agradable paseo por la orilla. En un ecosistema dunar, las vistas a la inmensidad azul del Cantábrico y la isla de Santa Marina son un regalo añadido que quienes visitan esta playa por primera vez no podían imaginar.

World.title: De la vivienda a la amenaza climática: así ha cambiado la forma de proteger las cosas que nos importan
World.content:
En los últimos 50 años, las prioridades aseguradoras de los españoles han evolucionado y compañías como Allianz se han amoldado dando un paso más: adaptarse al gran reto de anticipar los riesgos derivados de las nuevas amenazas digitales y el cambio climático.

En 1976, año en que EL PAÍS llegó a los quioscos, el gran sueño y prioridad de las familias españolas era la consolidación del hogar: el piso en propiedad, el patrimonio familiar construido con décadas de esfuerzo. En aquel momento, el sector seguros ya recaudaba 132.000 millones de pesetas (unos 793 millones de euros), y llegó un punto en el que ya no sólo se trataba de proteger cuatro paredes, sino toda una nueva forma de vida, con aventurados proyectos empresariales, con comodidades inéditas, con inmuebles y bienes materiales en abundancia, que se abría camino y requería ser asegurada. El estado de bienestar.

Esta relación entre progreso y riesgo viene de mucho antes. Hace casi cuatro mil años, un mercader babilonio que preparaba una travesía comercial ya sabía que un imprevisto podía arruinar de un plumazo su empresa. Para protegerse, los antiguos recurrían a un mecanismo recogido en el Código de Hammurabi, el llamado préstamo a la gruesa ventura, un contrato en el que un prestamista costeaba el viaje del comerciante y asumía el riesgo financiero de la misión. Si la expedición llegaba a buen puerto, el prestamista recibía de vuelta el dinero con intereses añadidos; en cambio, si la expedición fracasaba, el prestamista perdía el capital adelantado. Aquel sistema fue una de las primeras formas documentadas de transferencia (o reparto o división) del riesgo.

Desde Babilonia hasta hoy: el concepto de seguro a lo largo del tiempo Compartir el riesgo como cuestión de supervivencia En la Antigüedad, babilonios, griegos, romanos o comerciantes chinos ya idearon fórmulas para repartir las pérdidas entre varias personas. Préstamos marítimos, fondos comunes, diversificación y protección de las mercancías (con mecanismos como el que se recoge en el Código de Hammurabi, en la imagen) sentaron las bases de los tres principios que sigue definiendo el seguro: compartir el riesgo, dividirlo entre el máximo número de entidades posibles y compensar así las pérdidas. El comercio inventa el seguro moderno El auge del comercio marítimo hizo del riesgo en un elemento que podía calcularse. Entre los siglos XIV y XVIII, en ciudades como Génova, Venecia o Barcelona, nacieron las primeras pólizas, mientras que en Londres, Lloyd's (en la imagen) impulsó un sistema de corredores que revolucionó la forma de asegurar barcos y mercancías marítimas. Los avances en matemáticas y estadística permitieron, además, calcular las primas con criterios científicos. La Revolución Industrial multiplica los riesgos Ferrocarriles, fábricas y grandes ciudades trajeron nuevas oportunidades en el siglo XIX, pero también nuevos peligros. Se popularizaron los seguros para accidentes laborales, catástrofes (en la imagen, un perito de Allianz evalúa los daños del terremoto de San Francisco de 1906), responsabilidad civil o transporte. En este contexto, en 1890 nació Allianz como aseguradora especializada en transporte y accidentes, un reflejo de las necesidades de una economía cada vez más industrializada. Del patrimonio a la protección social Ya en el siglo XX, el seguro dejó de ser una herramienta exclusiva del comercio para convertirse en una pieza esencial de la vida cotidiana. Los sistemas públicos de salud y pensiones, junto con la expansión internacional de las aseguradoras, ampliaron la protección frente a los principales riesgos implícitos en la sociedad de masas y el estado de bienestar: el trabajo (como muestra la campaña de Allianz de 1958 que recoge la imagen), la vivienda, el automóvil o la jubilación. El reto de la anticipación En la actualidad, el sector afronta desafíos globales como los ciberataques o el cambio climática, con la inteligencia artificial, el análisis de datos o los seguros conectados como herramientas esenciales para anticipar problemas y personalizar coberturas. El seguro evoluciona y pasa de una lógica reactiva —indemnizar después del daño— a una cada vez más preventiva.

Es decir: la historia del seguro es la historia de lo que hemos necesitado proteger según el momento. El comercio marítimo, la industrialización, la expansión del automóvil, el estado de bienestar o la revolución digital, entre otros hitos históricos, han ido ampliando el mapa de riesgos y dirigiendo la brújula de los seguros. Allianz, una compañía alemana nacida en 1890 para cubrir los riesgos del transporte y los accidentes que se multiplicaron en plena revolución industrial, hoy opera en un escenario marcado por la conectividad, la inteligencia artificial y las amenazas climáticas. Lo hace en 70 países, entre los que se cuenta España, donde la compañía tomó su forma actual en 1999, fruto de la integración de varias aseguradoras nacionales. La filosofía, en un mundo acelerado e hiperconectado, es clara: servirse de la innovación para mejorar el servicio y anticiparse al riesgo antes de que suceda.

Una de las primeras agencias de Allianz en Bonn (Alemania), en 1907.

Veit Stutz, CEO de Allianz Seguros, entiende que esta transformación de los riesgos empuja a los seguros a repensarse y abrazar los últimos avances como la inteligencia artificial. Esta evolución de las empresas del sector, sin embargo, no depende únicamente de adoptar la tecnología de turno, sino que descansa en la sana combinación del avance con el conocimiento humano: “La inteligencia artificial no sustituye el talento comercial, lo acelera. Nuestro objetivo es que cada cliente reciba un asesoramiento de mayor calidad y que nuestros mediadores dispongan de las mejores herramientas para conseguirlo”.

La IA es una de las apuestas principales de Allianz, que ha desarrollado en España un modelo de entrenamiento en el que sus agentes se forman mediante avatares basados en el algoritmo, capaces de personificar diferentes roles para reproducir situaciones reales de asesoramiento y venta. Tal ha sido el éxito del programa que varios directivos de distintos países han viajado a Madrid para tratar de replicar este sistema en sus mercados: “Que esta iniciativa nacida en España se haya convertido en referencia para el Allianz demuestra nuestra capacidad de innovar y generar valor desde aquí”, explica Stutz.

1890 De asegurar transportes y accidentes… Allianz nació en Berlín el 5 de febrero de 1890 de la mano del actuario Carl Von Thieme (en la imagen) y el banquero Wilhelm Finck. Con un capital inicial de cuatro millones de marcos, comenzó ofreciendo seguros de transporte y accidentes en plena revolución industrial, cuando el crecimiento económico propició riesgos inéditos que requerían nuevas formas de protección. La empresa alemana se expandió con velocidad: en 1929 ya operaba en 30 países y, en 1956, se convirtió en la primera empresa privada europea en incorporar un ordenador IBM650, un hito que anticipaba la transformación tecnológica que estaba por llegar. 2026 …a asegurar un mundo conectado y en peligro climático Hoy, 136 años después, Allianz se ha convertido en uno de los principales grupos aseguradores y gestores de activos del mundo: está presente en cerca de 70 países, cuenta con alrededor de 97 millones de clientes particulares y empresas y supera los 156.000 empleados, además de patrocinar a múltiples entidades (como el estadio del FC Bayern de Múnich, club de fútbol alemán, en la imagen). El objetivo es repensar la protección del ciudadano frente a las dos amenazas más acuciantes de nuestro tiempo: los ciberataques (2.000 millones de dólares en primas en todo el mundo) y el impacto del cambio climático (con unas pérdidas aseguradas por catástrofes naturales que rondan los 130.000 millones de dólares anuales desde 2020.

Otro ejemplo muy gráfico de aplicación de la IA en Allianz es el que explica Victoria Medina, CTDO (jefa de tecnología) de la empresa: “Tenemos un proyecto al que coloquialmente llamamos Minority Report [como aquella película de ciencia ficción en la que Tom Cruise tenía el poder de anticiparse a los crímenes] que nos permite solventar la insatisfacción de los clientes antes de que se produzca”. ¿Cómo? “Gracias a la IA, podemos detectar cuando un cliente no está contento por cómo se está gestionando un siniestro, o recibir una alerta cuando la resolución de un siniestro se está demorando. Así, nos anticipamos antes de que el cliente nos llame enfadado, lo que propicia una gestión más rápida y ágil”, detalla Medina.

De la reacción a la anticipación: el nuevo paradigma de los seguros

Los riesgos a asegurar han ido cambiando a raíz del desarrollo tecnológico y los nuevos hábitos de consumo. Fenómenos como la exposición a los ciberataques, la vulnerabilidad de la identidad digital o el incremento de catástrofes meteorológicas extremas exigen hoy un paradigma distinto en el que ya no basta con indemnizar el daño: se busca prevenirlo antes de que se produzca.

Para abordar esta nueva realidad, Allianz está desarrollando y recurriendo a sistemas de vanguardia, con más de 600 aplicaciones de IA escalables que se sirven de la gran masa de información que generan los dispositivos conectados para fijar precios, evaluar riesgos o agilizar la gestión de los siniestros. El resultado: una protección en tiempo real, inteligente y a medida de cada persona. Un capítulo en el que la compañía aseguradora ha invertido cerca de 6.500 millones de euros en 2025.

El cliente tiene que poder acceder como y cuando quiera a nosotros. Si tiene que contratar una póliza a las once de la noche, debe ser posible hacerlo de forma rápida y sencilla” Veit Stutz, CEO de Allianz

Veit Stutz, CEO de Allianz, incide en cómo la IA está redefiniendo el mundo de los seguros a pasos agigantados: “Estamos pasando de compensar daños a anticipar riesgos, de cubrir problemas a prevenirlos. Queremos acompañar a las personas en momentos de incertidumbre”. En esta misma línea, Victoria Medina enfatiza la noción de tecnología al servicio del cliente: “Nos enfrentamos a un contexto marcado por la aceleración tecnológica y a clientes cada vez más exigentes. La esencia del trabajo no ha cambiado, pero podemos ser más eficaces apoyándonos en la innovación y las nuevas tecnologías”.

Así, Allianz ha desarrollado con éxito una solución que monitoriza en tiempo real más de 50 millones de hectáreas de terreno en España para prevenir incendios mediante el uso de IA, observación satelital avanzada y modelos predictivos. Esta solución, creada en colaboración con la empresa Satellites on Fire, es capaz de reducir el tiempo de detección en una media de 35 minutos e identificar hasta un 30% más incendios. Además, los datos que acumula esta herramienta sirven para avisar al cliente cuando sus bienes asegurados se encuentren próximos a focos de potencial propagación.

El objeto de nuestras preocupaciones, aquello que queremos proteger, ha mutado de forma constante al ritmo de la propia sociedad. Si hace cuatro mil años el reto era salvaguardar una mercancía babilónica en alta mar y hace medio siglo salvaguardar la vivienda, hoy la prioridad es la seguridad digital o la resiliencia climática. Dentro de esta gran transformación, la tecnología no altera el fin último del seguro, pero sí le proporciona un nuevo poder: la capacidad de otorgar una protección previsora, proactiva e inteligente que vaya por delante del siniestro.

World.title: Rosa Vañó (Castillo de Canena): “Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego con las que he trabajado”
World.content:
Economista de formación, dejó su exitosa carrera de directiva en Coca-Cola para desarrollar, junto a su hermano Francisco, la explotación olivarera que había creado su padre en Jaén. Además, conoce muy bien el mundo de las discográficas ya que trabajó para Warner Music y Universal

Es la gran dama del aceite español. Rosa Vañó (Madrid, 63 años), economista de formación, abandonó una exitosa carrera como directiva de Coca-Cola, donde se dedicaba al desarrollo de nuevas líneas de negocio, lanzamientos y reposicionamiento de productos, para dedicarse, junto a su hermano Francisco, al sueño que inició su padre, Luis Vañó: impulsar Castillo de Canena, una explotación olivarera con almazara situada en Canena (Jaén), propiedad de su familia y reconocida con numerosos premios nacionales e internacionales. Anteriormente trabajó en las discográficas Warner Music y Universal, “donde aprendí a gestionar egos y a entender que hay que contar con los medios de comunicación como embajadores y transmisores de la creatividad y el valor añadido de los músicos”. Ejerce también como tesorera de la Real Academia de Gastronomía.

Pregunta. Con este bagaje, decide desarrollar su propio negocio.

Respuesta. Sí, porque teníamos la enorme suerte de tener campo, almazara y también el castillo. Se puede empezar de cero, pero de distintas formas. Es un recorrido profesional que te va formando y quitando miedos. La ignorancia es muy valiente y te hace creer que puedes hacer las cosas mejor, de forma diferente y de manera especial. Todo esto cuesta mucho trabajo. Primero, porque no es fácil hacerlo y porque hay mucha gente que lo hace igual o mejor que tú. Al final, la fórmula no es otra que trabajo, pero bien entendido.

P. ¿Qué significa esto?

R. El trabajo no son horas, es calidad y flexibilidad. Los peores resultados los he tenido cuando he trabajado 14 horas al día. He sido menos resolutiva y creativa. Me parece importante la conectividad para mi conciliación como madre, como hija y como profesional. Son las tres prioridades de mi vida. El teléfono me permite tener mi sitio de trabajo en cualquier lugar.

P. Comentaba que sabe manejar los egos. ¿Se ha encontrado con muchos?

R. Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego que he conocido y con la que he trabajado en mi vida. Me tocó trabajar con ella en promoción y en gira. Por el contrario, con Phil Collins o los hermanos Young [Malcolm y Angus], de AC/DC, me he divertido mucho. Son personas que han dejado el ego a un lado. Y no tiene nada que ver con que sean hombres o mujeres. Por ejemplo, Prince era un hombre que tenía inseguridades, pero con una gestión muy peculiar de su ego. Porque el ego no es solo el de tipo Madonna, en el que tienes que interpretar su gestión, sino también cómo se siente, cómo es su timidez y cómo tienes que relacionarte con él. Seal tampoco era una persona fácil. Fue mi primer artista y era complicado de manejar.

P. ¿Qué se hace en esos casos?

R. Callar, entender y destensar la situación, aunque no tengas la culpa. Hay que intentar destensar y tratar de ser empático y resolutivo. El ego es más complejo que creerse superior, por eso hay que entender cómo es la personalidad de cada uno. Ha sido una gran escuela de vida.

P. Salir a vender aceite por el mundo habrá sido mucho más fácil, ¿no?

R. La primera vez que salí a vender aceite fue en España. Entré en un restaurante, que no voy a decir cuál, por la puerta principal. Me preguntaron a qué iba y les dije que a vender aceite. Me dijeron que eso era por la puerta de proveedores, que estaba por detrás, donde estaban los cubos de basura y los cascos de botellas. Entré por ahí. Hoy, si no me dicen lo contrario, siempre entro por la puerta de proveedores. Entiendo que, si el cocinero me tiene que recibir en su cocina para probar el aceite, esa es la puerta. Hay que entender cada situación.

P. ¿Ha hecho mucha calle?

R. Al principio hay que hacer mucha calle. Ahora también, pero tenemos más gente que te ayuda. Estoy en un momento de mi vida en el que tengo que mirarlo todo con mucha positividad. Lo mejor es hoy y tengo que estar preparada para el día de mañana. Debe haber un relevo. Hay decisiones que ya no me toca tomar a mí, sino al equipo, a mi sobrino y a mi hijo [ambos se llaman Luis y llevan el apellido Vañó]. Me pueden pedir opinión, pero no puedo empecinarme en que la decisión es mía porque hay gente alrededor que tiene que liderar. Odiaría ser la típica persona que es la primera que llega a la oficina y la última que se va. O la que va todos los días, con 80 años, a ver qué pasa.

P. ¿A qué dedica el resto del tiempo cuando no trabaja?

R. Voy a ir por orden de frivolidad. Me gusta jugar al golf; hago pilates tres días a la semana, que me divierte mucho, y camino. Soy una gran aficionada a viajar, pero con causa. Mi afición siempre ha sido la antropología, la arqueología y el arte antiguo. Me ha interesado saber cuándo el hombre deja de ser animal y adquiere un toque divino o humano. Me gusta viajar con contenido, por ejemplo, para ver el románico del norte de España, el misterio de las catedrales, conocer culturas antiguas... Es algo que no he hecho en los últimos años todo lo que me habría gustado y me gustaría retomarlo. Coger un barco y recorrer las esclusas francesas, pararte en los vignerons y vas viendo el paisaje, me gusta. Me voy a dedicar a viajar más. También he descuidado mucho mi afición a las exposiciones. Antes iba prácticamente todos los meses a ver dos exposiciones en Madrid y, si tenía que irme fuera, también lo hacía. Pero ahora, por mi situación personal, he descuidado un poco esa faceta. Me encantaba ir con toda la familia a ver una exposición y luego irnos a comer. Me parece gratificante. Adoro leer.

P. ¿Cuál es su género preferido?

R. Leo mucha historia, pero como formo parte de varias tertulias literarias me hacen leer todo tipo de libros. Uno de los más recientes ha sido Historia de una escalera. También acabo de leer varias obras de Hermann Hesse para una tertulia. Me esfuerzo por leer cosas diferentes de las que suelo leer durante el insomnio.

P. ¿Qué lee en esas noches en vela?

R. Leo a Agatha Christie y a sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Quiero lecturas ligeras para quedarme dormida. La ópera me ha encantado toda la vida. He estado en distintos teatros, como el Bolshói o La Scala de Milán. Verdi y Puccini me encantan porque mi madre me los ponía de pequeña. Voy a cuatro o cinco óperas al año. También me encanta la música barroca. No me pierdo los ciclos de Händel en el Auditorio Nacional de Música de Madrid.

P. ¿Qué restaurantes frecuenta?

R. Tanto de producto y muy clásicos como sorprendentes y de vanguardia. Me gustan los dos extremos. Estuve hace poco en Desde 1911 y trabaja con un gran producto. También me gustan las verduras de Saddle o el ganso de Navidad, que tomo con mis hijos. Los atunes guisados de El Campero me encantan. No me gustan los crudos. Estuve hace poco en Tetsu y me pareció espectacular y divertido. De Jaén me gustan Juan Carlos García, de Vandelvira, y Pedro Sánchez, de Bagá; también Dani Carnero, del restaurante Kaleja en Málaga. Son maravillosos. Y José Álvarez, en la costa de Almería, con su proyecto de tomates.

P. ¿Su desayuno preferido?

R. Una tostada de pan bien caliente, restregada con ajo, aceite de oliva virgen extra y sal. El ajo es maravilloso de todas las maneras. No soy muy cafetera, tomo uno al día. Me gusta su olor, pero no tanto el sabor.

P. ¿Le gusta darse caprichos?

R. No, salvo gastronómicos. Comprarme ropa siempre tiene que ser algo organizado. Hace años, una compañera de trabajo me dijo que salía con la misma ropa en todas las fotografías. Nunca se lo agradeceré lo suficiente porque no había caído en ello. Soy muy estructurada con lo que me pongo, pero ir de compras me aburre. También me aburren las obras en casa y comprar cosas para decorarla.

P. ¿Tiene algún viaje pendiente?

R. Cuando era pequeña leí los libros de Jack London y sus viajes a los mares del Sur. Por eso me atrae la Polinesia, aunque luego quizá sea un coñazo y tenga que llevarme 200 libros, preguntándome qué hago yo en un palafito. Me gustaría conocerla. También me gustaría ver una aurora boreal. La Antártida me resulta muy atractiva. Y me apetecería hacer un viaje en barco entre Moscú y San Petersburgo.

P. ¿Algún remedio para el insomnio?

R. La edad no perdona. He probado todo lo que no es químico y, a veces, funciona y otras no. Ya convivo con él, incluso cuando estoy de vacaciones en Granada, frente al mar Mediterráneo, al que tanto quiero. Lo que no me gusta es pensar por la noche porque es muy mala compañera. También escucho pódcasts ligeros y de true crime; eso me evade y evita que me invadan los malos pensamientos, porque soy una persona muy positiva y estable.

World.title: “Amsterdam’s gay tourism scene doesn’t stretch beyond the city”
World.content:

For over two decades, Michiel Hoogkamer has single-handedly managed Leiden’s sole gay bar. As it approaches its final weeks in business, he and others speak to Brandon Hartley about the challenges facing the country’s ‘homohoreca’ [gay nightlife scene].

Michiel Hoogkamer, the owner of De Roze Beurs, Leiden’s only gay bar, is ready

to call it quits.

After 24 years of catering for everyone from introverted university students to boisterous drag queens, the final night has been set for 15 August.

There’s no single reason why Hoogkamer decided to close down the bar he lovingly described as his child during an interview with Dutch News, but it comes at a difficult time for LGBTI+ oriented businesses all across the Netherlands.

While De Roze Beurs continues to host a stream of regulars, similar businesses across the country have struggled over the past decade.

“Here in the Netherlands, little bars like this one aren’t doing well,” Hoogkamer said. “Young people aren’t loyal to one place anymore. They go to monthly or quarterly parties at nightclubs instead or go to restaurants in the middle of the day.”

Hoogkamer and others say the country’s homohoreca is facing an increasing number of challenges.

Homohoreca is a Dutch term for hospitality businesses that cater for a gay, lesbian, transgender, and bisexual clientele, such as bars, saunas, nightclubs, and restaurants.

Saunas disappearing

Even Amsterdam is not immune. Cafe Getto, a popular gay-oriented restaurant that became famous for its ‘Diva Burgers,’ closed down a few years ago.

Lola the Green Aardvark, a queer food bar, and the lesbian/bisexual/queer café B’Femme both shuttered in 2025.

“The decline is drastic among gay saunas,” Peter Koop told Dutch News. “In 2020, there were still 12 gay saunas, but only eight remain.

“The closed saunas have not found successors. This is likely because there is hardly any interest in such establishments among young people anymore.”

Koop is the current writer and editor of homohoreca.nl, a website that has been tracking the industry since 2001.

However, a precise forecast of what’s to come could prove more difficult than predicting the weather in April.

“Although we do not have hard figures, we also have the impression that there are fewer bars and clubs aimed at the LGBTI+ community,” Philip Tijsma, spokesperson for the national LGBTQ+ rights group COC Nederland, said.

Changing habits

Many clientele are less reliant on these businesses to serve as safe spaces or

dating venues.

“We also have the impression that people’s nightlife behaviour has changed,’ Tijsma said.

“People go to a bar or club less often, and are more likely to attend a large LGBTI+ party or festival a few times a year. General nightlife venues have also sometimes become more inclusive and LGBTI+ people feel at home there more often.”

“In the Netherlands, there is indeed a decline in the number of gay bars, but that decline is very slow,” Koop said.

He said an average of two close in the Netherlands every year, but at least one new one usually appears.

Gay tourism

Koop also noted that, despite a downturn between 2010 and 2015, the number in Amsterdam has been holding steady.

“Amsterdam’s gay establishments benefit from gay tourism, which is not the case in the rest of the Netherlands,” he said.

The decrease is less severe than many people think, but the blow can be hard locally, as is the case with Leiden.”

The city still has a local chapter of COC Nederland but, aside from periodic club nights, it’s more of an advocacy centre than a social organisation.

Potential buyers

The building that houses De Roze Beurs has primarily served as a bar since it was built in 1636.

The name is somewhat difficult to translate into English, as beurs can mean various things such as stock exchange, marketplace and coin purse.

Hoogkamer said the name is partially a tribute to the years it was used as a meeting hall for officials and accountants from the Beestenmarkt, a nearby square where livestock was once sold.

He doesn’t know what the future holds for the building, but he doubts it will remain a gay bar.

A few interested parties have approached him about taking over De Roze Beurs, but the discussions didn’t go far. His landlord will make the ultimate decision about what happens next.

Homophobia increasing

Additional challenges new owners might face include what Hoogkamer says has been a rise in anti-gay hostility.

He said his first few years behind the bar could be rough at times. At one point in the early 2000s, the building was attacked by someone who threw paint bombs at the windows.

Things were largely quiet throughout the 2010s, but there’s been an uptick in aggression after De Roze Beurs reopened following the pandemic.

The rainbow flags out front have been stolen several times. On a busy Saturday night, a vandal smashed one of the windows and shouted anti-gay slurs at his customers.

Berlin attack

Hoogkamer also says there’s been an increase in passers-by heckling patrons seated outside on the terrace.

Recent studies suggest gay tolerance has declined in the Netherlands, especially among youths.

The Berlin Pride attack paints an even darker picture of the situation elsewhere

around the world.

“With the extreme right coming up, like Wilders and the FvD, it’s getting worse,” Hoogkamer said.

“They all say they’re woke and they’re attracting a lot of young people, but it simply isn’t true.”

Late nights

There’s also no denying that running any sort of bar can be incredibly difficult, especially once you enter middle age.

De Roze Beurs is essentially a one-man operation. “It’s hard work and I sometimes have 80-hour working weeks,” Hoogkamer said. “As you get older, you start to feel it, and there’s the long nights.

“I don’t get to bed until four or five in the morning. Everybody else gets to go home and I have to stay here and clean the toilets.”

When Dutch News recently visited De Roze Beurs, many of the rubber ducks that once stood watch over the bar itself had been packed up and placed into bags with other memorabilia.

Stripper pole

Along with an iconic stripper pole and pretty much everything else, the ducks will be sold at an auction scheduled for 20 August hosted by local drag queen Christine Carrington.

Hoogkamer will be sad to see it all go, but he said he was ready to move on.

“I’m going on sabbatical for a year,” he said. “I’m 46, I have good legs, and I want to see something of the world after managing a bar for so many years.”

While he himself wouldn’t take over a gay bar nowadays, he said Leiden could still use one, especially if there’s a person out there who knows what they’re getting themselves into.

“There’s plenty of potential in this city for a gay or queer bar, but you have to work hard,” he advised. “You’re not going to get rich and your social life is forever on hold.

“You can’t go to parties and you can’t go to birthdays because they’re all on Fridays and Saturdays. When do you make your money? On Fridays and Saturdays.”

World.title: Dutch unions call 24-hour public transport strike on September 9
World.content:
Public transport workers across the Netherlands are to stage a one-day strike on Wednesday, September 9, bringing buses, trains, trams and metro services almost to a standstill.

The FNV union has called the strike in the latest escalation of its campaign against the government’s social welfare reforms, which it says will lead to lower living standards for millions of working people.

The three major unions FNV, CNV and VCP have vowed to fight the cabinet’s social welfare reforms, which are designed to secure €6.5 billion in cost savings during the goverment’s four-year term.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief scrapped a plan to increase the statutory retirement age faster by raising it in step with life expectancy, but the unions want the cabinet to go further by abandoning cuts to unemployment pay and long-term disability benefits.

Staff working for NS, ProRail, urban and regional transport sevices and DB cargo will down tools for 24 hours on September 9, making it impossible to run timetables.

Delays inevitable

“We are aware that a 24-hour strike will cause disruption,” said FNV official Edwim Kuiper. “We regret that deeply. But the consequences of the dismantling of our social security are much greater for everyone and will last much longer.”

National train operator NS said it could not say exactly what the impact of the stoppage would be because it had not been officially notified by the union.

Lobby organisation OV-NL, which represents nine smaller public transport companies such as Arriva, QBuzz and the major city network operators GVB, RET and HTM, said it “understood up to a point” the reason to call a strike.

But it said it was “very unfortunate that passengers are being disadvantaged by a social and political debate”.

Union leader Henri Janssen said that the strike was being called on behalf of commuters. “Every working person has to deal with sickness, work incapacity or involuntary unemployment. They should be able to count on a decent social safety net,“ he said.

World.title: Amsterdam steps up Pride security in wake of attack in Berlin
World.content:
Amsterdam has stepped up security around this weekend’s WorldPride street parties and the annual canal parade in the wake of last week’s attack in Berlin.

A total of 250 concrete blocks have been placed along the canals and nightclubs are carrying out extra bag searches during the two-week event, which runs until August 8.

Richard Keldoulis of Club Church, one of Amsterdam’s best known gay clubs, told NOS: “I’ve never known anything like this.”

Venue owners are in constant contact with the police and intelligence services about appropriate security measures, although they conceded that it is almost impossible to prevent a so-called “lone wolf” attack by one person using a knife or a vehicle.

Last Sunday a woman was killed and 29 people were injured when a man drove a car into a crowd near the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where the annual Christopher Street Day parade, Germany’s main Pride event, was taking place.

The suspect, Abdul B., was later shot dead by police, who have said they are treating the incident as an Islamist terrorist attack.

Lone wolf attacks

“I come from Berlin and I was at the scene of the attack last week. I left the party few minutes before it all went wrong, but my friends were still there,” Keldoulis said.

“It’s always nice to feel safe, but ultimately you can never rule it out altogether. There were barriers and security measures in Berlin as well, but it still went wrong.”

Michel Peters, chair of the gay police association Roze in Blauw (“pink in blue”), said police would maintain a high-visibility presence during the weekend.

“We are there mainly to maintain contact with the [LGBTQI+] community,” he said. “We want to do more to show that we are there in the coming dys, so that people know they can approach us when something is going on.”

On Tuesday evening thousands of people in Amsterdam gathered at the Homomonument, the national memorial to victims of homophobic persecution, to commemorate the victims of Berlin.

City mayor Femke Halsema addressed the crowd, calling for courage and resilience. “We will win if we keep spreading hope loud and clear,” she said.

World.title: Dutch inflation rises to 3.1% in July as fuel costs soar
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Inflation rose slightly to 3.1% in July, sustaining the above-target trend of the last two and a half years, according to statistics agency CBS’s latest flash forecast.

A 9.7% spike in energy prices, including motor fuels, was the main driver of the increase as overall inflation ticked up from 2.9% in June.

Services inflation was measured at 4.1%, the same level as in June, while purchases abroad were 4.8% more expensive, down from 5.7% a month ago.

The harmonised European rate, which does not include the costs associated with owning or renting a home, was measured at 2.9%, up from 2.5% in June.

Since January 2024 inflation in the Netherlands has been persistently above the European Central Bank’s target level of 2%, peaking at 4.1% in December 2024 and April 2025. Its highest level so far this year was 3.5% in May.

The Dutch government has so far resisted calls to cut prices at the pumps, even though the Netherlands has the most expensive fuel in Europe, at €2.35 for a litre of petrol and €2.39 for diesel.

The CBS will publish the confirmed results with a more detailed breakdown on August 11.

World.title: Woman finds dinner-plate sized tarantula in her garden
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A woman in Twente was enjoying the sunshine in her garden on Wednesday when she came face to face with a tarantula the size of a dinner plate.

Dierenambulance Enschede posted photos of the poisonous spider on social media after they were called to the town of Oldenzaal to retrieve the arachnid.

The woman spotted the creature in her yard and informed the regional animal ambulance, who were able to capture it by placing a container over the creature and slowly sliding the lid underneath.

Tarantulas do not live in the wild in the Netherlands and it is suspected the spider escaped from a neighbour’s house.

According to the Dierenambulance Enschede, tarantulas are largely harmless. Their bites are akin to a wasp sting.

A number of people admitted they would not have had the woman’s composure. “If I had found the spider, this spider would now be the new owner of my former house,” one commenter wrote on the animal organisation Facebook post.

World.title: Arne Slot rules himself out as next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Former Liverpool and Feyenoord coach Arne Slot has ruled himself out as the next manager of the Dutch men’s national team, saying he wants to keep working in club football.

The 47-year-old was one of the names put forward to succeed Ronald Koeman, who resigned after the Netherlands were knocked out of the World Cup by Morocco in the round of 32.

Slot has also been courted by AC Milan and English Premier League side Fulham since he was sacked by Liverpool at the end of May after two seasons in charge.

The Dutchman, who arrived after steering Feyenoord to only their second Eredivisie title since the turn of the century, won the Premier League in his first season but could only manage fifth place last term.

The Dutch football association KNVB wants to appoint a manager well ahead of the next UEFA Nations League match against Germany on September 24.

Two other potential successors have also dropped out of the running. PSV manager Peter Bosz has extended his contract at the Eindhoven club, while former Ajax head coach Erik ten Hag recently joined his home town club Twente Enschede as director of football and has said he wants to continue in that role.

World.title: “I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”
World.content:
Originally from the Philippines, Deepa Paul moved to Amsterdam nearly 15 years ago after her husband took a job in the capital. Her book about opening up her marriage, Ask Me How It Works, was longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction. She loves how the Dutch do kids birthday parties, strongly advises tourists not to cycle and wishes she could have met Mata Hari.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I was born in the Philippines to a Bengali father and Filipina mother. I met my husband at university in Manila. I was studying communication but also had a crazy pipe dream of going to Europe to train as a classical singer. His first job ended up being in Singapore, so we had a long-distance relationship for four years while I lived in Manila. After we were married, I moved to Singapore to be with him and found work as a writer and producer in TV. But Singapore wasn’t really my bag.

I pitched my husband the idea of one last adventure before having a baby: a round-the-world trip, him on unpaid sabbatical, me writing freelance. He thought I was crazy and suggested finding a job abroad instead.

A friend working at a Dutch multinational offered to put him in touch with a VP at their Amsterdam HQ. I remember thinking that the cold email my husband wrote sounded way too direct and maybe a bit too much. Turns out the Dutch are a direct culture: it worked! One job offer and six months later, we were on a one-way flight to Amsterdam.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I am an immigrant.

How long do you plan to stay?

I don’t see an end date. I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam, although I often fantasise about living a parallel existence somewhere warm in the winter.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

There’s nothing glamorous about how I accumulated the Dutch I speak now, which I’d describe as pretty passable for daily social life. It was one awkward conversation with one school parent at a time, lots of listening to how people actually talk, and relying on context clues to fill in the 20-30% I might not be grasping accurately when people talk fast.

My husband had negotiated 30 hours of Dutch lessons for both of us, through his employer, when he started his job. I paused for a year or two after I gave birth to my daughter, then went back and took classes at the Volksuniversiteit.

I find that when Dutch people switch to English with me, I can push back. My go-to phrase is ‘ik ben grappiger in het Engels’ [I’m funnier in English]. Humour is disarming, it smooths over the switch in social situations..

My greatest achievement was being interviewed live on NPO Radio 1 about my book in Dutch. The segment was only supposed to last 8 minutes, but it was the longest 11 minutes of my life! Turns out talking about love, commitment, sex and open marriage is far more complicated than chatting about the weather.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

You’re asking a polyamorist to choose just one?! I love the mobility and freedom of cycling. Gezelligheid. The simplicity of young children’s birthday parties. The straightforward ease of voting — if you don’t come from a culture of systemically corrupt and murderous elections, as I do, you might not appreciate what a privilege and relief that is. The progression of flowers in the spring, from tulips to hyacinths to cherry blossoms to peonies to roses to dahlias: what a gift it is to have a reliable abundance of beauty.

How Dutch have you become?

Not much — I’m still too short (1.56m). I would argue that living in the Netherlands has given me the space and independence to become more myself, rather than more Dutch.

Having said that, I am a lot more direct now, and I not only can handle direct communication, I prefer it. It’s quite a relief actually, coming from a conflict-avoidant, high-context culture. I’ve been nearly cured of my lifelong affliction of Filipino time, which means I’m only mildly late most of the time, and actually punctual the rest of the time.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Anne Frank, who inspired me to start keeping a journal at the age of nine. She was the first person to show me that writing about my inner world and observing my own life, no matter how small and ordinary, is a worthy endeavour.

Rachel Ruysch, the most prolific and commercially successful female artist of the Dutch Golden Age, whose floral still life paintings sold for more than Rembrandt’s paintings in that time.

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Friesland, a bold free spirit who harnessed her eroticism, feminine power and artistic expression to live a courageous life and extraordinary life for a woman of her time. Later biographies exonerated her of espionage in World War I, but her image as a powerful and mysterious femme fatale endures to this day.

What’s your top tourist tip?

Please don’t cycle in Amsterdam, especially not with your selfie stick out. It’s not Disneyland with tulips and windmills along every cycle path. Some of us have things to do and places to get to.

On a less grumpy note, try to book a visit to the Six Collection in advance. It’s a private art collection that spans over three centuries and 10 generations of the wealthy and influential Six family, who have one of the most celebrated Rembrandt paintings you’ve never seen hanging right in their living room.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

When I gave birth in 2013, I was taken aback that official paternity leave was two days — one day for the actual birth and a second day for the father to register it. It ran completely counter to the image of the Netherlands in my mind as egalitarian, progressive and liberal. It turns out that it’s still deeply patriarchal in small, hidden and entrenched ways.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

If I’m not panicking about making sure everything is packed and ready to go, cycle around my neighbourhood and have a coffee at my favourite spots. If the weather allows, go for a walk and read in the sunshine at Westerpark, then go for a dip in the IJ.

Throw a big party at home for all the friends I’ve made over the last 15 years, all the people who have become part of my story (except those I’ve revoked access to). My husband will cook enough Filipino food to feed everyone one last time. Eat, drink, laugh, cry, hug and dance, maybe stay up talking until the sun comes up.

If we make it out early enough, go dancing until my legs give out or the club kicks us out. Cycle home as the sun rises and enjoy one last sleep in my own bed—or not.

Deepa was speaking to Molly Quell.

Dutch drug criminal Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, has been convicted by a Belgian judge and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The 35-year old was not present at the court in Antwerp when the verdict was announced on Thursday, having been on the run since 2024.

Leijdekkers was sentenced for his part in the Costa drugs case, in which a total of 56 people were accused of smuggling 25 tonnes of cocaine through Antwerp and money laundering. The drugs had a street value of €3.5 billion.

An investigation by Follow The Money revealed that the Brabant drugs baron has been living in Sierre Leone and is in a relationship with the president’s daughter.

Two years ago, a Dutch judge sentenced him to 24 years in 2024 for cocaine trafficking through the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam.

In total, he has been sentenced to 103 years in prison across 10 trials.

The Dutch have requested his extradition from Sierre Leone, but the government denies any knowledge of his presence in the country.

According to drugs experts, the West African country has become a major logistical hub for the smuggling of drugs from South America to Europe.

Earlier this year, Spanish authorities intercepted a ship that had departed from the country and discovered 30,215 kilograms of cocaine, the largest intercepted cocaine shipment ever.

A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut. Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. Alimentation Couche-Tard has already secured commitments to acquire at least 57.2% of the company. Heket, an entity linked to CVC Capital Partners owning 37.6% of Żabka’s shares, and PG Investment Company, holding 10%, have agreed to sell their entire stakes. A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives. They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares. The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction. Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year. The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand. Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%. Żabka, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores, has made its stock market debut in one of Europe’s biggest listings this year.
