World.title: ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave
World.content:
Members of the Guardia Civil USECIC guard migrants on Tarajal beach after crossing the border between Spain and Morocco in Ceuta.

Tens of thousands of Moroccans broke into Ceuta, a Spanish territory that neighbours Morocco. By the following evening, most of them had left, hungry and disappointed.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ceuta, Spain: Like so many others in Morocco, Mohammed Ahmidho saw on his social media feeds early Thursday that the heavily guarded border his country shared with the Spanish territory of Ceuta was open. Soon enough, he joined a crowd in the tens of thousands, many of whom were astonished to see Moroccan police urge them, as he recalled, to “come to Spain.” Some climbed over the fence, as he did, or dove through holes in the chain-link, or swam across the maritime border. Some wore wet-suits, sometimes kicking with flippers, or floated to the Spanish coast in orange life preservers, pink inflatable doughnuts around their waists. At least 60 people died in the mayhem. “A lot of people came,” said Ahmidho, 37. “A lot.” He was among roughly 50,000 people who crossed the border into a Spanish town of only 84,000 residents on Thursday and early Friday, local time, according to the Spanish interior ministry. That was a more intense surge than in any equivalent period during the peak of the European migration crisis in 2015. Loading By Friday morning, the city looked like the emergency that Europe has been trying to avoid since that era of mass migration 11 years ago, the last time so many non-Europeans surged into European-held territory, upended the continent’s politics and spurred the rise of its anti-immigrant right. As the city’s residents hunkered down and shuttered their stores, groups of mostly young men with nowhere to go filled squares and avenues, condominium courtyards, hilltop overlooks and bridge underpasses. Some took dips in waters patrolled by a Spanish naval ship or waded through a band of floating detritus – plastic bags and water bottles – caught in the current. Others marched across a beach littered with the things their fellow arrivals had carried: single shoes, a shed wet-suit, mobile phone cases, an ID card from Casablanca.



Spanish soldiers, many of whom had been mobilised on Thursday to deal with the crisis, stood on nearby tanks. They watched the migrants drink water from beach showers, each shaped like vertical surfboards and branded with the slogan, “Ceuta, where you feel the emotions.” Nearby, young teens laughed under the whirl of patrol helicopters as they tried out the exercise equipment at a beach playground. Ahmidho wore a pink bathing suit and stood bare-chested, his black T-shirt slung over his shoulder. The soles of his feet were cut, he said, from clambering over rocks near the border. Belongings left behind by migrants float in the sea. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Migrants from Morocco run from Spanish police officers. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere His voyage had been a disappointment, he said. Like so many, he had come to find work, only to find soldiers and policemen harrying him to leave. “There’s no water, there’s no food, there’s no place to sleep,” he said. “There’s nothing.” As the migrants took over the streets, residents mostly stayed hidden in their homes, keeping their shops and businesses closed. Emerging briefly, Francisco Pérez, 68, rushed his grandchildren into car seats as the migrants walked around him. He said his granddaughter had asked why they couldn’t go to the beach, and why there were “so many Moroccans.” The locals, he said, were “scared” and furious with the Spanish government, which, he said, had abandoned them.



Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, tried to avert such reactions by rushing to Ceuta on Friday morning to show his support for its citizens and also to condemn the influx as a “violation of Spain’s territorial integrity.” For Sánchez’s right-wing critics – both at home, around Europe and throughout the world, including at the White House – the surge of migrants was an indictment of his pro-immigration policies. His government allowed more than 1 million migrants illegally living in Spain to apply for legal residency this year – a move that his opponents said had helped to entice the migrants this week. Migrants wait for a shop to open so they can buy food after crossing from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Migrants rest outside the Temporary Centre for Immigrants (CETI) after crossing from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere To opponents of immigration, the footage of migrants sweeping into the tiny Spanish territory amounted to Exhibit A for their case. Ceuta, all of a sudden, became an international emblem for the perils of unchecked illegal immigration. In response, Sánchez blamed human traffickers for misleading the migrants about how easy it would be to claim asylum in Spain – and noted that, despite his migrant-friendly policies, Spain has attracted fewer migrants trying to enter illegally in recent years than some European neighbours. It is still unclear why so many people came to Ceuta. Many of the Moroccans who wandered around Ceuta on Friday wondered if the doors hadn’t opened because of some unknown plan by Morocco, which has been accused of using immigrant flows in the past for political pressure.



“I don’t know why they let us through,” said Ajoub el-Arrot, 24, who said he heard about the open border on social media. “Maybe they had some political reason. They opened the border and let everyone go by.” Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right He added, “When there are political problems, Morocco opens the doors and tells us to go.” Douae Tabit, 19, who also said she heard about the unchecked crossing on social media, said it went “viral” and passed by word-of-mouth, attracting people from all around Morocco. Fluent in English, French and Spanish, she said she worked as a nurse and photographer and spontaneously decided to take advantage of the opportunity. She climbed over a fence and swam to the Spanish shore, she said, but she had expected something more welcoming: No one had food, water or a place to sleep. Still, she said, “I’m not going back.” Many seemed not to know exactly what they were doing there.



Young men, shirtless or in soccer jerseys, marched barefoot or sometimes in a single sandal, as if in an aimless parade. One teenager gently knocked on the grate of a closed food market while others hovered longingly around the city’s locked supermarkets. As morning turned to afternoon and the harsh sun burned away the clouds, men sought shade wherever they could. One group gathered under a hulking statue of Hercules near the port terminal. Others leaned against gas station pumps or reclined under the tents of abandoned stalls that had been raised for a local food fair. Still more looked in trash bins for food, or begged passersby for water. One woman fainted by a Zara store. Sulayman Ahmed, 15, a resident of Ceuta who is of Moroccan descent, said he couldn’t believe that Morocco was letting so many people through. Related Article Updated

Immigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe “They have to put more resources to stop people from coming,” he said, complaining that the appearances of politicians at the border, including that of Sánchez, amounted to “theatre.” As the day progressed, it became clear many of the migrants were leaving. By the boardwalk, they hovered around Spanish soldiers who had hooked a mobile phone to stereos that played messages in Arabic telling them to go home. Other Spanish soldiers and police officers threatened the migrants, waving their sticks to push them back to the border. In town, a roving band of young Spanish men chased down and intimidated Moroccan stragglers. Even as a sprinkling of late arrivals waded through the water, a mass return was underway.

World.title: ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: In another at-times heated press conference, St Kilda coach Ross Lyon was optimistic Jack Silvagni would face his old side Carlton next weekend.

Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend Leigh Matthews has taken a major swipe at his famous rivals, Essendon.

Alastair Clarkson had another frustrating day against his former club, Hawthorn. Matthews takes aim at Bombers’ administration in hunt for new coach Jon Pierik Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend Leigh Matthews has taken a major swipe at Essendon, declaring anyone who has a choice wouldn’t apply for the Bombers’ vacant coaching role, and he would have no confidence in heading there under the current administration. Matthews, a four-time premiership coach who also featured in three-straight grand finals against the Bombers as a player with arch-rival Hawthorn, declared he “wouldn’t be going to Essendon” if he was still a coach.



No confidence: AFL coaching great Leigh Matthews said he would have no confidence in heading to Essendon under the current administration. Bombers great Kevin Sheedy has backed James Hird to win the role. Justin McManus “From the outside I said, ‘Oh well, good luck’. If I was a coach, I wouldn’t be going to Essendon. If you desperately want a job, you just go for it, right? But, anyone who has choices ain’t going to Essendon,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘What boxes does James tick?’ The blunt assessment of Hird’s credentials The Bombers, led by president Andrew Welsh and chief executive Tim Roberts, have narrowed the search for their next senior coach to four candidates: club legend James Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis, a former long-time Brisbane Lions assistant. Essendon caretaker coach Dean Solomon, a friend and former teammate of Hird and McVeigh, will this week have his first formal discussions with club hierarchy about the full-time job. But Solomon has remained tight-lipped on whether he’ll seek the head coaching role.



“The other coaches, whether it be Jaymie Graham, now Murray Davis, Mark McVeigh, they have been in for jobs to a degree, they have just got to get a job if they can get it ... but I don’t have any idea who would be good or bad,” Matthews said. “A coach is only as good as what’s around him in players and staff, and support from the top. For me, from the outside, I don’t know the Essendon people that well, but I would have no confidence to coach under that regime.” The Bombers declined to comment. Essendon have been rebuffed by other potential candidates, including Geelong assistant James Kelly, Hawthorn assistant Daniel Giansiracusa and St Kilda assistant Corey Enright. Back then: James Hird and Dean Solomon speak with then Giants interim coach Mark McVeigh during the 2022 season. Hird and McVeigh are now seeking to coach the Bombers, while Solomon is yet to indicate his intentions. Getty Images



Matthews, who is a Brisbane Lions board member and won three-straight flags there as a coach, was befuddled by the Bombers using soccer coach Kevin Muscat to interview candidates over Zoom while he is coaching Chinese club Shanghai Port. Related Article AFL 2026 Geelong reach settlement with Stengle as Hill departs Collingwood “He is going to do a Zoom meeting from Japan with these individual candidates and get some kind of feedback from that. It’s not so much window dressing, I reckon it’s like trying to stab with a dartboard – it’s so hard,” Matthews said. Matthews said Carlton “looked like they knew what they were doing” in their hunt for a new coach, and Tasmania had as well before appointing Ken Hinkley as coach. But, when it came to Essendon, he questioned, “how qualified are they to make an informed decision?” Long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop is also part of the process alongside the panel.



Essendon’s football boss Daniel McPherson will leave the club at the end of the season. Getty Images Hird, with the support of fellow club great Kevin Sheedy, is seeking his third stint in charge. His first was from the end of 2010 until the end of 2013, when he was banned from coaching for his role in the supplements saga. He returned for the 2015 season, but quit after a 5-14 start. “To be honest, if Hird had been an assistant coach at another club for the last three or four years, you would think he would have already been appointed,” Matthews said. The Bombers are also on the hunt for a new football manager after the resignation of Daniel McPherson. McPherson, who came to the Bombers with former coach Brad Scott, will leave the club at season’s end. The appointment of a new football boss will be made alongside that of a new senior coach, as the Bombers review their football structure.



‘He is a Silvagni, he is tough’ Jon Pierik and Danny Russell St Kilda coach Ross Lyon is optimistic Jack Silvagni will line up against his former club Carlton next week in a finals-shaping, Sunday-night blockbuster despite dislocating his shoulder in a 19-point loss to Sydney on Saturday. Silvagni had to be helped from the field in pain in a 42-minute final term which also had play suspended after Swans defender Will Edwards suffered a badly broken ankle in a marking contest. He required a green whistle for pain relief and was taken from the field at Marvel Stadium on a motorised cart. Hoping for a quick return: Jack Silvagni leaves the ground with a dislocated shoulder on Saturday. AFL Photos



Swans forward Charlie Curnow booted three goals after Silvagni, his direct opponent and a former Blues teammate, left the field, highlighting the importance of the off-season recruit with the fabled family history at Princes Park. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects “He has a dislocated shoulder, [but] it went back in. He said he had a dislocated shoulder before, in round one, and he played the next week,” Lyon said. “He is a Silvagni, he is tough, we see his spirit, can’t believe we have got him in our club, but we are thrilled. But we will take no risk … we have got to get on to Carlton.” Silvagni had his shoulder in a sling post-match when chatting in the change rooms with father Steve and mother Jo.



After a short dinner break following the Saints’ defeat, Lyon returned to Marvel Stadium to watch the Blues host the Brisbane Lions on Saturday night. With three rounds remaining, the Saints (with nine wins) and Blues are jostling for 10th spot, and a wildcard berth, under the new top-10 finals system. In another entertaining press conference when he sparred with journalists, Lyon denied he had spoken sternly with Mattaes Phillipou in a break during play, insisting it had been a typical conversation. “I spoke to him calmly and rationally, but you [a journalist] have turned it into strong feedback. I was teaching him on a leading pattern when he went shallow, [and] could have gone to the top of the square like Hugo [Garcia], so I am OK, you can interpret it how you want,” he said. Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos



Lyon said ruckman Tom De Koning was dealing with a hip pointer issue, as was superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, who spent time off the ground with the ailment. The Swans booted the first two goals of the game, but then trailed by nine points at quarter-time, 13 points at half-time and 12 points at the final break, as the Saints dominated possession and Wanganeen-Milera booted three goals. But with the St Kilda gun clearly hampered in the final term, finishing the game out as a forward, Sydney’s midfielders went on a rampage and the Swans kicked seven last-quarter goals to the Saints’ two. Lyon lamented his team’s poor work at stoppages, declaring the Saints need more quality in the starting 23, and need to be better for longer. View post on X



The Saints have had a series of tough defeats this season, but Lyon said he wasn’t hiding from the raw facts. “The facts are there and are laid bare. Until you get it done, it’s two points up there against Sydney, it’s one point against Adelaide … the Dockers, I think we kicked the first goal of the last quarter, then it was ‘Wharfie Time’ [when the Dockers electrify the crowd with loud music],” Lyon said. “The feedback is, we need to get better – I am not shying away from it. But there is no doubt we have improved, that’s indisputable, but on our win-loss, I think our percentage tells us we know where are, but against [Sydney], we are just a bit short of that on our journey.” Play was stopped for 10 minutes while medical staff attended 23-year-old Edwards for what appeared to be a compound fracture. The promising Swan did not make his AFL debut until this year after a serious leg infection and then a broken leg threatened his career. Sydney also lost James Rowbottom with a broken hand in the first term. Swans coach Dean Cox described Edwards’ latest injury as “devastating”.



“To see a player battle like he has for so long to get a chance at AFL with some of the injuries he’s already had, to dislocate his ankle and be required to go to hospital and get surgery, is devastating for him and the football club and his family,” Cox said. “To forge out to be a really strong key defender for a young man is great. It’ll just be another hurdle that he has to jump, and we’ll support him all the way through it.” Watson’s career-high as Hawks down gritty Roos AAP Nick Watson kicked an equal career-best five goals to keep Hawthorn firmly in the hunt for a top-two spot with a 16-point win over a plucky North Melbourne.



The Hawks trailed by one point heading into the final quarter in Launceston on Saturday against an opposition needing a victory to boost their AFL finals hopes. Nick Watson was at his brilliant best yet again for the Hawks. Getty Images But they did enough to hold on for the 14.15 (99) to 12.11 (83) result, with Mabior Chol getting a crucial breathing-space goal at the back end of the game. With his side ahead by 11 and less than six minutes on the clock, Chol earned a free kick with a tackle and then nailed a goal from about 50m out near the boundary line. North cut the margin to 10 points with less than three minutes left thanks to Harry Sheezel but were left to rue several key misses in the fourth quarter.



Watson’s haul gives him 52 goals for the season, putting him right in the hunt for the Coleman Medal. “Every week he gets a fair bit of attention and for a player so young he works his way through it really well,” Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said. “It’s very difficult to be consistent. He was really important.” Alastair Clarkson and his Roos had a frustrating day against his former club, Hawthorn. AFL Photos Jai Newcombe was also heavily involved for the Hawks and picked up a game-high 34 disposals, plus 12 clearances and one goal assist.



Hawthorn, who are in third spot and just two points behind Sydney, have won four in a row ahead of a blockbuster against reigning premiers the Brisbane Lions on Friday. The Kangaroos have slumped to five losses on the trot and sit 13th on the ladder. “Finn O’Sullivan at the 20-minute mark of the last quarter, snaps, should be a goal,” North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson said. “Jack Darling takes a mark 30 metres out [in the] last quarter, [that] should be a goal. “We’re competing, and we’re getting closer to some of those sides, but it also tells us that we’ve got a way to go.



“At AFL level those shots and opportunities should be executed.” Hawthorn nabbed the opening goal of the game through Will Day before the Kangaroos got four straight for a 26-9 lead at the first break. North Melbourne’s Nick Larkey, who has struggled for accuracy in recent times, produced a shocking first shot but nailed his second from off-centre. Teammate Zac Banch squeezed one through from the goal square in the last minute of the first quarter to give his side a boost. Hawthorn came to life early in the second with Watson, who only picked up one touch in the first term, getting three goals in a row including two in 60 seconds.



The lead then changed hands multiple times before a behind after the halftime buzzer to Chol levelled the scores at 46-46. Watson fired again with two goals early in the third before a major to Chol broke the run of tit-for-tat scores as Hawthorn threatened to pull away. But the Kangaroos rallied and Larkey’s second gave his side a 69-68 lead heading into the final quarter. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’: Urgent care clinics failing to relieve pressure on hospitals, say doctors
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaHealthcare ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’: Urgent care clinics failing to relieve pressure on hospitals, say doctors Melissa Cunningham and Henrietta Cook August 1, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of multimillion-dollar urgent care clinics set up around Victoria and touted by politicians as a silver bullet for the state’s healthcare crisis are doing “absolutely nothing” to ease pressure on overstretched hospitals, while threatening the viability of GP practices, doctors warn. There are 38 urgent care clinics in the state, many of which were opened in 2023 by the federal government in a bid to take pressure off Victoria’s overrun hospital system by providing bulk-billed services for urgent, but not life-threatening, injuries and illnesses. Melbourne emergency physician Dr Sarah Whitelaw said urgent care clinics were having a “minuscule” effect on Victoria’s overrun emergency departments, which are being flooded. Louis Trerise The federal government has argued the clinics are reducing the number of people turning up at emergency departments with non-life-threatening but urgent conditions by about 10 per cent, but this figure is strongly disputed by doctors on the front line. Melbourne emergency physician Dr Sarah Whitelaw said the clinics were having a “minuscule” effect on Victoria’s overwhelmed emergency departments, which are being flooded by a wave of sicker, more complex patients requiring urgent care and hospital admission.



“The clinics do nothing to solve our problems,” said Whitelaw, who is the emergency medicine representative on the Australian Medical Association’s federal council. Related Article Exclusive

Hospitals Booted from hospital and dumped on the street: Patients on secret blacklist being refused treatment “It is so frustrating every time we hear the phrase ‘reducing emergency department pressures’ because they haven’t decreased our waiting times in any way.” The federal government’s own reporting on the system has found the introduction of urgent care clinics has not reduced emergency department waiting times. In many metropolitan hospitals only 1 to 2 per cent of emergency department arrivals were being diverted to urgent care clinics, Whitelaw said.



This figure has come from emergency departments nationally, where staff have begun recording the number of patients opting to use urgent care clinics instead. Official data shows emergency department arrivals have risen by about 4.4 per cent since the urgent care centres opened. In 2024-25 there were 1,978,267 arrivals in Victoria, about 84,000 higher than in 2022-23, when there were 1,894,732 visits to the state’s emergency departments. Emergency physician Dr Simon Judkins, who works in rural and metropolitan emergency departments, said hospitals in regional areas including Bendigo and Ballarat were “really, really struggling”.



“It’s not because of patients who need lacerations fixed up; they’re full of patients who’ve got complex care issues, who need hospital admission, and the hospitals are completely full,” said Judkins, also the Victorian president of the Australian Medical Association. He said emergency departments were being left with wards full of patients who needed to be immediately admitted to hospital, but there were often no beds available. The federal government oversees 29 of the clinics, while the state government manages the rest. In this year’s state budget, the Victorian government allocated $20.9 million for the clinics, describing the funding as a way to “help reduce the demand on busy hospital emergency departments”. The federal government announced a $1.8 billion national boost to the clinics in May this year and previously committed more than $88 million in direct grants for Victoria’s clinics.



Emergency doctors argue that funding would have been better spent on GPs, who manage chronic and complex illnesses to keep patients out of hospital, as well boosting staff numbers and increasing the number of hospital beds. Related Article Opinion

Medicare I ended up in a Medicare urgent care clinic … and I liked it Millie Muroi Economics Writer “Imagine what we could have done with those billions of dollars, investing it into GP clinics and providing them the capacity to do after-hours care,” Judkins said. “That would have been a much better choice.” An evaluation of urgent care centres around Australia is underway, the federal government confirmed. An interim report found the clinics were costing taxpayers up to five times more per patient than a standard GP consultation. Each presentation cost taxpayers more than $250 compared with a standard GP consultation, which cost roughly $47.



However, the federal government said the net saving from avoiding an emergency department presentation was estimated to be $381 per patient. In April, Carmel Misale called an ambulance after a sudden, intense pressure in her head caused her to briefly pass out. Instead of taking her to an emergency department, paramedics redirected her to an urgent care clinic in Northcote, warning of massive hospital waiting times. Carmel Misale was taken by ambulance to an urgent care clinic in Northcote but was shocked to be told no doctors were available. Wayne Taylor But when she arrived at the clinic she was shocked to discover it was in effect closed. It was 2pm on a weekday afternoon, and Misale said the clinic’s only nurse told paramedics there were no doctors available.



“I was flabbergasted,” the mother of two from Reservoir in Melbourne’s north recalled. “I said, ‘What do you mean you aren’t open?’” Misale’s husband then drove her to the Epworth’s emergency department, where she underwent urgent testing, including a CT scan and an MRI of her brain. After 10 hours, she was diagnosed with vestibular migraines. She’s concerned urgent care clinics are passing too many patients on to emergency departments. Others who have used the medical clinics for urgent care are fierce advocates of the service, including people unable to afford the increasing cost of visiting a GP, or parents of children who find themselves caring for a sick or injured child out of hours.



However, Associate Professor Julian Rait, the Australian Medical Association’s federal vice president, warned that urgent care clinics were sucking doctors out of rural areas and hospitals, offering much higher pay and more sociable hours. “It has a very distorting effect on the workforce basically; it’s robbing Peter to pay Paul,” Rait said. Dr Robin O’Neill said enormous amounts of federal funding meant urgent care clinics were able to offer doctors between $250 and $400 an hour. Ruby Alexander It is something Robin O’Neill, a GP in Camperdown in the state’s south-west, has experienced firsthand. He said enormous amounts of federal funding meant urgent care clinics were able to offer doctors between $250 and $400 an hour. O’Neill said regular general practices were unable to offer this sort of pay under current Medicare rebates, which made it difficult for them to attract doctors, particularly in regional and rural areas.



“The government has now created a two-tier system where federally funded urgent care centres can afford to bulk bill and offer higher rates of pay to doctors,” he said. “This in turn is causing pressure and workforce shortages in regular general practice clinics, which is most acute in rural and regional locations.” Dr Aadhil Aziz, Victorian deputy co-chair of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, warned that underfunded GP practices were closing daily, noting his own Melbourne clinic recently shut down due to financial pressure. He said increasing Medicare rebates was crucial. “General practice is severely underfunded,” he said. “But if you fund it better we will be able to deliver a better-class healthcare system for everyone, which will reduce the number of people needed going to EDs.”



Federal Health Minister Mark Butler said doctors had embraced the urgent care clinics and the government had been told they were having a positive impact on hospital emergency departments. Related Article Healthcare More free urgent care clinics part of $8.5 billion health commitment “When you need urgent but not life-threatening care, instead of waiting for hours at the local emergency department you can go to your local clinic,” Butler said. Official figures showed there have been more than 722,800 visits to urgent care clinics in Victoria since they were opened in 2023, including more than 9000 visits for the week of July 21. Victorian opposition health spokeswoman Georgie Crozier said the clinics were not operating as promised and had failed to ease pressure on emergency departments.



“Our health system is struggling to meet growing demand,” she said. “Labor should scrap the GP tax and provide greater support to our primary healthcare providers to keep people out of our busy emergency departments.” A Victorian government spokeswoman said the urgent care units were needed to fill a hole in the nation’s healthcare system. “The former federal Coalition government spent a decade gutting Australia’s primary care system, leaving too many Victorians unable to secure an appointment or afford to see a GP,” she said. World.title: AFL Super Saturday Live: Blues, Lions clash in Marvel blockbuster; Lyon tees off at reporters after Swans’ comeback
World.content:
A stern Ross Lyon has taken aim at a journalist in a post-match press conference for the second week in a row.

The grumpy St Kilda coach took umbrage at a suggestion that he offered “stern feedback” to Mattaes Phillipou during his side’s disappointing 19-point loss to Sydney at Marvel Stadium after the Saints led by two goals at three-quarter-time.

A serious-looking Ross Lyon speaks to the St Kilda players. via Getty Images

“Can I dive into that? That’s the media narrative,” Lyon shot back at the Phillipou question. “Anytime I speak to a player, it’s strong feedback. What I was on about was a leading pattern, so you can create the identity that you want.”

Lyon was obviously disappointed that his side had coughed up nine of the game’s last 11 goals as his side struggles to maintain wildcard relevance this year.

“So, [when it comes to] Mattaes, I spoke to him calmly and rationally. You’ve turned it into strong feedback,” Lyon said.

“I’m OK, but at the end of the day, you guys interpret it how you want. [Channel 7 reporter] Mitch Cleary did it the year before, and I said, ‘Mitch, I spoke to the group and walked off calmly’.

“But when we are up, and I walk off calmly, it’s like, you don’t say anything. But when we are down, and I do the same timing, it’s like, ‘Ross gave them a serve’. It gets a bit monotonous and boring.”

Lyon asked the journalist why he used the word “stern”. He was told it was because he looked serious during his interaction with Phillipou.

“I always look serious,” the Saints coach said. “It’s a serious business. I don’t sit there eating party pies and putting on headphones, listening to [the] Fox studio to get my insights to the game, like a lot of people do, don’t they?

“They walk into the media box and put their headsets on, they don’t even watch the game, and they listen to the other experts to get their opinion. I know that because a senior journo has told me that happens.

“It happens a lot, and I haven’t got time for that. And if I give them feedback, it’s not stern. If everything was stern, do you think these kids would be growing? I’ll leave it with you. That’s probably stern feedback.”

World.title: European fires bring into focus climate emergency
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters European fires bring into focus climate emergency August 1, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Climate work crisis

Your correspondent (Letters, 31/7) answers her own question on the Bordeaux fires. Should we recognise the more frequent disasters like this, or risk hitting the tourism industry?

Of course, the world needs to acknowledge the direct link of extreme weather to fossil fuels burning.

People and governments have been complacent for many reasons. Problems like cost of living take precedence when results are wanted by the next election.

Individual floods and droughts are complex, not caused by global warming alone. Australia has always been a land “of droughts and flooding rains”.

But these are excuses, demolished for years by science, and recently by unprecedented fires in places like Bordeaux.

More needs to be done now to reduce the even worse impacts that will come in the second half of this century.

John Hughes, Mentone AI as a subject

Kylie Moore-Gilbert (Comment, 30/7) expresses deep concerns about the use of AI in high schools, worrying that children whose brains are still developing will become deskilled in thinking for themselves. I recognise these concerns, but wonder whether it is possible to safely and proactively equip students to responsibly use AI by focusing on process more than outcome. Prompts are key to AI use. Students could start by looking at a question from numerous angles to elicit a large number of prompts, explaining their reasoning along the way. No one achieves a final draft immediately, so students could submit their drafts as well with their own evaluation of them. Hopefully, by incorporating AI as a compulsory subject in the curriculum, the next gen – ″⁣AI natives″⁣ – will have the knowledge and understanding to ethically, creatively and confidently function in an uncertain future.

Sue Fisher, Coburg A depressendon thought

Depressendon–- couldn’t have picked a better word, Kate Halfpenny (Comment, 01/8). If James Hird gets another crack after two previous failed attempts, I’m out, too. Will make it to the Fitzroy ground and barrack for the Royboys in the amateur league. Maybe that’s where the Bombers should be.

Moira Macdonald, Daylesford



Outsourcing to the client

Waleed Aly has hit the nail on the head (Comment, 31/7). One wonders sometimes, how some people manage tasks that used to be so straightforward. The reality is that businesses have, in effect, outsourced to us what used to be their service offering or obligation. We now do the work, carry the risk, do the waiting and experience the frustrations while they claim ″⁣efficiency″⁣! The organisation that comes up with a better ″⁣digital solution″⁣ will be a winner.

Charles Griss, Balwyn Learn the new ways

Remember the abacus and ″⁣log books″⁣ of logarithmic and trigonometric functions? In the ’70s, my mentor began teaching me how to repair three-legged transistors, diodes, resistors and some capacitors operating as a four function 20kg lump of desktop calculator.

Decades later, I lifted the lid on an Intel Pentium microprocessor and with a decent microscope you could probe a subminiature world for two etched signatures left by the ″⁣artwork″⁣ engineers. Presumably there are still people who understand how (now) billions of transistors connect and operate in modern devices.

A friend is trying to guide me through the mathematics of crude image recognition AI. It troubles me that few people understand or care how anything actually works in our brave new world.

Ronald Elliott, Sandringham City needs the SRL

Melbourne 2050 – population nine million. Hundreds of thousands of more cars on the streets. Gridlock wherever you go. Why didn’t we build the SRL, like every other major world city which has one? It’s there for generations to come.

George Djoneff, Mitcham Longer vision needed

The SRL is a perfect example of the moral and political dilemmas those politicians with a long-term vision always face (“Carroll considers rail loop’s future”, 30/7).

There will always be a choice between spending money to benefit future generations and the immediate needs of the voters, especially in health, education, and housing. The benefits of the SRL will not be felt until there is appropriate supporting development and people start to see the need to rely on public transport far more than we currently do.

When we say we should leave the world in good condition for future generations, most people are thinking about their children, grandchildren and maybe even their great grandchildren, when inreality we should be thinking more like Indigenous peoples around the world.

They think about the impact of their behaviour on the next seven generations or beyond. As current representatives of humanity, we are far too self-focused.

There was much ongoing opposition to London’s underground rail system when it was first proposed in the mid-19th century.

Howard Tankey, Box Hill North Widen commission

At best, SRL East would rank at the bottom of a top 10 priority strategic infrastructure projects list, if the best interests of all Victorians were considered, not least jobs, economic productivity and air quality for the western suburbs and growth corridor to Geelong and beyond.

With news of yet more cost blow-outs on this project too, this project should also come within the purview of the royal commission, along with all these dubious planning approvals for excessive height and site coverage around train stations.

There’s no reason Melbourne has to become a mega city of highrise towers leaving no room for sunshine and trees, certainly not if it means trashing liveability, so the question remains, who benefits?

Bernadette George, Mildura



Recall Kennett years

Your correspondent (Letters, 31/7) confidently suggests that “the Liberals would never be so reckless with taxpayer money” as they imply Labor has been. We might also reflect on the short-term budget gains over long-term public value of the privatisations and public sector restructures prioritised by the Kennett Liberal government (1992-99).

Bruce Watson, Clifton Springs Weighing the risks

Cartoonist Cathy Wilcox (1/8) has captured the irony of modern technology by showing how ludicrous it is to use a valuable resource to cool down data centres and the risk of more wildfires? What is the balance between supporting these digital services that rely on water and the use of a resource that is essential for people, agriculture and the environment?

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East The pleasure of trees

Like columnist Melissa Hoyer (Comment, 30/7) I find it extremely sad when mature trees are cut down, whatever the reason given – the beautiful mature peppercorn trees near the tennis courts next to the council gym in Gleadell Street, Richmond, for example.

I’ve been going to the gym for nearly 40 years and I’ve always passed those trees with a feeling of intense pleasure at the sight of them: they’ve provided deep shade and beauty to generations of tennis players and passers-by, and heaven knows we need them in such a heavily concreted area.

Bill Mack, Kew The bee all and end all?

With the escalation of climate difficulties being so vivid across the planet, how are bees fairing?

Richard Pentony, Hawthorn

World.title: ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave
World.content:
Members of the Guardia Civil USECIC guard migrants on Tarajal beach after crossing the border between Spain and Morocco in Ceuta.

Tens of thousands of Moroccans broke into Ceuta, a Spanish territory that neighbours Morocco. By the following evening, most of them had left, hungry and disappointed.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ceuta, Spain: Like so many others in Morocco, Mohammed Ahmidho saw on his social media feeds early Thursday that the heavily guarded border his country shared with the Spanish territory of Ceuta was open. Soon enough, he joined a crowd in the tens of thousands, many of whom were astonished to see Moroccan police urge them, as he recalled, to “come to Spain.” Some climbed over the fence, as he did, or dove through holes in the chain-link, or swam across the maritime border. Some wore wet-suits, sometimes kicking with flippers, or floated to the Spanish coast in orange life preservers, pink inflatable doughnuts around their waists. At least 60 people died in the mayhem. “A lot of people came,” said Ahmidho, 37. “A lot.” He was among roughly 50,000 people who crossed the border into a Spanish town of only 84,000 residents on Thursday and early Friday, local time, according to the Spanish interior ministry. That was a more intense surge than in any equivalent period during the peak of the European migration crisis in 2015. Loading By Friday morning, the city looked like the emergency that Europe has been trying to avoid since that era of mass migration 11 years ago, the last time so many non-Europeans surged into European-held territory, upended the continent’s politics and spurred the rise of its anti-immigrant right. As the city’s residents hunkered down and shuttered their stores, groups of mostly young men with nowhere to go filled squares and avenues, condominium courtyards, hilltop overlooks and bridge underpasses. Some took dips in waters patrolled by a Spanish naval ship or waded through a band of floating detritus – plastic bags and water bottles – caught in the current. Others marched across a beach littered with the things their fellow arrivals had carried: single shoes, a shed wet-suit, mobile phone cases, an ID card from Casablanca.



Spanish soldiers, many of whom had been mobilised on Thursday to deal with the crisis, stood on nearby tanks. They watched the migrants drink water from beach showers, each shaped like vertical surfboards and branded with the slogan, “Ceuta, where you feel the emotions.” Nearby, young teens laughed under the whirl of patrol helicopters as they tried out the exercise equipment at a beach playground. Ahmidho wore a pink bathing suit and stood bare-chested, his black T-shirt slung over his shoulder. The soles of his feet were cut, he said, from clambering over rocks near the border. Belongings left behind by migrants float in the sea. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Migrants from Morocco run from Spanish police officers. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere His voyage had been a disappointment, he said. Like so many, he had come to find work, only to find soldiers and policemen harrying him to leave. “There’s no water, there’s no food, there’s no place to sleep,” he said. “There’s nothing.” As the migrants took over the streets, residents mostly stayed hidden in their homes, keeping their shops and businesses closed. Emerging briefly, Francisco Pérez, 68, rushed his grandchildren into car seats as the migrants walked around him. He said his granddaughter had asked why they couldn’t go to the beach, and why there were “so many Moroccans.” The locals, he said, were “scared” and furious with the Spanish government, which, he said, had abandoned them.



Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, tried to avert such reactions by rushing to Ceuta on Friday morning to show his support for its citizens and also to condemn the influx as a “violation of Spain’s territorial integrity.” For Sánchez’s right-wing critics – both at home, around Europe and throughout the world, including at the White House – the surge of migrants was an indictment of his pro-immigration policies. His government allowed more than 1 million migrants illegally living in Spain to apply for legal residency this year – a move that his opponents said had helped to entice the migrants this week. Migrants wait for a shop to open so they can buy food after crossing from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere Migrants rest outside the Temporary Centre for Immigrants (CETI) after crossing from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere To opponents of immigration, the footage of migrants sweeping into the tiny Spanish territory amounted to Exhibit A for their case. Ceuta, all of a sudden, became an international emblem for the perils of unchecked illegal immigration. In response, Sánchez blamed human traffickers for misleading the migrants about how easy it would be to claim asylum in Spain – and noted that, despite his migrant-friendly policies, Spain has attracted fewer migrants trying to enter illegally in recent years than some European neighbours. It is still unclear why so many people came to Ceuta. Many of the Moroccans who wandered around Ceuta on Friday wondered if the doors hadn’t opened because of some unknown plan by Morocco, which has been accused of using immigrant flows in the past for political pressure.



“I don’t know why they let us through,” said Ajoub el-Arrot, 24, who said he heard about the open border on social media. “Maybe they had some political reason. They opened the border and let everyone go by.” Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right He added, “When there are political problems, Morocco opens the doors and tells us to go.” Douae Tabit, 19, who also said she heard about the unchecked crossing on social media, said it went “viral” and passed by word-of-mouth, attracting people from all around Morocco. Fluent in English, French and Spanish, she said she worked as a nurse and photographer and spontaneously decided to take advantage of the opportunity. She climbed over a fence and swam to the Spanish shore, she said, but she had expected something more welcoming: No one had food, water or a place to sleep. Still, she said, “I’m not going back.” Many seemed not to know exactly what they were doing there.



Young men, shirtless or in soccer jerseys, marched barefoot or sometimes in a single sandal, as if in an aimless parade. One teenager gently knocked on the grate of a closed food market while others hovered longingly around the city’s locked supermarkets. As morning turned to afternoon and the harsh sun burned away the clouds, men sought shade wherever they could. One group gathered under a hulking statue of Hercules near the port terminal. Others leaned against gas station pumps or reclined under the tents of abandoned stalls that had been raised for a local food fair. Still more looked in trash bins for food, or begged passersby for water. One woman fainted by a Zara store. Sulayman Ahmed, 15, a resident of Ceuta who is of Moroccan descent, said he couldn’t believe that Morocco was letting so many people through. Related Article Updated

Immigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe “They have to put more resources to stop people from coming,” he said, complaining that the appearances of politicians at the border, including that of Sánchez, amounted to “theatre.” As the day progressed, it became clear many of the migrants were leaving. By the boardwalk, they hovered around Spanish soldiers who had hooked a mobile phone to stereos that played messages in Arabic telling them to go home. Other Spanish soldiers and police officers threatened the migrants, waving their sticks to push them back to the border. In town, a roving band of young Spanish men chased down and intimidated Moroccan stragglers. Even as a sprinkling of late arrivals waded through the water, a mass return was underway.

World.title: ‘I wouldn’t be going to Essendon’: Matthews slams Bombers; Lyon again eyeballs reporters in presser
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: In another at-times heated press conference, St Kilda coach Ross Lyon was optimistic Jack Silvagni would face his old side Carlton next weekend.

Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend Leigh Matthews has taken a major swipe at his famous rivals, Essendon.

Alastair Clarkson had another frustrating day against his former club, Hawthorn. Matthews takes aim at Bombers’ administration in hunt for new coach Jon Pierik Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend Leigh Matthews has taken a major swipe at Essendon, declaring anyone who has a choice wouldn’t apply for the Bombers’ vacant coaching role, and he would have no confidence in heading there under the current administration. Matthews, a four-time premiership coach who also featured in three-straight grand finals against the Bombers as a player with arch-rival Hawthorn, declared he “wouldn’t be going to Essendon” if he was still a coach.



No confidence: AFL coaching great Leigh Matthews said he would have no confidence in heading to Essendon under the current administration. Bombers great Kevin Sheedy has backed James Hird to win the role. Justin McManus “From the outside I said, ‘Oh well, good luck’. If I was a coach, I wouldn’t be going to Essendon. If you desperately want a job, you just go for it, right? But, anyone who has choices ain’t going to Essendon,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘What boxes does James tick?’ The blunt assessment of Hird’s credentials The Bombers, led by president Andrew Welsh and chief executive Tim Roberts, have narrowed the search for their next senior coach to four candidates: club legend James Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis, a former long-time Brisbane Lions assistant. Essendon caretaker coach Dean Solomon, a friend and former teammate of Hird and McVeigh, will this week have his first formal discussions with club hierarchy about the full-time job. But Solomon has remained tight-lipped on whether he’ll seek the head coaching role.



“The other coaches, whether it be Jaymie Graham, now Murray Davis, Mark McVeigh, they have been in for jobs to a degree, they have just got to get a job if they can get it ... but I don’t have any idea who would be good or bad,” Matthews said. “A coach is only as good as what’s around him in players and staff, and support from the top. For me, from the outside, I don’t know the Essendon people that well, but I would have no confidence to coach under that regime.” The Bombers declined to comment. Essendon have been rebuffed by other potential candidates, including Geelong assistant James Kelly, Hawthorn assistant Daniel Giansiracusa and St Kilda assistant Corey Enright. Back then: James Hird and Dean Solomon speak with then Giants interim coach Mark McVeigh during the 2022 season. Hird and McVeigh are now seeking to coach the Bombers, while Solomon is yet to indicate his intentions. Getty Images



Matthews, who is a Brisbane Lions board member and won three-straight flags there as a coach, was befuddled by the Bombers using soccer coach Kevin Muscat to interview candidates over Zoom while he is coaching Chinese club Shanghai Port. Related Article AFL 2026 Geelong reach settlement with Stengle as Hill departs Collingwood “He is going to do a Zoom meeting from Japan with these individual candidates and get some kind of feedback from that. It’s not so much window dressing, I reckon it’s like trying to stab with a dartboard – it’s so hard,” Matthews said. Matthews said Carlton “looked like they knew what they were doing” in their hunt for a new coach, and Tasmania had as well before appointing Ken Hinkley as coach. But, when it came to Essendon, he questioned, “how qualified are they to make an informed decision?” Long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop is also part of the process alongside the panel.



Essendon’s football boss Daniel McPherson will leave the club at the end of the season. Getty Images Hird, with the support of fellow club great Kevin Sheedy, is seeking his third stint in charge. His first was from the end of 2010 until the end of 2013, when he was banned from coaching for his role in the supplements saga. He returned for the 2015 season, but quit after a 5-14 start. “To be honest, if Hird had been an assistant coach at another club for the last three or four years, you would think he would have already been appointed,” Matthews said. The Bombers are also on the hunt for a new football manager after the resignation of Daniel McPherson. McPherson, who came to the Bombers with former coach Brad Scott, will leave the club at season’s end. The appointment of a new football boss will be made alongside that of a new senior coach, as the Bombers review their football structure.



‘He is a Silvagni, he is tough’ Jon Pierik and Danny Russell St Kilda coach Ross Lyon is optimistic Jack Silvagni will line up against his former club Carlton next week in a finals-shaping, Sunday-night blockbuster despite dislocating his shoulder in a 19-point loss to Sydney on Saturday. Silvagni had to be helped from the field in pain in a 42-minute final term which also had play suspended after Swans defender Will Edwards suffered a badly broken ankle in a marking contest. He required a green whistle for pain relief and was taken from the field at Marvel Stadium on a motorised cart. Hoping for a quick return: Jack Silvagni leaves the ground with a dislocated shoulder on Saturday. AFL Photos



Swans forward Charlie Curnow booted three goals after Silvagni, his direct opponent and a former Blues teammate, left the field, highlighting the importance of the off-season recruit with the fabled family history at Princes Park. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects “He has a dislocated shoulder, [but] it went back in. He said he had a dislocated shoulder before, in round one, and he played the next week,” Lyon said. “He is a Silvagni, he is tough, we see his spirit, can’t believe we have got him in our club, but we are thrilled. But we will take no risk … we have got to get on to Carlton.” Silvagni had his shoulder in a sling post-match when chatting in the change rooms with father Steve and mother Jo.



After a short dinner break following the Saints’ defeat, Lyon returned to Marvel Stadium to watch the Blues host the Brisbane Lions on Saturday night. With three rounds remaining, the Saints (with nine wins) and Blues are jostling for 10th spot, and a wildcard berth, under the new top-10 finals system. In another entertaining press conference when he sparred with journalists, Lyon denied he had spoken sternly with Mattaes Phillipou in a break during play, insisting it had been a typical conversation. “I spoke to him calmly and rationally, but you [a journalist] have turned it into strong feedback. I was teaching him on a leading pattern when he went shallow, [and] could have gone to the top of the square like Hugo [Garcia], so I am OK, you can interpret it how you want,” he said. Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos



Lyon said ruckman Tom De Koning was dealing with a hip pointer issue, as was superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, who spent time off the ground with the ailment. The Swans booted the first two goals of the game, but then trailed by nine points at quarter-time, 13 points at half-time and 12 points at the final break, as the Saints dominated possession and Wanganeen-Milera booted three goals. But with the St Kilda gun clearly hampered in the final term, finishing the game out as a forward, Sydney’s midfielders went on a rampage and the Swans kicked seven last-quarter goals to the Saints’ two. Lyon lamented his team’s poor work at stoppages, declaring the Saints need more quality in the starting 23, and need to be better for longer. View post on X



The Saints have had a series of tough defeats this season, but Lyon said he wasn’t hiding from the raw facts. “The facts are there and are laid bare. Until you get it done, it’s two points up there against Sydney, it’s one point against Adelaide … the Dockers, I think we kicked the first goal of the last quarter, then it was ‘Wharfie Time’ [when the Dockers electrify the crowd with loud music],” Lyon said. “The feedback is, we need to get better – I am not shying away from it. But there is no doubt we have improved, that’s indisputable, but on our win-loss, I think our percentage tells us we know where are, but against [Sydney], we are just a bit short of that on our journey.” Play was stopped for 10 minutes while medical staff attended 23-year-old Edwards for what appeared to be a compound fracture. The promising Swan did not make his AFL debut until this year after a serious leg infection and then a broken leg threatened his career. Sydney also lost James Rowbottom with a broken hand in the first term. Swans coach Dean Cox described Edwards’ latest injury as “devastating”.



“To see a player battle like he has for so long to get a chance at AFL with some of the injuries he’s already had, to dislocate his ankle and be required to go to hospital and get surgery, is devastating for him and the football club and his family,” Cox said. “To forge out to be a really strong key defender for a young man is great. It’ll just be another hurdle that he has to jump, and we’ll support him all the way through it.” Watson’s career-high as Hawks down gritty Roos AAP Nick Watson kicked an equal career-best five goals to keep Hawthorn firmly in the hunt for a top-two spot with a 16-point win over a plucky North Melbourne.



The Hawks trailed by one point heading into the final quarter in Launceston on Saturday against an opposition needing a victory to boost their AFL finals hopes. Nick Watson was at his brilliant best yet again for the Hawks. Getty Images But they did enough to hold on for the 14.15 (99) to 12.11 (83) result, with Mabior Chol getting a crucial breathing-space goal at the back end of the game. With his side ahead by 11 and less than six minutes on the clock, Chol earned a free kick with a tackle and then nailed a goal from about 50m out near the boundary line. North cut the margin to 10 points with less than three minutes left thanks to Harry Sheezel but were left to rue several key misses in the fourth quarter.



Watson’s haul gives him 52 goals for the season, putting him right in the hunt for the Coleman Medal. “Every week he gets a fair bit of attention and for a player so young he works his way through it really well,” Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said. “It’s very difficult to be consistent. He was really important.” Alastair Clarkson and his Roos had a frustrating day against his former club, Hawthorn. AFL Photos Jai Newcombe was also heavily involved for the Hawks and picked up a game-high 34 disposals, plus 12 clearances and one goal assist.



Hawthorn, who are in third spot and just two points behind Sydney, have won four in a row ahead of a blockbuster against reigning premiers the Brisbane Lions on Friday. The Kangaroos have slumped to five losses on the trot and sit 13th on the ladder. “Finn O’Sullivan at the 20-minute mark of the last quarter, snaps, should be a goal,” North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson said. “Jack Darling takes a mark 30 metres out [in the] last quarter, [that] should be a goal. “We’re competing, and we’re getting closer to some of those sides, but it also tells us that we’ve got a way to go.



“At AFL level those shots and opportunities should be executed.” Hawthorn nabbed the opening goal of the game through Will Day before the Kangaroos got four straight for a 26-9 lead at the first break. North Melbourne’s Nick Larkey, who has struggled for accuracy in recent times, produced a shocking first shot but nailed his second from off-centre. Teammate Zac Banch squeezed one through from the goal square in the last minute of the first quarter to give his side a boost. Hawthorn came to life early in the second with Watson, who only picked up one touch in the first term, getting three goals in a row including two in 60 seconds.



The lead then changed hands multiple times before a behind after the halftime buzzer to Chol levelled the scores at 46-46. Watson fired again with two goals early in the third before a major to Chol broke the run of tit-for-tat scores as Hawthorn threatened to pull away. But the Kangaroos rallied and Larkey’s second gave his side a 69-68 lead heading into the final quarter. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’: Urgent care clinics failing to relieve pressure on hospitals, say doctors
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaHealthcare ‘Robbing Peter to pay Paul’: Urgent care clinics failing to relieve pressure on hospitals, say doctors Melissa Cunningham and Henrietta Cook August 1, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of multimillion-dollar urgent care clinics set up around Victoria and touted by politicians as a silver bullet for the state’s healthcare crisis are doing “absolutely nothing” to ease pressure on overstretched hospitals, while threatening the viability of GP practices, doctors warn. There are 38 urgent care clinics in the state, many of which were opened in 2023 by the federal government in a bid to take pressure off Victoria’s overrun hospital system by providing bulk-billed services for urgent, but not life-threatening, injuries and illnesses. Melbourne emergency physician Dr Sarah Whitelaw said urgent care clinics were having a “minuscule” effect on Victoria’s overrun emergency departments, which are being flooded. Louis Trerise The federal government has argued the clinics are reducing the number of people turning up at emergency departments with non-life-threatening but urgent conditions by about 10 per cent, but this figure is strongly disputed by doctors on the front line. Melbourne emergency physician Dr Sarah Whitelaw said the clinics were having a “minuscule” effect on Victoria’s overwhelmed emergency departments, which are being flooded by a wave of sicker, more complex patients requiring urgent care and hospital admission.



“The clinics do nothing to solve our problems,” said Whitelaw, who is the emergency medicine representative on the Australian Medical Association’s federal council. Related Article Exclusive

Hospitals Booted from hospital and dumped on the street: Patients on secret blacklist being refused treatment “It is so frustrating every time we hear the phrase ‘reducing emergency department pressures’ because they haven’t decreased our waiting times in any way.” The federal government’s own reporting on the system has found the introduction of urgent care clinics has not reduced emergency department waiting times. In many metropolitan hospitals only 1 to 2 per cent of emergency department arrivals were being diverted to urgent care clinics, Whitelaw said.



This figure has come from emergency departments nationally, where staff have begun recording the number of patients opting to use urgent care clinics instead. Official data shows emergency department arrivals have risen by about 4.4 per cent since the urgent care centres opened. In 2024-25 there were 1,978,267 arrivals in Victoria, about 84,000 higher than in 2022-23, when there were 1,894,732 visits to the state’s emergency departments. Emergency physician Dr Simon Judkins, who works in rural and metropolitan emergency departments, said hospitals in regional areas including Bendigo and Ballarat were “really, really struggling”.



“It’s not because of patients who need lacerations fixed up; they’re full of patients who’ve got complex care issues, who need hospital admission, and the hospitals are completely full,” said Judkins, also the Victorian president of the Australian Medical Association. He said emergency departments were being left with wards full of patients who needed to be immediately admitted to hospital, but there were often no beds available. The federal government oversees 29 of the clinics, while the state government manages the rest. In this year’s state budget, the Victorian government allocated $20.9 million for the clinics, describing the funding as a way to “help reduce the demand on busy hospital emergency departments”. The federal government announced a $1.8 billion national boost to the clinics in May this year and previously committed more than $88 million in direct grants for Victoria’s clinics.



Emergency doctors argue that funding would have been better spent on GPs, who manage chronic and complex illnesses to keep patients out of hospital, as well boosting staff numbers and increasing the number of hospital beds. Related Article Opinion

Medicare I ended up in a Medicare urgent care clinic … and I liked it Millie Muroi Economics Writer “Imagine what we could have done with those billions of dollars, investing it into GP clinics and providing them the capacity to do after-hours care,” Judkins said. “That would have been a much better choice.” An evaluation of urgent care centres around Australia is underway, the federal government confirmed. An interim report found the clinics were costing taxpayers up to five times more per patient than a standard GP consultation. Each presentation cost taxpayers more than $250 compared with a standard GP consultation, which cost roughly $47.



However, the federal government said the net saving from avoiding an emergency department presentation was estimated to be $381 per patient. In April, Carmel Misale called an ambulance after a sudden, intense pressure in her head caused her to briefly pass out. Instead of taking her to an emergency department, paramedics redirected her to an urgent care clinic in Northcote, warning of massive hospital waiting times. Carmel Misale was taken by ambulance to an urgent care clinic in Northcote but was shocked to be told no doctors were available. Wayne Taylor But when she arrived at the clinic she was shocked to discover it was in effect closed. It was 2pm on a weekday afternoon, and Misale said the clinic’s only nurse told paramedics there were no doctors available.



“I was flabbergasted,” the mother of two from Reservoir in Melbourne’s north recalled. “I said, ‘What do you mean you aren’t open?’” Misale’s husband then drove her to the Epworth’s emergency department, where she underwent urgent testing, including a CT scan and an MRI of her brain. After 10 hours, she was diagnosed with vestibular migraines. She’s concerned urgent care clinics are passing too many patients on to emergency departments. Others who have used the medical clinics for urgent care are fierce advocates of the service, including people unable to afford the increasing cost of visiting a GP, or parents of children who find themselves caring for a sick or injured child out of hours.



However, Associate Professor Julian Rait, the Australian Medical Association’s federal vice president, warned that urgent care clinics were sucking doctors out of rural areas and hospitals, offering much higher pay and more sociable hours. “It has a very distorting effect on the workforce basically; it’s robbing Peter to pay Paul,” Rait said. Dr Robin O’Neill said enormous amounts of federal funding meant urgent care clinics were able to offer doctors between $250 and $400 an hour. Ruby Alexander It is something Robin O’Neill, a GP in Camperdown in the state’s south-west, has experienced firsthand. He said enormous amounts of federal funding meant urgent care clinics were able to offer doctors between $250 and $400 an hour. O’Neill said regular general practices were unable to offer this sort of pay under current Medicare rebates, which made it difficult for them to attract doctors, particularly in regional and rural areas.



“The government has now created a two-tier system where federally funded urgent care centres can afford to bulk bill and offer higher rates of pay to doctors,” he said. “This in turn is causing pressure and workforce shortages in regular general practice clinics, which is most acute in rural and regional locations.” Dr Aadhil Aziz, Victorian deputy co-chair of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, warned that underfunded GP practices were closing daily, noting his own Melbourne clinic recently shut down due to financial pressure. He said increasing Medicare rebates was crucial. “General practice is severely underfunded,” he said. “But if you fund it better we will be able to deliver a better-class healthcare system for everyone, which will reduce the number of people needed going to EDs.”



Federal Health Minister Mark Butler said doctors had embraced the urgent care clinics and the government had been told they were having a positive impact on hospital emergency departments. Related Article Healthcare More free urgent care clinics part of $8.5 billion health commitment “When you need urgent but not life-threatening care, instead of waiting for hours at the local emergency department you can go to your local clinic,” Butler said. Official figures showed there have been more than 722,800 visits to urgent care clinics in Victoria since they were opened in 2023, including more than 9000 visits for the week of July 21. Victorian opposition health spokeswoman Georgie Crozier said the clinics were not operating as promised and had failed to ease pressure on emergency departments.



“Our health system is struggling to meet growing demand,” she said. “Labor should scrap the GP tax and provide greater support to our primary healthcare providers to keep people out of our busy emergency departments.” A Victorian government spokeswoman said the urgent care units were needed to fill a hole in the nation’s healthcare system. “The former federal Coalition government spent a decade gutting Australia’s primary care system, leaving too many Victorians unable to secure an appointment or afford to see a GP,” she said. World.title: NPC: Mo'unga scores match-winning try for Canterbury against Auckland
World.content:
Richie Mo'unga has scored the winning try for Canterbury in his first NPC match since 2020, with the defending champions beating Auckland 38-31.

Mo'unga, who has spent the last three years playing in Japan, came on as a replacement in the second half on Saturday night, and while he had a few awkward moments, he turned on the class to split the Auckland defence in the 78th minute, when the scores were deadlocked.

The first half was helter-skelter, with Canterbury starting off where they left off last season, with early dominance at the breakdown seeing them score two tries in the first 11 minutes.

But Auckland stormed back when the red-and-blacks made a couple of errors, leaving a hole in their lineout for Sam Hainsworth-Fa'aofo to score and then gifting an intercept to Xavier Tito-Harris.

Canterbury then scored two more tries, but Auckland claimed one back to trail 26-21 at halftime.

There was a big cheer when Mo'unga took the field but he looked a bit rusty early, knocking forward a ball that bounced just in front of him and then missing a conversion he normally would have nailed.

Auckland had taken the lead for the first time in the 60th minute, but Canterbury hit back seven minutes later.

It was 31-all with 12 minutes to go and stayed that way, until Canterbury's forwards charged towards the Auckland line from a lineout after winning a penalty and Mo'unga got his hands on the ball playing halfback, fooling the defence with a dummy and scoring by the posts. He then converted it.

In earlier games today, Otago beat Southland 41-14, and Taranaki beat Counties Manukau 20 points to five.

On Friday night, Tasman pipped North Harbour 31-29 in Nelson, while Waikato opened the season with a 38-26 win over Bay of Plenty on Thursday.

World.title: Country Life: Hydroponics in Horowhenua
World.content:
There's no need for extra washing when it comes to these salad greens. The plants from Waikawa fresh are harvested straight from their trays where they're grown hydroponically.

"There's no bugs, there's no soil, there's no dirt. We don't clean these plants with any chemicals or chlorine, so we eat those lettuce straight out of the channels. They're just absolutely crispy clean ... and they haven't been touched by anyone the whole time it's been growing," Tony Dale-Low told Country Life.

He and wife Lisa Dale-Low made the move to growing salad greens and herbs almost a decade ago, trading in city life and corporate jobs for horticulture in Horowhenua.

Hydroponics in Horowhenua: Growing with water Country Life Download MP3 17m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The couple had no growing experience before starting.

They'd spent a couple of years travelling around the country in a bus with their three children before coming up with a checklist of what they wanted for their next chapter.

"We wanted to be doing something productive, rather than something paper or computer-based. We wanted to be rural and we wanted to have a bit more flexibility with the kids. None of that was really sector specific or even location-specific," Lisa said.

The couple grow fancy lettuces and other herby greens hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Hydroponic growing systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The water sourced from the 4500m2 of rooves of the many greenhouses, and the recent addition of solar power is also helping cut down on energy bills. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

After narrowing it down to the North Island they came across an existing hydroponic growing business near Levin - hydroponic systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution.

That was in 2018 and after learning the ropes from the previous owners they've made it their own.

They grow the plants from seedlings themselves, also using hydroponics on a 'flood and drain table'.

"So this is set up on a timer. It runs three times a day and these tables will fill with nutrients or liquid with some fertilizer," Tony explained.

Seedlings, like these little basil sprouts, are also grown hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The seedlings are easily plugged into the next growing space. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It sits there for a few minutes before draining. Being fully automated means the team don't need to do any manual watering.

He said it helps the plants up well - making them more resistant to diseases and pests.

"[It] all definitely starts here in the propagating house. If we get it wrong here, then we have issues later. If we get it right, then we have so much more success."

Once the seedlings reach about three weeks, they're transferred to larger growing trays called 'gullies'.

"They look like downpipes, which in fact I think they are, actually straight off someone's house," Tony told Country Life.

"They've been drilled with a lot of little round holes and we plant the plant inside the holes. The nutrients get pumped around the greenhouse through these small whiskers."

Among some of the 'fancy' lettuces they grow, the oak leaf in red and green varieties. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The couple learned the art of hydroponics from the previous owners. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Over the cooler winter months, it gets too cold to grow basil so they replace this with growing watercress instead. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The system they use only requires liquid to be pumped to the top of the gully before gravity does the rest, drawing it down the channel, through the gutter back to the holding tank which is topped up with the water sourced from the 4500m2 of greenhouse rooves.

The water is reticulated meaning they only need to add more to account for evaporation or absorption by the plants.

In the central tank, a computer system checks to make sure the water has the right balance of nutrients and the right pH level - the acid or alkaline concentration - and runs a dosing system to adjust this when needed.

Tony and his green 'lettuce' Leaf - the old Nissan Leaf gets its power from solar panels on the farm and is used to run around the property for the many maintenance jobs. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Sustainability is a key part of Waikawa Fresh' operations.

The recent addition of solar power at the end of last year is also helping cut down on energy bills - it's even used to power an old Nissan 'lettuce' leaf they use on farm to run the maintenance gear around.

About two months after the plants have finished growing they'll be ready to be picked straight from the gullies with no extra washing required - "lovely and crunchy and and fresh".

From their hands where they're packed straight into bags, the harvested plants are taken straight to the chiller ready to be picked up by a truck that same day. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Getting the product to the market as fresh as possible is a key focus. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke
